Synthesis of Results Our methodology adhered to established guidelines (Cochrane Handbook for Systematic Reviews of Interventions [ ] and the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic reviews and Meta-Analyses [PRISMA] 2020 statement [ ]). Bias risk assessment is described in the . We evaluated the performance characteristics of DTs, including pathogen yield or detection rates, accuracy metrics (sensitivity, specificity, positive predictive values [PPV]/negative predictive values [NPV]), and turnaround time. We also assessed whether studies reported the following measures: clinical course (including antimicrobial management), clinical outcomes (including morbidity, graft loss, and mortality), healthcare resource utilization (HCRU), and cost. Finally, we examined whether studies evaluated the impact of infection DT on these metrics. RESULTS Study Selection The database searches identified 2362 unique records. After classification using the original Population, Intervention, Comparators, Outcomes, Timing, and Study design ( ), applying additional exclusion criteria ( ), and conducting a full-text review, 70 records were deemed eligible ( , PRISMA flow diagram). We identified 2 additional studies through supplementary searches ( ). Thus, 72 unique studies were included. Study Characteristics Study characteristics are shown in ( ). Median patient sample size was 102 (range, 11–1307; Q1/Q3, 57.5/200; ). Studies were stratified by SOT type as follows: lung (pediatric [ , ], n = 2; adult [ , ], n = 12), liver (pediatric [ ], n = 4; adult [ ], n = 22), kidney (pediatric [ ], n = 1; adult [ ], n = 19), heart (pediatric, n = 0; adult [ ], n = 1), pancreas (pediatric, n = 0; adult [ ], n = 1), and >1 organ (pediatric [ ], n = 1; adult [ ], n = 9; ). Studies originated from diverse regions (North America, n = 16; Europe, n = 23; and Asia, n = 22; ). Most studies (n = 45, 62.5%) evaluated standard cultures ( ); 11 (15.3%) evaluated blood biomarkers ( Aspergillus GM, BDG, or C-reactive protein [CRP], n = 5; serology, n = 6). Overall, 21 studies (29.2%) examined MDT: PCR (n = 17, 23.6%), bacterial BRPCR (n = 1), and metagenomics (n = 3, 4.2%). The 3 metagenomic studies utilized the Illumina platform and internal, center-specific pipelines for pathogen identification; no other commercial platforms were reported [ , , ]. Biospecimens tested varied widely and included blood, BALF, nasopharyngeal swabs, intra-abdominal samples, surgical site samples, and stool. BALF testing was performed in all lung transplant studies. Although all studies (n = 72, 100%) reported percent pathogen detected, only 6 (8%) provided sensitivity, specificity, PPV, or NPV. Furthermore, while clinical course (n = 59, 82%), clinical outcomes (n = 44, 61%), and HCRU and cost (n = 19, 26%) were frequently reported ( ), only 6 studies (8%) directly assessed the impact of infection DT on clinical course (antimicrobials) or HCRU [ , , , ]. Test Performance Percent Pathogen Detected Among the 45 studies using standard cultures, 39 reported culture yield, which was positive in a median of 27.7% (range, 0%–88.3%; Q1/Q3, 17.0%/49.6%) ( ). Eleven studies evaluated blood cultures (median positive yield, 21.7%; range, 2.2%–55%) [ , , , , , , , , , , ], and 5 evaluated BALF cultures (median positive yield, 36%; 5.3%–67%) [ , , , , ]. Only 5 studies assessed pathogen yield for nonculture diagnostics (fungal biomarkers, n = 1; multiplex PCR, n = 3; metagenomic sequencing, n = 1), and primarily used culture as a comparator. In a study of lung transplant recipients, obtaining both standard culture and GM increased the diagnosis of invasive aspergillosis to 36%, compared with 23.3% and 16.1% for each test alone, respectively [ ]. In a study of kidney transplant recipients with diarrhea, stool multiplex PCR outperformed microscopy and culture combined (yield 85% vs 32.3%, respectively) in detecting Norovirus, Giardia lamblia , Cryptosporidium , and enteropathogenic Escherichia coli , and others [ ]. A multiplex PCR for bloodstream infections in heart or lung transplant recipients demonstrated 90.8% concordance with blood culture, with combined testing detecting pathogens in more specimens than blood culture alone (13.1% vs 6.1% of specimens tested, respectively) [ ]. However, another multiplex PCR for suspected airway infections in lung transplant recipients failed to detect infections caused by pathogens not included in the platform, such as Haemophilus parainfluenzae and molds [ ]. Of the 3 metagenomic testing studies, only one reported diagnostic yield: metagenomic sequencing of BALF from lung transplant recipients detected pathogens in 83.4% of cases versus 55.8% using CDM, which included culture (bacterial, mycobacterial, fungal), staining (fungal smear and Grocott's methenamine staining [GMS]), PCR, serologies, and GM/BDG [ ]. This approach led to antimicrobial changes in 21% (23/107) of cases, including infections with Pneumocystis jirovecii

respectively) [ ]. However, another multiplex PCR for suspected airway infections in lung transplant recipients failed to detect infections caused by pathogens not included in the platform, such as Haemophilus parainfluenzae and molds [ ]. Of the 3 metagenomic testing studies, only one reported diagnostic yield: metagenomic sequencing of BALF from lung transplant recipients detected pathogens in 83.4% of cases versus 55.8% using CDM, which included culture (bacterial, mycobacterial, fungal), staining (fungal smear and Grocott's methenamine staining [GMS]), PCR, serologies, and GM/BDG [ ]. This approach led to antimicrobial changes in 21% (23/107) of cases, including infections with Pneumocystis jirovecii (not detected by GMS staining and not targeted by the PCR platform), Mycobacteria spp. (nontuberculous mycobacteria and Mycobacterium tuberculosis ), Legionella spp., Strongyloidiasis stercoralis , and Aspergillus spp [ ]. PCR later verified the 7 metagenomic tests that were positive for P jirovecii ; GeneXpert MTB/RIF confirmed the 2 metagenomic tests showing M tuberculosis . However, cases with positive metagenomic sequencing results required adjudication by 2 expert clinicians to distinguish colonization from infection and to determine which pathogens were clinically relevant when results of metagenomic sequencing and CDM were discordant. Another study suggested that plasma metagenomic sequencing may complement culture for early detection of invasive fungal infection (IFI) following liver transplant, although diagnostic yield was not reported [ ]. Test Accuracy Sensitivity, specificity, PPV, and NPV were reported in 6 studies ( ) [ , , , ], evaluating biomarkers (BDG or CRP, n = 2) or PCR (n = 4). In a study primarily involving lung transplant recipients, BDG demonstrated low to moderate PPV for early IFI diagnosis (BALF, 26.2%; serum, 69.2%) [ ]. Another study assessed CRP thresholds to predict bacterial infections following pediatric kidney transplant [ ]. Four studies compared multiplex PCR assays with standard diagnostics in lung or kidney transplant recipients ( ) [ , ]. One study examined 7 commercial multiplex PCR assays in kidney transplant recipients with severe diarrhea [ ]. Viral detection correlated well with reference methods, but detection of bacteria was potentially limited by poor specificity. For instance, molecular methods resulted in a 50% increase in detecting enteropathogenic E coli compared with stool culture, but the validity of these results could not be confirmed using reference methods [ ]. Three studies assessed expanded multiplex PCR of BAL samples to diagnose lower respiratory infections in lung transplant recipients. Two were conducted in patients with suspected infection [ , ], whereas 1 described patients undergoing routine surveillance [ ]. Sensitivity varied depending on assay and pathogen, but PPV was generally high ( ). Turnaround Time Five studies reported TAT, which was statistically significantly shorter for molecular compared with nonmolecular tests but also varied by test type. In lung transplant recipients, median TAT for multiplex bacterial PCR was 21.2 hours, compared with 23 hours for bacterial culture [ ]. Similarly, multiplex PCR and directed RNA-viral PCR had TATs of 3.8 and 13 hours, respectively, versus 48 hours for bacterial culture [ ]. Another study reported a median TAT of 2.3 hours for multiplex PCR versus 21.4–47.6 hours for usual care diagnostics, which included immunofluorescence and standard PCR [ ]. In thoracic transplant recipients with suspected bloodstream infections, PCR results were available 1.5 days earlier than blood cultures [ ]. Metagenomic sequencing also had a significantly shorter TAT than CDM in lung transplant recipients with various infections (2.7 vs 5.5 days, respectively) [ ]. No studies reported TAT for other DTs. Clinical Course Clinical course (primarily antimicrobial use) was reported in 59 studies, although only 4 specifically evaluated the impact of infection DT on antimicrobial-related decisions. In 1 study of 50 pediatric liver transplant recipients undergoing 157 percutaneous cholangiography procedures, prophylactic antimicrobials were administered universally and continued in 73.2% (115/157) of procedures due to cholangitis, sepsis, or colonization with drug-resistant pathogens [ ]. However, in 12% (14/115) of these cases, antimicrobials were optimized based on positive blood or biliary cultures [ ]. In 3 studies of lung transplant recipients, antimicrobial modification or discontinuation followed multiplex PCR [ ], GM [ ], and/or culture [ , ] of respiratory samples. Clinical Outcome, HCRU, and Cost Mortality was reported in all 44 studies that described clinical outcomes. However, none evaluated the direct impact of infection DT results on mortality, and reporting methods varied (eg, different follow-up durations posttransplant). Median all-cause mortality (ie, including but not limited to infections) posttransplant was 15.2% (range, 0%–80%; Q1/Q3, 6.8%/27.2%). Eighteen studies reported all-cause mortality rates >20% [ , , , , , , , , , , , , , , , , , ]. Graft loss was reported in 4 studies, [ , , , ] but none explored potential relationships between graft loss, DT results, and antimicrobials. Eighteen studies reported HCRU outcomes ( ), including hospital length of stay (LOS;

none evaluated the direct impact of infection DT results on mortality, and reporting methods varied (eg, different follow-up durations posttransplant). Median all-cause mortality (ie, including but not limited to infections) posttransplant was 15.2% (range, 0%–80%; Q1/Q3, 6.8%/27.2%). Eighteen studies reported all-cause mortality rates >20% [ , , , , , , , , , , , , , , , , , ]. Graft loss was reported in 4 studies, [ , , , ] but none explored potential relationships between graft loss, DT results, and antimicrobials. Eighteen studies reported HCRU outcomes ( ), including hospital length of stay (LOS; n = 16) [ , , , , , , , , , , , ], intensive care unit admission (n = 2), [ , ] and intensive care unit LOS (n = 9) [ , , , , , , , , ]. However, none directly assessed the influence of positive DT results on HCRU because positive results served as a proxy for infection. No studies reported cost. DISCUSSION This SLR of 72 studies evaluating infection DT in SOTR identified several key findings. First, significant heterogeneity existed across studies, which varied in design, SOTR populations, infections, DT methods, and specimens tested. Second, while most studies evaluated cultures, and some included PCR assays, novel MDT like BRPCR and metagenomics were rarely examined. Third, despite faster TATs, PCR tests were limited by their fixed array of detectable organisms. Although BRPCR and metagenomics could overcome this limitation, data on these MDT were scarce. Fourth, only 6 studies reported sensitivity, specificity, PPV, and NPV. Finally, few studies reported the impact of infection DT on clinically relevant outcomes like antimicrobial use, mortality, LOS, HCRU, and cost. These findings highlight significant knowledge gaps in infection DT for SOTR, underscoring the need for prospective studies to evaluate the performance and clinical impact of advanced MDT compared with conventional DT methods in SOTR. Diagnosing infections in SOTR typically involves a stepwise approach [ ], starting with basic microbiological assessment and consideration of empiric antimicrobials, followed by more extensive testing and changes in antimicrobial therapy if the patient deteriorates or opportunistic infection is suspected. The diagnostic journey often includes a combination of modalities such as imaging, cultures, antigen tests, serology, and PCR, with advanced pathogen-agnostic diagnostics like BRPCR and metagenomics reserved as last resort measures. A paradigm shift toward earlier use of pathogen-agnostic diagnostics in SOTR is appealing because such approaches could potentially help overcome cognitive biases and facilitate timely treatment of fastidious organisms. However, our data indicate that advanced pathogen-agnostic diagnostics require additional validation. Indeed, despite growing interest, research on these novel DT modalities in SOTR remains limited [ , ]. This paradox—frequent clinical use despite limited supporting evidence—was highlighted by the American Society of Transplantation [ ]. Furthermore, we identified no cost-effectiveness analyses to determine whether the increased cost of pathogen-agnostic MDTs can be offset by other cost savings, for instance from a reduction in the total number of tests ordered; we also identified no studies evaluating the cost of combining multifaceted diagnostic approaches (eg, culture, antigens, histology, PCR, either sequentially or simultaneously). While BDG and GM assays were designed to rapidly diagnose IFI, few studies have examined their performance in SOTR. BDG has poor specificity, cannot identify specific fungi, and can yield false positives [ , , ]. Although serum GM is accurate in neutropenic cancer patients (70–82% sensitivity, 86–92% specificity), it is less sensitive in SOTR (22% sensitivity, 84% specificity) [ ]. Thus, a negative serum GM result cannot exclude invasive aspergillosis in SOTR with lung nodules [ ]. Conversely, BAL GM has >80–90% sensitivity and specificity in both neutropenia and SOTR [ ]. No studies evaluated antigen-based biomarkers for endemic mycoses or Cryptococcus in SOTR. Fungal antigen tests also exhibit cross-reactivity, and no commercial antigen tests exist for resistant mycoses like Mucorales and Scedosporium [ ]. While PCR assays for these molds exist [ , ], we identified no studies focused solely on SOTR. One study with ∼25% SOTR found that serum Mucorales PCR identified mucormycosis earlier than CDM (primarily histopathology), leading to earlier treatment with amphotericin B and improved survival [ ]. However, pathogen-directed PCR requires clinicians to suspect the specific pathogen. Whether pathogen-agnostic MDT will outperform conventional methods and PCR for diagnosing IFI remains unknown, highlighting the need for further study and for proper diagnostic stewardship. Ju et al evaluated the utility of pathogen-agnostic MDT for diagnosing P jirovecii pneumonia (PJP) in lung transplant recipients [ ] and highlight important considerations for rational use of metagenomics-based DT. GMS staining, a conventional and commonly used test for PJP despite its poor sensitivity in persons without HIV [ ], missed all 7 PJP cases, and the PCR assay used was not designed to detect P jirovecii . The diagnosis of PJP was made

Whether pathogen-agnostic MDT will outperform conventional methods and PCR for diagnosing IFI remains unknown, highlighting the need for further study and for proper diagnostic stewardship. Ju et al evaluated the utility of pathogen-agnostic MDT for diagnosing P jirovecii pneumonia (PJP) in lung transplant recipients [ ] and highlight important considerations for rational use of metagenomics-based DT. GMS staining, a conventional and commonly used test for PJP despite its poor sensitivity in persons without HIV [ ], missed all 7 PJP cases, and the PCR assay used was not designed to detect P jirovecii . The diagnosis of PJP was made through metagenomic sequencing and subsequently verified by a P jirovecii –specific PCR. Importantly, clinical adjudication confirmed that all 7 of these cases were consistent with PJP, underscoring the critical role of clinical judgment, which should never be replaced by DT results. This is particularly true for pathogens such as P jirovecii , where DNA detection may indicate colonization not disease [ ]. Rational interpretation of metagenomic tests requires nuanced clinical expertise to avoid reflexive interpretation of results. However, such expertise may not be readily available. Whether genome copies or cycle threshold values can further refine medical decision-making in patients with positive metagenomic testing results remains to be determined [ ]. Although PCR can accurately diagnose CMV and EBV infection after SOT [ , ], diagnosing other DNA viruses remains challenging. We identified no studies focused on this issue. For example, diagnosing HHV-8 after SOT is difficult because of low clinical suspicion and limited commercial assays with variable turnaround times, despite the increasing incidence of donor-derived HHV-8 [ , ]. A recent study using plasma microbial cell-free DNA (mcfDNA) sequencing to monitor for infections after lung transplant identified one case where HHV-8 was detected in posttransplant plasma samples. This individual, whose pretransplant sample was negative for HHV-8, subsequently developed disseminated Kaposi sarcoma with allograft involvement, which was diagnosed on autopsy and strongly suggested DDI [ ]. Such data remain anecdotal, and whether pathogen-agnostic testing will have a role in DDI surveillance remains unknown but should be studied. Diagnosing rare CNS viruses like HHV-6 and JC after SOT is also challenging [ ] and relies on a high index of suspicion. We identified no studies evaluating novel DT for these viruses in SOT. Metagenomic sequencing holds promise for diagnosing infections in immunocompromised patients but requires further validation. Bergin et al [ ] showed that in patients with hematologic malignancies and suspected infectious pneumonia, combining mcfDNA sequencing with usual care testing improved the infectious diagnostic yield to 42% (from 30% and 28%, respectively). Plasma mcfDNA sequencing alone provided an additive diagnostic value of 12%, detecting P jirovecii , rare molds, Nocardi, and others. mcfDNA sequencing also detected organisms often dismissed as commensals but which can cause disease in hematological cancer. Importantly, an expert committee adjudicated the significance of all microbes detected. However, this study also revealed limitations of plasma mcfDNA sequencing. The proportion of plasma mcfDNA tests yielding the same pathogen as usual care was highest for DNA viruses and bacteria but lowest for Aspergillus . Most cases of pulmonary aspergillosis were diagnosed exclusively because of compatible imaging and a positive serum GM result, but plasma mcfDNA results were negative in nearly all these cases. Potential causes of false-negative metagenomics testing results include low pathogen DNA concentrations or thick fungal cell walls [ ]. Another study in hematopoietic cell transplant recipients showed that mcfDNA sequencing had variable sensitivity for detecting different mold species, with improved performance for non- Aspergillus molds and in early samples [ ]. Importantly, in the study by Bergin et al [ ] ∼58% of participants lacked a microbiologically confirmed cause of their pulmonary process. Whether these cases are “false negatives” or “true negatives” is currently difficult to determine definitively but is an important research question. Because individuals with a confirmed diagnosis (infectious or otherwise) were excluded, the study may have included many participants with (1) difficult-to-diagnose infections (in whom the negative DT results are false negatives) or (2) a noninfectious etiology of their pulmonary process (in whom the negative DT results are true negatives); this premise should be explored in future studies. Finally, current tests may miss some pathogens, particularly RNA viruses, which may not be included in certain testing platforms [ ]. Ultimately, further refinement of diagnostic technologies is needed. Clinicians using pathogen-agnostic MDT must interpret results (both positive and negative) cautiously and in the context of the patient's clinical presentation. Transplant centers adopting such technologies should develop algorithms for rational use and employ diagnostic stewardship with infectious disease expertise. Study Limitations This SLR, although conducted using established guidelines, has limitations. Search criteria may have been too restrictive or did not match selected MeSH terms, despite a supplemental manual search. The included studies (N = 72) were of

particularly RNA viruses, which may not be included in certain testing platforms [ ]. Ultimately, further refinement of diagnostic technologies is needed. Clinicians using pathogen-agnostic MDT must interpret results (both positive and negative) cautiously and in the context of the patient's clinical presentation. Transplant centers adopting such technologies should develop algorithms for rational use and employ diagnostic stewardship with infectious disease expertise. Study Limitations This SLR, although conducted using established guidelines, has limitations. Search criteria may have been too restrictive or did not match selected MeSH terms, despite a supplemental manual search. The included studies (N = 72) were of varied quality, including retrospective and noncomparative designs. While our exclusion criteria encompassed studies evaluating only a single pathogen or exclusively RNA viruses, all such studies (N = 13 and N = 3, respectively) were also excluded for other reasons, including not addressing the research question ( and ). Notably, studies evaluating RNA viruses alongside other pathogens were still included [ , , , , , , ]. Variability in diagnostic approaches reflects the diverse clinical practices and DT access across different regions and institutions. Heterogeneity in the “gold” standard complicates interpreting test performance across studies. This review focused on hospitalized patients and did not evaluate diagnostics for unrecognized donor-derived infection. Thus, findings cannot be generalized to all SOTR or diagnostic approaches. CONCLUSION This SLR reveals a critical gap: although noninvasive monitoring for allograft rejection has progressed [ ], the development of advanced molecular diagnostics for infection in SOTR lags behind. However, transplant clinicians frequently use novel infectious DT [ ], despite limited supporting evidence. Thus, future prospective studies must prioritize evaluating the performance and clinical impact of novel tests like metagenomic sequencing and broad-range PCR following transplantation. Study endpoints should include diagnostic accuracy, antimicrobial use, mortality, healthcare resource utilization, and cost. Novel molecular diagnostic tests should be studied in the context of donor-derived infections. Finally, clinicians and medical centers should recognize the critical role of diagnostic stewardship and clinical expertise in interpreting the results of novel molecular diagnostics. chunks.content: 1 Introduction Sleep is a common and crucial requirement for all living beings. It is defined as the alteration in consciousness, restriction in sensory movements, and reduced muscle movements [ ]. It is also found in all living beings, such as reptiles, mammals, Pisces, animals and humans. Some animals sleep with one eye open, and some sleep with both eyes closed. Sleep is categorized into four categories, including REM, NREM, wake and sleep. Lack of sleep influences the person's health, leading to various mental disorders like mood swings, memory loss, lack of concentration, heart disorders, enhanced risk of stroke and brain hemorrhages, obesity, and diabetes. Lack of sleep disastrously affects a person's ability to function, their health and the mental and emotional balance of the body. Good quality of sleep is a symbol of good health. It is generally said that reduced sleep can lead to decreased efficiency, reduced ability to handle stress and mood swings. Continuously ignoring sleep can damage a person's health as much as caused by accidents, frustration, and lack of performance and according to AASM (American Academy of sleep medicine), USA and their physicians reported that 50–70 million people are affected by sleep disorders ( https://www.cdc.gov/sleep/data_statistics.html ). According to an Indian report, about 93 per cent of people are affected by sleep disorders [ ]. About 70–75 per cent of people in the UK and European countries are affected by sleep disorders. Sleep disorders are mainly categorized as sleep disorders, sleep apnea, and unusual sleep patterns [ ]. chunks.content: 1. Introduction Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) is a chronic inflammatory lung disease characterized by airflow limitation. Its pathophysiological mechanisms are complex, involving multiple factors such as genetics, environment, and lifestyle. [ ] Recent studies have shown that gut microbiota plays an important role in the development and progression of various chronic diseases, including respiratory diseases such as asthma, cystic fibrosis, and lung cancer. [ ] Gut microbiota is a microbial community that resides in the human intestine for an extended period. They play crucial roles in immune regulation. [ , ] Research indicates that the interaction between gut microbiota and the host immune system may influence the development of COPD. For example, supplementing the COPD mice with specific probiotics (such as Lactobacillus rhamnosus and Bifidobacterium breve ) can alleviate airway inflammation and alveolar damage [ ] ; in vitro experiments have also demonstrated that these probiotics exhibit similar anti-inflammatory effects against cigarette smoke-induced inflammation in human macrophages. [ ] This suggests a close connection between gut microbiota and COPD. Interestingly, gut microbiota can also regulate the expression of circulating cytokines in the host, thereby affecting systemic inflammatory responses. [ , ] Circulating cytokines have been shown to be closely associated with the severity of illness and inflammatory response in COPD patients. [ ] Multiple studies have shown that the levels of certain pro-inflammatory cytokines in the serum of COPD patients, such as interleukin-6 (IL-6) and tumor necrosis factor-alpha (TNF-α), are significantly elevated, and these cytokines are considered to be involved in the exacerbation and progression of COPD. [ , ] It appears that both gut microbiota and circulating cytokines can influence the development of COPD. However, the causal relationships among various gut microbiota, circulating cytokines, and COPD remain unclear, limiting our understanding of the pathological mechanisms of COPD and the formulation of treatment strategies. Therefore, it is of great significance to explore which gut microbiota influences the risk of COPD and how the gut microbiota affects the occurrence and development of COPD by altering the levels of certain circulating cytokines. Herein, we preliminarily hypothesize that circulating cytokines may act as mediators in the pathway from gut microbiota to COPD. Even though randomized controlled trials can assist in determining the causal links between gut microbiota or cytokines and COPD, they are hard to conduct in humans because of objective constraints, like screening suitable strains and modulating cytokine levels. Mendelian randomization (MR) is a genetic epidemiological approach. As a complementary method for studying causal relationships, MR based on genome-wide association studies (GWAS) employs 1 or more genetic markers as instrumental variables (IVs). These markers are strongly genetically associated with the exposure of interest and are considered unaffected by potential confounders. [ ] Currently, MR is widely used as an alternative method to test causal associations among variables. [ - ] In this study, we conducted a comprehensive MR analysis to explore the causal effects among 473 species of gut microbiota, 91 types of cytokines, and the development of COPD. The aim of this study is to provide new insights and theoretical evidence for the prevention and treatment of COPD. 2. Materials and methods 2.1. Study design This study comprises 3 main components, as illustrated in Figure : analyzing the causal relationships of 473 gut microbiota on COPD (step 1A); analyzing the causal relationships of 91 cytokines on COPD (step 2A); and performing mediation MR analyses for gut microbial taxa that were identified through the above screening as having significant causal associations with COPD, using circulating cytokines as potential mediators (step 3). Single-nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) were defined as IVs. MR is founded on 3 core assumptions: firstly, the IVs exhibit a strong correlation with the exposure factors; secondly, there is no association between the IVs and confounding factors; and thirdly, the IVs exert no direct influence on the outcome, with their impact on the outcome being mediated solely through the exposure. [ , ] 2.2. Data source The detailed summary statistics for gut microbiota with genome-wide significant findings are publicly available in the NHGRI-EBI GWAS Catalog (ranging from accession GCST90032172 to GCST90032644.1). Genetic variants linked to the gut microbiota were identified through genome-wide association analyses conducted on 79,79,834 human genetic variants from 5959 participants from the FINRISK 2002 cohort. GWAS of gut microbial taxa reveal 567 independent SNP-taxon associations. [ ] Circulating cytokine levels were derived from a recent study that included 11 cohorts and a total of 14,824 participants of European descent. The specific study design and data management protocols have been described in other publications. [ ] The levels of all 91 cytokines were assessed using the Olink Target Inflammation panel, and genome-wide genetic data were also collected. Considering parameters such as sample size, sequencing depth, ethnicity, and data update time, the dataset for this study was sourced from the

5959 participants from the FINRISK 2002 cohort. GWAS of gut microbial taxa reveal 567 independent SNP-taxon associations. [ ] Circulating cytokine levels were derived from a recent study that included 11 cohorts and a total of 14,824 participants of European descent. The specific study design and data management protocols have been described in other publications. [ ] The levels of all 91 cytokines were assessed using the Olink Target Inflammation panel, and genome-wide genetic data were also collected. Considering parameters such as sample size, sequencing depth, ethnicity, and data update time, the dataset for this study was sourced from the twelfth version of the Finngen consortium, consisting of 24,138 cases and 4,09,070 controls (gs://finngen - public - data - r12/summary_stats/release/finngen_R12_J10_COPD.gz). The current research is a secondary analysis based on publicly accessible GWAS summary statistics. Each of the original GWAS studies had obtained ethical approval. Moreover, this study did not involve the use of individual-level data. As a result, there was no need for additional ethical review board approval. 2.3. Instrumental variables selection Initially, we selected SNPs significantly associated with gut microbiota ( P < 1 × 10 −6 ). To maximize the number of instruments available for each cytokine, we also included SNPs with a P -value threshold of 5 × 10 −6 . We then removed the SNPs that exhibited linkage disequilibrium (LD) from the analysis. The LD of SNPs strongly associated with gut microbiota should satisfy the condition that r 2 < 0.001 and distance > 10,000 kb. [ ] A crucial aspect of MR analysis is to verify that the effects of SNPs on the exposure variable align with the same allele as their effects on the outcome variable. Following the matching of the outcome data, we eliminated palindromic SNPs. We obtained the necessary information, including chromosome, effect allele (EA), other allele, effect allele frequency (EAF), effect sizes (β), standard error (SE), and P -value. Finally, we computed the explained variance ( R 2 ) and F -statistic to assess whether the identified IVs were strongly associated with the exposure. Typically, SNPs with an F -statistic value < 10 are regarded as weak instruments. [ ] In this study, R 2 was calculated using the formula R 2 = 2 × EAF × (1 − EAF) × β 2 /[2 × EAF × (1 − EAF) × β 2 + 2 × EAF × (1 − EAF) × N × SE 2 ], where N represents the sample size of the GWAS for F . The F -statistic was derived using the formula F = R 2 (N − 2)/(1 − R 2 ). [ ] 2.4. MR analysis 2.4.1. Primary analysis To assess the causal relationships between gut microbiota and cytokines with COPD, we conducted 2-sample MR analyses for each association (step 1A and step 2A in Fig. ). The inverse variance weighted (IVW) method was utilized as the primary analytical approach, while the Wald ratio test was applied for variables with only one IV. [ ] The MR findings were reported as odds ratios (ORs) with their respective 95% confidence intervals (CIs). Statistical significance was determined when the P -value of IVW analysis was below 0.05 and the effect directions of IVW and MR-Egger were concordant. 2.4.2. Mediation analysis For gut microbiota and cytokines with significant causal relationships on COPD identified through the 2-sample analysis (step 1A and step 2A in Fig. ), we included them in the mediation analysis. We first investigated whether gut microbiota had a causal effect on cytokines (step 3, path a in Fig. ). If a causal effect was identified, we would then conduct a multiple MR analysis to determine whether cytokines acted as mediating factors in the causal pathway from gut microbiota to COPD. To ensure valid inference in our 3-step mediation MR framework, we enforced strict consistency in the instrumental SNP set used across all 3 causal paths: microbiota (exposure) → cytokine (mediator), cytokine → COPD (outcome), and microbiota → COPD (total effect). Specifically, for each gut microbial taxon identified as causally associated with COPD in step 1, we extracted its genome-wide significant instrumental SNPs ( P < 5 × 10 −6 , clumped at r 2 < 0.001, kb = 10,000). We then retained only those SNPs that: were present in the cytokine GWAS summary statistics; were present in the COPD GWAS summary statistics; passed allele harmonization across all 3 datasets; showed no evidence of horizontal pleiotropy in the exposure–outcome association. This stringent filtering yielded a common SNP set that satisfies the core IV assumptions for all 3 paths in the causal chain. Prior to calculating the indirect effect as β(indirect) = β(A) × β(B), we rigorously harmonized the EAs of instrumental SNPs across the exposure (gut microbiota), mediator (circulating cytokines), and outcome (COPD) datasets. Specifically, for

Specifically, for each SNP used as an instrument for a gut microbial taxon (exposure), we first aligned its EA with that reported in the cytokine GWAS (mediator) using the TwoSampleMR R package. [ ] SNPs with ambiguous strand orientation (A/T or G/C SNPs) were excluded to avoid allele misalignment. For remaining SNPs, we ensured that the EA for the exposure–mediator association (β(A)) and the mediator–outcome association (β(B)) referred to the same nucleotide. If the EA in the cytokine GWAS was the reverse complement of that in the microbiota GWAS, we flipped the sign of β(B) accordingly. This harmonization guarantees that the product β(A) × β(B) correctly reflects the directional causal pathway from gut microbiota through cytokine to COPD. 2.4.3. Bidirectional causality analysis To assess the bidirectional causal relationships between gut microbiota, cytokines, and COPD, we designated COPD as the “exposure” and considered gut microbiota or cytokines associated with COPD as the “outcomes” (step 1B and step 2B in Fig. ). We chose the SNPs that were significantly linked to COPD ( P < 5 × 10 –6 ) to serve as IVs. 2.5. Sensitivity analysis To assess the heterogeneity of each SNP, we conducted Cochran’s Q test. [ ] We also created scatter plots to illustrate the associations between SNPs and exposures, as well as SNPs and outcomes, thereby visualizing the MR results. Leave-one-out analysis was carried out to determine whether each SNP could influence the results. Furthermore, we employed MR-PRESSO and MR-Egger regression to examine potential horizontal pleiotropy. MR-PRESSO was utilized to identify significant outliers and to adjust for the horizontal plural effect by eliminating these outliers. [ ] All data analysis packages were obtained from the open-access repository in the R software environment (version 4.3.2; Ningbo, China; https://www.r-project.org/ ). 3. Results 3.1. Selection of IVs Initially, we detected 5259 SNPs linked to 473 gut microbiota taxa, with a significance threshold of P < 1 × 10 −6 . These SNPs were designated as IVs for the corresponding gut microbiota taxa (Table S1, Supplemental Digital Content, https://links.lww.com/MD/R569 ). Likewise, we found 1818 SNPs associated with 91 cytokines at a significance level of P < 5 × 10 −6 (Table S2, Supplemental Digital Content, https://links.lww.com/MD/R569 ). In the reverse MR analysis targeting COPD, a total of 115 SNPs were ultimately chosen (Table S3, Supplemental Digital Content, https://links.lww.com/MD/R569 ). 3.2. MR results of gut microbiota on COPD The IVW method was employed as the primary analytical approach. Taxonomic classifications followed GTDB release 89. In the forward MR analysis, we initially identified 26 bacterial taxa potentially exhibiting a causal effect on COPD. Sensitivity checks using the MR-Egger intercept indicated horizontal pleiotropy for two of these taxa; after excluding them, 24 taxa remained robustly linked to COPD (Table S4, Supplemental Digital Content, https://links.lww.com/MD/R569 ; Figure ). Among these, 11 taxa conferred an elevated risk. The details are as follows: Francisellales abundance in stool (OR = 1.9056, 95% CI: 1.3410–2.7080, IVW: P = .0003), Francisellaceae abundance in stool (OR = 1.5949, 95% CI: 1.1567–2.1991, IVW: P = .0044), Pandoraea abundance in stool (OR = 1.3544, 95% CI: 1.0124–1.8119, IVW: P = .0411), UBA1446 sp002329245 abundance in stool (OR = 1.2899, 95% CI: 1.0326–1.6114, IVW: P = .0249), Comamonas B abundance in stool (OR = 1.2852, 95% CI: 1.0162–1.6255, IVW: P = .0363), Staphylococcus A fleurettii abundance in stool (OR = 1.1880, 95% CI: 1.0141–1.3917, IVW: P = .0329), Coprobacter secundus abundance in stool (OR = 1.1690, 95% CI: 1.0142–1.3475, IVW: P = .0312), Brevibacillus B abundance in stool (OR = 1.1658, 95% CI: 1.0057–1.3513, IVW: P = .0418), Bacteroides faecis abundance in stool (OR = 1.1228, 95% CI: 1.0306–1.2233, IVW: P = .0081), Lachnospira sp000437735 abundance in stool (OR = 1.1106, 95% CI: 1.0149–1.2152, IVW: P = .0225) and Leuconostoc mesenteroides abundance in stool (OR = 1.1067, 95% CI: 1.0100–1.2128, IVW: P = .0298). Conversely, 13 gut microbial taxa were found to have a protective effect against COPD. Conversely, 13 gut microbial taxa were found to have a protective effect against COPD. The MR-Egger regression intercept method suggested that genetic pleiotropy had no significant impact on the results. Furthermore, MR-PRESSO analysis confirmed the absence of horizontal pleiotropy in the MR study (Table S4, Supplemental Digital Content, https://links.lww.com/MD/R569 ). Cochran’s Q tests also indicated no significant heterogeneit, and “leave-one-out” analyses confirmed the robustness of the MR results. Visual inspection of funnel and scatter plots revealed no notable asymmetry or heterogeneity (Figs. S1–S4,Supplemental Digital Content, https://links.lww.com/MD/R568 ). 3.3. MR results of cytokines on COPD Seven circulating cytokines were found to have a causal relationship with COPD (Table S5, Supplemental Digital Content, https://links.lww.com/MD/R569 , Fig. ). Specifically, 6 cytokines were likely to increase the risk of COPD: interleukin-7 levels (IL-7; OR = 1.1990, 95% CI: 1.0138–1.4182, IVW: P = .0340), protein S100-A12 levels (EN-RAGE; OR = 1.1231, 95% CI: 1.0394–1.2136, IVW: P = .0033), leukemia inhibitory factor levels (LIF; OR = 1.0950, 95% CI: 1.0137–1.1828, IVW: P = .0211), interleukin-1-alpha levels (IL-1A; OR = 1.0833, 95% CI: 1.0132–1.1582, IVW: P = .0191), C-X-C motif chemokine 10 levels (CXCL10; OR = 1.0665, 95% CI: 1.0072–1.1292, IVW: P = .0273) and T-cell surface glycoprotein CD6 isoform levels (CD6; OR = 1.0636, 95% CI: 1.0266–1.1019, IVW: P = .0006). One cytokine was found to potentially reduce the risk of COPD: CUB domain-containing protein 1 levels (CDCP1; OR = 0.9489, 95% CI: 0.9069–0.9929, IVW: P = .0234). The results of the sensitivity analysis indicated no evidence of heterogeneity or pleiotropy. The “leave-one-out” analysis, funnel plot, and scatter plot further verified the reliability of our results (Table S5 and Figs. 5 to 8, Supplemental Digital Content, https://links.lww.com/MD/R568 ). 3.4. Association of gut microbiota and cytokines Next, we performed MR analysis on 24 selected gut microbiota and 7 cytokines to further investigate the potential mediating role of gut microbiota exposure in these important mediators. Our analysis yielded several noteworthy results. Specifically, 11 gut microbial taxa showed strong correlations with the 7 cytokines (Table S6, Supplemental Digital Content, https://links.lww.com/MD/R569 , Fig. ). It was observed that different gut microbiota can have varying effects on the same cytokine. This phenomenon was evident for T-cell surface glycoprotein CD6 isoform levels (CD6), CUB domain-containing protein 1 levels (CDCP1), leukemia inhibitory factor levels (LIF), and onterleukin-1-alpha levels (IL-1A). The results of the sensitivity analysis indicated no evidence of heterogeneity or pleiotropy. The “leave-one-out” analysis, funnel plot, and scatter plot further confirmed the reliability of our findings (Table S6, Supplemental Digital Content, https://links.lww.com/MD/R569 ; Figs. S9–S12, Supplemental Digital Content, https://links.lww.com/MD/R568 ). 3.5. Sensitivity analysis did not detect potential level multiplicity or heterogeneity. These findings underscore the complex interplay between gut microbiotas, cytokines, and COPD, corroborating previous research indicating that COPD patients often experience dysbiosis of the gut microbiota. Discussion To elucidate the causal effects of gut microbiota and cytokines in the pathogenesis and development of COPD, we employed MR analysis to conduct a comprehensive and detailed genetic analysis. We analyzed the causal relationships between the latest 473 gut microbiota and 91 circulating cytokines and COPD. As a result, 24 different gut microbiota and 7 cytokines were found to be closely related to COPD. This enhances our understanding of the complex interactions among gut microbiota, cytokines, and the pathogenesis of COPD. We utilized the IVW method as the primary approach. Specifically, there are 11 gut microbial taxa that may increase the risk of COPD. Among them, there is relatively limited research on the direct association between Francisellales and Francisellaceae and COPD. Bacteria of the genus Pandoraea can be detected in patients with pulmonary diseases and are considered one of the important pathogens causing acute exacerbations of the disease. [ ] Pandoraea can produce a variety of extracellular enzymes and toxins, damage lung tissue and promote inflammatory responses. [ , ] Although its pathogenic mechanism in the lungs is relatively clear, its role in the gut and its impact on COPD still require further investigation. Bacteria of the genus Staphylococcus have a high detection rate in the lungs of COPD patients, especially Staphylococcus aureus , which has been widely studied. [ ] However, the role of Staphylococcus A fleurettii in COPD has not been reported yet. Considering the pathogenic mechanisms of Staphylococcus bacteria, such as toxin production and induction of inflammatory responses, [ - ] Staphylococcus A fleurettii may affect the development of COPD through similar mechanisms. The role of C secundus in COPD can be understood from its presence and changes in the gut microbiota. The study found that C secundus is more common in the healthy control group, while it is significantly reduced in COPD patients. [ ] This may be related to the relatively small sample size of the population examined, and more population-based studies are needed to clarify the specific mechanisms and functions of C secundus in COPD. Bacteria of the genus Brevibacillus are widely present in the environment and the human body. Some studies have found that Brevibacillus and Proteus in the upper respiratory tract microbiota of COPD patients are associated with COPD exacerbations. [ - ] . However, the specific mechanism of action of Brevibacillus in the gut has not been clearly elucidated in current research. B faecis belongs to the genus Bacteroides and is a common gut microbiota. Studies have shown that Bacteroides undergoes significant changes in the gut microbiota composition of COPD patients. For example, some studies have found that the relative abundance of Bacteroidetes is higher in the gut of COPD patients. [ , ] In patients with COPD and lung cancer, research indicates that smoking significantly alters the composition of gut bacteria. Specifically, smoking tends to reduce the abundance of Firmicutes and Proteobacteria, while simultaneously increasing the levels of Prevotella, Bacteroides, and Bacteroidetes. [ , ] However, there is controversy regarding the role of this bacterium in the acute exacerbation of COPD. On the one hand, Bacteroides is considered a major commensal microbiota in the gut, with anti-inflammatory properties that can reduce systemic inflammatory responses by decreasing the levels of the pro-inflammatory cytokine IL-8. [ ] Additionally, the weakly agonistic lipopolysaccharide (LPS) produced by Bacteroides has anti-inflammatory functions, which may improve COPD symptoms. [ ] On the other hand, an imbalance in the microbial community may lead to increased intestinal permeability, allowing bacteria and toxins to enter the

of Prevotella, Bacteroides, and Bacteroidetes. [ , ] However, there is controversy regarding the role of this bacterium in the acute exacerbation of COPD. On the one hand, Bacteroides is considered a major commensal microbiota in the gut, with anti-inflammatory properties that can reduce systemic inflammatory responses by decreasing the levels of the pro-inflammatory cytokine IL-8. [ ] Additionally, the weakly agonistic lipopolysaccharide (LPS) produced by Bacteroides has anti-inflammatory functions, which may improve COPD symptoms. [ ] On the other hand, an imbalance in the microbial community may lead to increased intestinal permeability, allowing bacteria and toxins to enter the circulatory system, exacerbating systemic inflammation and worsening COPD. [ ] Regarding Lachnospira sp000437735, some studies have found that an increase in Lachnospira is also associated with a decrease in lung function and may play a certain role in the pathological process of COPD. [ , ] This is consistent with our research findings, but the underlying mechanism remains to be explored. As for Comamonas, Francisella, and Leuconostoc mesenteroides, their roles in the gut and in COPD have not been reported yet. Our findings provide new insights into the study of their roles in COPD. On the contrary, 13 gut microbial taxa exhibit a protective effect against COPD. Among them, only Bacillus has been reported in the field of COPD. Most bacteria of the genus Bacillus are generally not considered human pathogens. Bacillus can regulate the gut microbiota and restore the intestinal epithelial barrier. [ ] Compared with healthy controls, the levels of culturable Bacillus species in COPD patients are significantly reduced. [ ] A COPD mouse model treated with Lactobacillus showed an increase in short-chain fatty acid levels in the cecum, especially acetic acid and propionic acid. [ ] In addition, poly-γ-glutamic acid derived from Bacillus has been shown to have anti-inflammatory effects in animal models through a Toll-like receptor 4-dependent pathway. [ ] Another study found that supplementing Bacillus in a mouse model of ovalbumin (OVA)-induced pulmonary inflammation reduced the levels of type 2 helper T cell (Th2) cytokines at both the transcriptional and protein levels in the lungs. [ ] This suggests that Bacillus may play a protective role by regulating inflammatory responses. In summary, the gut microbiota is one of the key factors in the occurrence and development of COPD, which can affect the progression of COPD through various pathways such as cytokines and immune responses. Similar to gut microbiota, circulating cytokines also play a crucial role in the onset and progression of COPD. Our research identified 7 circulating cytokines that appear to have a causal relationship with COPD. Specifically, 6 cytokines – interleukin-7 (IL-7), protein S100-A12 (EN-RAGE), leukemia inhibitory factor (LIF), interleukin-1-alpha (IL-1A), C-X-C motif chemokine 10 (CXCL10), and T-cell surface glycoprotein CD6 (CD6) – were associated with an increased risk of COPD. IL-1A is a well-known pro-inflammatory cytokine, and its involvement in COPD has been confirmed by multiple studies. In COPD, IL-1A may exacerbate airway inflammation by promoting the activation of inflammatory cells and the release of inflammatory mediators. [ , ] IL-7, a cytokine critical for T-cell development and immune responses, has been less extensively studied in COPD. However, research indicates that IL-7 plays a significant role in various inflammatory diseases and may contribute to the immunopathological processes of COPD by influencing T-cell differentiation and survival. [ , ] Leukaemia inhibitory factor (LIF), typically associated with hematopoietic function, may contribute to COPD by affecting alveolar epithelial cells and mesenchymal cells. Elevated LIF expression may be linked to lung tissue repair and remodeling processes. [ , ] CXCL10, a chemokine that recruits T cells and other immune cells to sites of inflammation, has been shown to be significantly elevated in COPD patients and is thought to exacerbate airway inflammation and tissue damage, driving disease progression. [ , ] CD6, a T-cell surface glycoprotein, although the specific role of CD6 in COPD remains unclear, its known function in T-cell activation suggests it may influence COPD pathogenesis by regulating T-cell-mediated immune responses. [ ] EN-RAGE, a member of the S100 protein family, primarily acts in inflammatory processes. While specific studies on EN-RAGE in COPD are limited, its involvement in oxidative stress and inflammatory cell activation in other diseases implies a potential role in COPD pathogenesis. [ , ] Conversely, CUB domain-containing protein 1 (CDCP1) was found to be associated with a reduced risk of COPD. CDCP1 has been implicated in diverse cellular stress responses; however, its specific role in COPD remains largely unexplored. Studies indicate that CDCP1 gene expression is up-regulated in COPD patients. [ ] CDCP1 mediates cellular antiapoptotic capacity by inhibiting the PI3K/AKT pathway. Moreover, the Ras/ERK signaling pathway can activate CDCP1, thereby enhancing resistance to anoikis-induced apoptosis. [ ] These findings suggest that CDCP1 may contribute to COPD pathogenesis by modulating cellular stress responses

CDCP1 has been implicated in diverse cellular stress responses; however, its specific role in COPD remains largely unexplored. Studies indicate that CDCP1 gene expression is up-regulated in COPD patients. [ ] CDCP1 mediates cellular antiapoptotic capacity by inhibiting the PI3K/AKT pathway. Moreover, the Ras/ERK signaling pathway can activate CDCP1, thereby enhancing resistance to anoikis-induced apoptosis. [ ] These findings suggest that CDCP1 may contribute to COPD pathogenesis by modulating cellular stress responses and antiapoptotic mechanisms. Additional basic and clinical studies are needed to further elucidate the roles of these cytokines in COPD. COPD not only affects the lungs, but may also impact the gut microbiota and systemic inflammatory status through the gut-lung axis. To verify whether COPD in turn leads to imbalanced gut microbiota or changes in cytokine levels, we conducted reverse MR analysis. The results revealed that COPD was positively correlated with 46 gut microbiota and 9 cytokines, and negatively correlated with 17 gut microbiota ( P < .05). This is consistent with previous studies, suggesting that patients with COPD often experience gut microbiota dysbiosis. [ ] However, it should be noted that in the subsequent exploration of whether cytokines play a mediating role in the “microbiota-COPD” pathway, it is necessary to first exclude the reverse effects of COPD on microbiota and cytokines to avoid causal inversion. Although the mechanisms by which gut microbiota contribute to COPD remain unclear, we hypothesize that gut microbiota may influence the onset and progression of COPD through the modulation of cytokine levels. Our mediation analyses identified 4 circulating cytokines – LIF, IL-1A, CXCL10, and CD6 – as significant mediators linking specific gut microbiota taxa to COPD risk. Notably, LIF mediated a substantial proportion of the total causal effects, with mediation proportions ranging from 9.34% to 18.84% across 4 distinct bacterial exposures, with the strongest mediation observed for ER4 sp002437735 abundance in stool. IL-1A also exhibited relatively strong mediating role, accounting for approximately 12% of mediation proportions of both Brevibacillus B abundance in stool and C secundus abundance in stool on COPD. In contrast, CXCL10 and CD6 showed more modest mediation proportions (4.24% and 5.60%, respectively), suggesting that while these cytokines contribute to the gut-lung axis in COPD pathogenesis, a portion of the microbial effects likely operates through alternative, non-cytokine-mediated pathways. These findings offer new insights that may inform future intervention strategies targeting gut microbiota and cytokines. This study is the first to systematically investigate the associations among gut microbiota, circulating cytokines, and COPD risk using large-scale MR methods. However, there are also several limitations that need further improvement. First, the summary data from GWAS on COPD, cytokines, and most gut microbiota utilized in this analysis are primarily derived from European populations. As MR estimates can be sensitive to cohort-specific biases or technical artifacts, our findings require replication using independent, large-scale GWAS datasets. Second, to ensure an adequate number of SNPs as IVs, we adopted a relatively lenient significance threshold ( P < 1 × 10 −6 ) rather than the more stringent threshold ( P < 5 × 10 −8 ) commonly used in MR studies. While this approach increases the number of available genetic variants, it may also introduce additional noise or potential biases. Finally, although our analysis explored the mediating role of cytokines between different gut microbiota and COPD, these findings require validation through rigorous scientific experiments before they can be directly translated into clinical practice. Moreover, the pathological mechanisms through which gut microbiota influence COPD are highly complex. This study only begins to uncover these mechanisms, and further in-depth research is necessary to fully elucidate them. 5. Conclusion In this study, we systematically investigated the genetic associations among gut microbiota, circulating cytokines, and COPD risk. Our analyses provided evidence suggestive of associations between 11 gut microbiota taxa and increased COPD risk, and 13 taxa with decreased risk. Similarly, we observed associations of 6 cytokines with higher COPD risk and 1 cytokine with lower risk. Reverse MR analyses provided evidence for genetic associations between genetically predicted COPD and 64 gut microbial taxa, as well as 9 cytokines. Furthermore, mediation analysis highlighted 4 cytokines – LIF, IL-1A, CXCL10, and CD6 – as potential mediators in the pathways linking specific gut microbiota to COPD. Our research findings provided new insights for early diagnosis, intervention, and understanding the progression of COPD. chunks.content: Introduction Malignant hyperthermia (MH) is an acute pharmacogenetic disorder, which while uncommon is potentially fatal [ , ]. In humans, susceptibility to MH is an inherited disorder and it has an autosomal dominant pattern [ - ]. To date, genes located at six chromosomal loci associated with MH have been described: 1) Ryanodine receptor type 1 ( RyR1 ) gene, ryanodine receptor found in skeletal muscle (chromosomal locus 19q13.1.); 2) CACNA1S gene, which encodes for the alpha-1S subunit of dihydropyridine (chromosomal locus 1q32); 3) A variant of the STAC3 gene, which encodes an important protein for excitation-contraction coupling via trafficking the voltage sensor into the correct T-tubular location (chromosomal locus 7q21-q22); 4) SCN4A gene (possible), related to voltage-dependent sodium channel of skeletal muscle (chromosomal locus 17q11.2-q24); and, not yet identified genes for 5) chromosomal loci 3q13.1 and 6) 5p [ , , - ]. However, these genes associated with MH show incomplete penetrance and variable expression [ , , ]. MH is related to muscle function and calcium levels. A muscle contraction starts when the action potential arrives at the neuromuscular junction, starting a muscle depolarization and causing a conformational change in the T-tubular L-type voltage-dependent calcium channel (dihydropyridine calcium channel receptor, DHPR). This conformational change activates the RyR1 leading to a rapid release of Ca 2+ , from sarcoplasmic reticulum, increasing the intracytoplasmic Ca 2+ concentration [ , - ]. Muscle relaxation occurs when stimulation of the motor nerve stops and the intracellular adenosine triphosphate (ATP)-dependent Ca 2+ pump transports intracytoplasmic Ca 2+ into the sarcoplasmic reticulum lumen [ , , , ]. MH is a calcium channelopathy of skeletal muscle [ ] in which a constant increase of intracytoplasmic Ca 2+ concentration occurs causing a change in cellular metabolism [ , - , ]. A hypermetabolic state develops when susceptible patients are exposed to halogenated volatile inhalational anesthetic agents (halothane, isoflurane, enflurane, sevoflurane, desflurane and methoxyflurane), depolarizing muscle relaxants (e.g., succinylcholine), and/or extreme physical activity in hot environments [ , , , - ]. The MH clinical incidence is estimated to be from 1 in 10,000 - 30,000 to 1 in 100,000 - 250,000 in patients undergoing anesthesia, depending on geographic localization and age [ , ]. Nevertheless, the prevalence of genetic variants or mutations of an individual susceptible to MH is estimated to be 1 in 2,000 - 3,000 [ , , ]. MH affects all ethnic groups and both sexes, although there is a greater predisposition for men and children, and it is atypical in the elderly [ , - ]. The MH episode can occur both in the first exposure to the substances that triggers the crisis and in subsequent contacts [ , , ]. MH presents variable clinical expression [ , ]. During an episode of MH, the patient may present clinical signs and laboratory findings including masseter muscle spasm, tachycardia, rise in end-tidal CO 2 concentration (EtCO 2 ), tachypnea, hyperthermia, cyanosis, metabolic acidosis, rhabdomyolysis, hyperkalemia, myoglobinuria, hyperlactacidemia and acute renal failure [ , , , , , ]. When the pathology is diagnosed, the exposure to the triggering agents should be discontinued followed by immediate intravenous administration of dantrolene sodium, a hydantoin-derived skeletal muscle relaxant drug [ , , , , ]. Dantrolene remains the drug of choice for MH prophylaxis and treatment [ , , ]. In addition, protocols must be established to control or prevent complications associated with the clinical condition of the disease. These include external (if necessary, internal) cooling of the patient’s body, hyperventilation with 100% oxygen, correction of metabolic acidosis, adjustment of cardiac arrhythmias, dialysis to remove anesthetic residues and aid in blood filtration to revert metabolites to normal levels [ , , , ]. Several tests have been proposed or are being investigated as less invasive diagnostic tests to determinate MH susceptible patients [ ], including: 1) Evaluation of creatine kinase concentrations; 2) In vitro measurement for the concentrations of ATP, phosphocreatine or other phosphomonoesters, along with pH, in muscle and other tissue by nuclear magnetic resonance spectroscopy; 3) Evaluation of calcium flow at RYR1 receptors on B lymphocytes; 4) Assessment of the enhanced intracellular calcium from cultured muscle tissue; and 5) Molecular genetic tests to look for mutations in the genes associated with MH susceptibility. However, the caffeine-halothane contracture test (CHCT) remains the standard method used in Brazil [ , , , ]. CHCT must be performed on a biopsy of approximately 2 g of muscle from the vastus lateralis or vastus medialis [ , , ]. The muscle fragment is longitudinally dissected into strips and the level of muscle contraction is assessed before and after exposure to caffeine and halothane ( RYR1 agonists) [ , ]. Individuals who are susceptible to MH have a CHCT positive result when abnormally high levels of contractile force

The aim of this case report is to describe an episode of MH associated with the use of halogenated anesthetic during bariatric surgery. The case study is intended to serve as inclusive knowledge and a reference tool for healthcare professionals and academic-scientific area with respect to clinical, pathophysiological, biochemical, and biophysical correlations. Case Report Informed consent was obtained from the patient’s family as well as authorization to use and disclose protected health information. L.R.M.S was a 29-year-old man, born in Jau, Sao Paulo, Brazil but with European ascendance. He was admitted to the Hospital Santa Casa de Jahu to undergo a bariatric surgery, vertical gastroplasty to Roux-en-Y gastric bypass without a ring, using the conventional technique (not performed by laparoscopy). The patient’s relevant medical history included morbid obesity grade III, allergy to sulfa-based drugs and severe obstructive sleep apnea (i.e., apnea and hypopnea index greater than 30 hypopneas and apneas per hour). The patient complained of episodes of gastroesophageal reflux and the repeated occurrences of calf cramps. In addition, due to the obesity condition, the patient possessed a lack of energy, impaired mobility, episodes of peak hypertension, and mood changes. The patient was using antidepressant medications to treat anxiety. Preoperative evaluations with cardiopulmonary exercise testing, echocardiogram with color Doppler and electrocardiogram showed no anatomical and functional changes of the patient’s heart. However, some signs of hepatic steatosis were detected from a total abdominal ultrasound and spirometry test showed a mild obstructive ventilatory defect. On pre-anesthetic evaluation, the patient reported that he had never undergone general anesthesia. Furthermore, none of his family members had presented complications in surgical procedures with general anesthesia. Upon arriving at the operating room, the patient’s preoperative blood pressure was 200/130 mm Hg with an oxygen saturation of 94%. Although the patient’s oxygen saturation showed normal in the preoperative exams, while lying down a significant drop in this saturation was observed. Surgical procedures started at approximately 8 am on February 14, 2011 and ended at 12:50 pm, without complications. General anesthesia was induced and maintained with the following agents as described in . After the end of the surgical procedures, the patient remained in the operating room for another hour until he responded to stimuli. Then, the patient was taken to the recovery room, where he stayed until 2 pm. According to medical reports, the evolution of the patient’s condition indicated oliguria and acute breathing insufficiency. Therefore, the patient was placed under mechanical ventilation in the intensive care unit (ICU). Five hours after the patient arrived at the ICU, he started to present clinical signs of hypermetabolic state, with tremors, excessive sweating, and rapid body temperature increases. In early postoperative, the temperature was being adjusted with an antipyretic (dipyrone) administration. On postoperative days 0 (02/14), 1 (02/15), 2 (02/16) and 3 (02/17), nursing reports described an unstable blood pressure, tachycardia and persistent hyperthermia, as shown in . In the early postoperative, a chest X-ray was performed, which indicated an elevation of diaphragmatic domes. In addition, the routine tracheal aspiration for intubated patients was carried out and the patient had serosanguinolent secretion. Some laboratory tests and arterial-blood gas analyses were performed to monitor the patient’s clinical conditions ( ). The blood sugar levels were measured in the pre- and post-operative periods and hyperglycemia was observed in postoperative tests. Postoperative changes in creatine phosphokinase (CPK) concentration were also observed. The first CPK test was carried out on February 15 at 08:26 am, indicating a high CPK concentration, more than 2,380 U/L. After 5 h, a new CPK evaluation was done showing an increase of 164%. The level of serum calcium was normal in the preoperative evaluation; however, the calcium test performed on postoperative day 1 (morning) showed hypocalcemia, whereas in the following postoperative tests the concentration of this ion was returned to the normal level. Serum sodium levels increased from postoperative day 2, while hyperkalemia was observed in the afternoon of postoperative day 1. The level of serum calcium was normal in the preoperative evaluation; however, the calcium test performed on postoperative day 1 (morning) showed hypocalcemia, whereas in the following postoperative tests the concentration of this ion was returned to the normal level. Serum sodium levels increased from postoperative day 2, while hyperkalemia was observed in the afternoon of postoperative day 1. Serum levels of urea and creatinine were evaluated in the pre- and post-operative periods. Urea and creatinine concentrations were normal in the preoperative tests; however, on postoperative day 1, urea was 78% higher and creatinine increased more than 350%. On the following postoperative days, both urea and creatinine concentrations kept increasing. Aspartate aminotransferase (AST) and alanine aminotransferase (ALT) enzymes were evaluated in the pre- and postoperative periods. In the preoperative test, the AST and ALT levels were normal. On postoperative day 1 (morning) the AST and ALT levels were approximately 22 and 15 times higher, respectively. A new AST and ALT test were carried out after 5 h and the values almost doubled. Two arterial-blood gas analyses were performed on postoperative day 1. The first arterial-blood gas analysis (08:26 am) showed normal rates, although the partial pressure of oxygen (PaO 2 ) increased due to the patient being on mechanical ventilation with pure oxygen. The second arterial-blood gas analysis (01:18 pm) indicated acidification of the blood pH and significant changes in both the concentration of base excess and in arterial-blood distribution of gases. In addition, the bicarbonate concentration remained in a normal range and the partial pressure of carbon dioxide (PaCO 2 ) increased in both arterial-blood gas analyses ( ). Preoperative and postoperative blood counts were performed. In the preoperative blood counts, the absolute number of leukocytes was 7,900 mm 3 (level range: 4,000 - 10,000 mm 3 ). On postoperative day 1, two blood counts were carried out; the first one showed a significant increase of leukocytes (14,700 mm 3 ), characterizing a leukocytosis. After 2 h, a new leukocyte count was performed and the absolute number decreased to 12,000 mm 3 . On postoperative day 2, the absolute number of leukocytes was 13,800 mm 3 , while the last blood count performed on postoperative day 3 showed 13,000 leukocytes per mm 3 . On the postoperative day 1, an echocardiogram was performed and showed mild symmetric hypertrophy. On the same day, a new chest X-ray was carried out and indicated little pulmonary inspiration, bilateral basal interstitial infiltrate, veiled left diaphragmatic dome, and globose cardiac area. On the postoperative day 2, an abdominal ultrasound was carried out and did not indicate any anatomical alteration of the liver, gallbladder, spleen, kidneys, and bladder. In addition, it did not indicate signs of ascites or pleural effusion. A third chest X-ray was performed revealing a veiling of the base of the right lung, cardiomegaly, aortic stretching, permeable costophrenic sinuses and free diaphragmatic domes. On the postoperative day 3 (08:15 am), an urinalysis was accomplished and showed traces of proteinuria, presence of ketones, leukocytes (17,600/mL), red blood cells (12,000/mL), and urobilinogen (0.2 UE). On the same day (3:50 pm), the medical records reported the establishment of multifactorial acute respiratory and renal failures, rhabdomyolysis, systemic inflammatory process and, for the first time, MH crisis was assumed. At night, nursing reports recorded edema formation of lower limbs, cold and cyanotic extremities, distended abdomen, paleness, and septic shock a few hours before the death of the patient. The MH diagnosis of L.R.M.S. was conducted less than 5 h before his death, and the administration of dantrolene sodium was not performed. The patient’s exposure to the substances that triggered the crisis was completed when the surgical procedures were over. External body cooling and hyperventilation with pure oxygen were administered in the following postoperative days. Dialysis was done a few hours before the patient’s death; however, according to medical reports this procedure caused decompensation of several of the patient’s clinical and laboratory parameters. The patient died at 9:20 pm on February 17, 2011 in the Hospital Santa Casa de Jahu. Discussion In MH crises, there is a persistent increase in the intracytoplasmic calcium concentration. The initial manifestations of a hypermetabolic state induce fast depletion of ATP causing increased carbon dioxide production, increased oxygen demands, respiratory acidosis, and increased temperature [ , , ]. The constant rise in oxygen consumption will lead to a hypoxia and progressive lactic acidosis, while depletion of ATP due to hypermetabolism of skeletal muscle cells will result in metabolic acidosis [ , ]. Based on the clinical and lab findings, a late diagnosis of MH crisis was established for patient L.R.M.S. According to Litman et al (2008) [ ], a MH crisis may occur at any time during anesthesia as well as in the early

hypermetabolic state induce fast depletion of ATP causing increased carbon dioxide production, increased oxygen demands, respiratory acidosis, and increased temperature [ , , ]. The constant rise in oxygen consumption will lead to a hypoxia and progressive lactic acidosis, while depletion of ATP due to hypermetabolism of skeletal muscle cells will result in metabolic acidosis [ , ]. Based on the clinical and lab findings, a late diagnosis of MH crisis was established for patient L.R.M.S. According to Litman et al (2008) [ ], a MH crisis may occur at any time during anesthesia as well as in the early postoperative period, although not usually 1 h after discontinuation of volatile agents. However, in our case the patient displayed initial symptoms of MH after 11 h of isoflurane administration, a late postoperative crisis. Hyperthermia is a key indicator of MH, since the rapid increase in body temperature occurs due to the process of sustained muscle contraction [ , , ]. In the initial postoperative period, the patient’s temperature increase was being controlled with the administration of antipyretic. Thereafter, hyperthermia no longer responded with the antipyretic administration, and the patient’s body was cooled externally. However, even with measures taken to control the temperature, it continued to increase. Tachycardia is another clinical sign characteristic of MH and it has been registered since the early postoperative period, as described in . Constant muscle contraction causes a decrease in ATP levels and consequent difficulty in muscle relaxation, which explains the masseter rigidity presented by patients during the MH crisis [ , , , ]. The patient L.R.M.S. was placed on spontaneous ventilation after the surgical procedure but was maintained with Montgomery T-tube due to his morbid obesity. After being transferred to the ICU, the patient presented a drop in oxygen saturation and needed to be placed on a mechanical respirator, in which he remained until his death. However, it was not observed whether the patient showed masseter rigidity as described in other MH case reports. High temperatures (at times over 42 degrees) achieved during MH crisis, together with the toxins released due to rapid and severe catabolism. It causes profound and acute inflammatory and functional changes of internal organs, leading to changes in the information contained in the blood [ , , - ]. If diagnosed late, MH causes multiple organ dysfunction (e.g., kidneys, pancreas and liver), disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC), cardiac dysrhythmias (cardiac arrest), and can progress to multiple organ failure [ , , , , ]. The pre- and early post-operative patient’s blood sugar tests were normal. After the afternoon of postoperative day 1, the glucose concentration increased. The hyperglycemia presented by the patient could be due to both a dysfunction of the pancreas caused by the hypermetabolic state and the need of the body to try to supply glucose for the ATP production and, consequently, muscle relaxation. Creatine phosphokinase is one of the most sensitive indicators of muscular damage. High serum levels of CPK observed after general anesthesia is a strong indicator of an MH crisis [ ]. Expressively high values in the serum CPK concentration indicate damage to contractile cells [ , ], since this enzyme plays an important role in regulation of muscle contraction [ ]. Although serum CPK levels were not evaluated during the intraoperative period, our patient presented high levels in all dosages performed in the postoperative period. The increase in serum CPK concentration occurs due to cell lysis, as this enzyme is not able to naturally cross the sarcoplasmic membrane [ , , ]. Calcium is essential for the integrity and structure of cell membranes, proper conduction of electrical stimuli (cardiac and muscular) blood clotting, and bone formation growth [ ]. When serum calcium levels decrease, excitability of nerve and muscle cells increases significantly [ ]. Given the abundance of calcium in the body, hypocalcemia always means failure in the regulatory mechanisms and can have several causes such as rhabdomyolysis, cardiac arrhythmias, and incessant muscle contractions [ , ]. The patient’s hypocalcemia detected on postoperative day 1 could be directly related to the renal failure and with increased muscle cell excitability presented. Sodium is a cation found in high concentration in extracellular fluids [ , ]. Hypernatremia is always associated with plasma hyperosmolarity and is usually caused by a water deficit (low intake or abnormal losses) or excessive sodium intake [ , ]. The patient’s hypernatremia observed from postoperative day 2 may be related to renal failure, elevated temperature and hyperventilation. Potassium is the main intracellular cation and it is critical in many physiological functions, such as in the regulation of neuromuscular excitability and muscle contraction [ , ]. Acid-base balance can affect the balance between cellular and extracellular potassium concentration.
