Given that the panel recommended against the intervention, issues related to feasibility, acceptability, and health equity were not discussed. Research needs Additional well-designed clinical trials with large sample sizes, conducted in real-life situations, could provide the needed robust evidence to determine whether the benefits of maintenance oral steroid therapy might outweigh its harms. In the meantime, the use of maintenance oral steroid therapy in COPD treatment could be considered by clinicians and well-informed patients, underscoring the need for shared decision-making. Question 6: In Patients with COPD Who Experience Advanced Refractory Dyspnea despite Otherwise Optimal Therapy, Is Opioid-based Therapy More Effective than and as Safe as No Additional Therapy? Recommendation In individuals with COPD who experience advanced refractory dyspnea despite otherwise optimal therapy, we suggest that opioid-based therapy be considered for dyspnea management within a personalized shared decision-making approach (conditional recommendation, very low certainty evidence). Critical outcomes Outcome prioritization by the panel resulted in ranking emergency department visits, dyspnea, exacerbations, health-related QOL, falls/accidents, overdose, and exercise capacity as critical outcomes. Summary of the evidence The expert medical librarian initially identified 576 citations in MEDLINE ( n = 267), Embase ( n = 193), and the Cochrane Library ( n = 116), with deduplication resulting in n = 370 warranting abstract screening. The majority (96.2%) were ineligible either because of a nonrigorous study methodology or lack of relevance to the PICO question, and this resulted in screeners identifying 14 studies for final review inclusion. All of the 14 identified studies were RCTs, and 13 of these studies used a crossover design ( – ). Each RCT had a relatively small sample size and the total sample size for the 14 studies was 366 participants. There were 184 participants in the treatment/intervention arms (opioid-based treatment) across the trials (50.2%) and 182 (49.7%) in the control (comparator) arms. The majority of the 14 studies were single-center studies. Exacerbations One study ( n = 30) assessed exacerbation risk ( ). The study revealed no significant difference in exacerbations between the opioid and nonopioid groups (RR, 1.38; 95% CI, 0.74–2.55; P = 0.31). There was low certainty in estimates of effect based on GRADE (absolute risk effect was 190 more exacerbations per 1,000 patients; 95% CI, 130 fewer to 775 more). Emergency department visits One study ( n = 30) assessed the risk of emergency department visits ( ). However, the small number of events and small sample size, as well as zero events in one arm, resulted in an excessively wide 95% CI, with unstable estimates of effect. The study revealed no significant difference in risk between the opioid and nonopioid groups (RR, 4.41; 95% CI, 0.23–84.79; P = 0.33). There was low certainty in estimates of effect based on GRADE (absolute risk effect was 125 more admissions per 1,000 patients; 95% CI, 66 fewer to 316 more per 1,000 patients). Falls/accidents One study ( n = 38) with a small sample size assessed the risk of falls/accidents ( ). The evidence from this study is very limited and underpowered. The study revealed no significant difference in risk of falls between the opioid and nonopioid groups (RR, 0.37; 95% CI, 0.02–8.51; P = 0.53). There was low certainty in estimates of effect based on GRADE (absolute risk effect was 32 fewer per 1,000 patients; 95% CI, 49 fewer to 376 more). Overdose One study ( n = 38) assessed the risk of overdose/oversedation ( ). The study revealed no significant difference in risk between the opioid and nonopioid groups (RR, 3.32; 95% CI, 0.14–76.6; P = 0.45). There was low certainty in estimates of effect based on GRADE (absolute risk effect was 56 more per 1,000 patients; 95% CI, 82 fewer overdoses per 1,000 patients to 193 more per 1,000 patients). Health-related QOL: assessed using a visual analog scale One study ( n = 40) assessed health-related QOL ( ). The study revealed a significant difference in the visual analog scale, with an increased score in the group that was randomized to opioids (MD = 1.50; 95% CI, 0.66–2.34; P = 0.03), indicating improved QOL. There was very low certainty in estimates of effect based on GRADE (absolute risk effect was 1.50 fewer; 95% CI, 2.34 more to 0.66 more fewer). Dyspnea: assessed using a variety of methods, including diary cards, visual analog scales, Medical Research Council scale, and Chronic Respiratory Disease Questionnaire dyspnea subscale Twelve studies ( n = 240) assessed dyspnea ( , , – , – ). The studies revealed a significant difference in dyspnea, favoring the group that received opioids (SMD = −0.60; 95% CI, −1.08 to

to opioids (MD = 1.50; 95% CI, 0.66–2.34; P = 0.03), indicating improved QOL. There was very low certainty in estimates of effect based on GRADE (absolute risk effect was 1.50 fewer; 95% CI, 2.34 more to 0.66 more fewer). Dyspnea: assessed using a variety of methods, including diary cards, visual analog scales, Medical Research Council scale, and Chronic Respiratory Disease Questionnaire dyspnea subscale Twelve studies ( n = 240) assessed dyspnea ( , , – , – ). The studies revealed a significant difference in dyspnea, favoring the group that received opioids (SMD = −0.60; 95% CI, −1.08 to −0.13; P = 0.01), and this exceeded the MCID threshold. There was low certainty in estimates of effect based on GRADE (absolute difference was 0.60 SDs lower; 95% CI, 1.08 lower to 0.13 lower). No subgroup differences were noted when systemic versus nebulized administration subgroups were analyzed ( P = 0.08). Exercise capacity Nine studies ( n = 103) assessed exercise capacity ( , , , – , ). The data were pooled across distance in meters, duration in minutes, and workload capacity in watts. The studies revealed no significant difference between the opioid and no-opioid groups (SMD = 0.14; 95% CI, −1.42 to 1.70; P = 0.86), and this did not reach the MCID threshold. There was moderate certainty in estimates of effect based on GRADE (absolute difference was 0.14 SDs higher; 95% CI, 1.42 lower to 1.70 higher). No subgroup differences were noted when systemic versus nebulized administration subgroups were analyzed ( P = 0.10). Summary Based on the eight critical outcomes and completion of the GRADE evidence table, the overall certainty of evidence was judged to be “very low” and this certainty was assigned to the final recommendation as per GRADE guidance. Committee discussion The panel noted that in patients with advanced refractory dyspnea, there was a statistically and clinically meaningful improvement in dyspnea with opioid treatment. The panel believed that a conditional recommendation in favor of opioid use was reasonable for dyspnea management given the accumulated evidence, and that well-informed patients might place a higher value on the improvement in dyspnea and less value on the uncertain harms of exacerbations, hospitalizations, falls, or overdoses. The panel believed that the observed benefit in dyspnea outweighed the uncertain risks. However, many of these studies were undertaken when there was a relative paucity of maintenance medications available to treat COPD, and the presumed effects of opioids might differ in today’s clinical context. Therefore, given the very low certainty of evidence, the use of opioids must be evaluated by clinicians and patients in a shared decision-making process. The panel debated the issues of feasibility, acceptability, and health equity, and felt confident that a trial of opioid therapy to determine if there was individual benefit could be implemented, would be acceptable to patients, and would pose limited (if any) health-equity challenges. A cost-effectiveness analysis was not performed, and the literature evidence was not fully examined in this regard. However, the panel also believed that opioid treatment would not be prohibitively expensive in terms of access to treatment. The burden of use for patients was also not deemed to be a factor that would preclude patients from taking opioids for advanced refractory dyspnea despite otherwise optimal COPD therapy if prescribed. After considering these issues, and armed with very low certainty evidence, the panel concluded that in individuals with COPD who experience advanced refractory dyspnea despite otherwise optimal therapy, the balance of benefits of opioid therapy may outweigh the risks when compared with no opioid use. The panel suggested that the use of opioid treatment in COPD should be carefully considered by both the clinician and the well-informed patient, underscoring the need for shared decision-making. Research needs Adequately powered, well-designed studies with larger sample sizes should be conducted in real-life situations, which could provide needed robust evidence. These studies could also allow for the inclusion of patients >80 years of age and those with multiple comorbidities in conjunction with opioid treatment. Conclusions In developing this guideline, we performed a rigorous, PICO-driven distillation of the scientific evidence to provide recommendations pertaining to key questions regarding the pharmacologic treatment of COPD. We hope that clinicians and researchers will find this guideline useful; however, it is important to apply these recommendations along with clinical assessments and shared decision-making to ensure that patients receive optimal clinical care. We also recognize that slowing the progression of disease and improving mortality are important goals of therapy; however, pharmacotherapy has not definitely been proven to affect these outcomes. Improvements in COPD mortality and disease progression have thus far only been achieved through smoking cessation. The panel recognizes that there are limitations to this clinical practice guideline. The recommendations were based on the available scientific evidence. In many cases, the available

and researchers will find this guideline useful; however, it is important to apply these recommendations along with clinical assessments and shared decision-making to ensure that patients receive optimal clinical care. We also recognize that slowing the progression of disease and improving mortality are important goals of therapy; however, pharmacotherapy has not definitely been proven to affect these outcomes. Improvements in COPD mortality and disease progression have thus far only been achieved through smoking cessation. The panel recognizes that there are limitations to this clinical practice guideline. The recommendations were based on the available scientific evidence. In many cases, the available clinical trials did not include certain COPD populations, such as patients over 80 years of age, those with chronic comorbid conditions, and those with COPD/asthma overlap. In addition, the available evidence did not risk stratify patients with exacerbations or those with eosinophilia. It is also important to note that the panel did not include patient representatives or family/caregiver representatives. Their participation might have been important in prioritizing clinical outcomes. Many questions remain regarding the optimal pharmacologic therapy for patients with varying risks of exacerbations and varying levels of eosinophilia, as well as potentially different responses to medication among current and former smokers. We hope that the research priorities outlined in this document will prompt new research to identify more specific patient profiles and enable personalized, patient-centered care. He has received grants from the National Institutes of Health and the Alpha-1 Foundation. 2016 6 6 2016 3 3 296962 668 682 4 2 2016 06 06 2016 28 08 2017 12 12 2020 JCOPDF © 2016 Background: The diagnosis and clinical management of adults with alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency (AATD) have been the subject of ongoing debate, ever since the publication of the first American Thoracic Society guideline statement in 1989. In 2003, the “American Thoracic Society (ATS)/European Respiratory Society (ERS) Statement: Standards for the Diagnosis and Management of Individuals with Alpha-1 Antitrypsin Deficiency” made a series of evidence-based recommendations, including a strong recommendation for broad-based diagnostic testing of all symptomatic adults with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD). Even so, AATD remains widely under-recognized. To update the 2003 systematic review and clinical guidance, the Alpha-1 Foundation sponsored a committee of experts to examine all relevant, recent literature in order to provide concise recommendations for the diagnosis and management of individuals with AATD. Purpose: To provide recommendations for: (1) the performance and interpretation of diagnostic testing for AATD, and (2) the current management of adults with AATD and its associated medical conditions. Methods: A systematic review addressing the most pressing questions asked by clinicians (clinician-centric) was performed to identify citations related to AATD that were published since the 2003 comprehensive review, specifically evaluating publications between January 2002 and December 2014. Important, more recent publications were solicited from the writing committee members as well. The combined comprehensive literature reviews of the 2003 document and this current review comprise the

management of individuals with AATD. Purpose: To provide recommendations for: (1) the performance and interpretation of diagnostic testing for AATD, and (2) the current management of adults with AATD and its associated medical conditions. Methods: A systematic review addressing the most pressing questions asked by clinicians (clinician-centric) was performed to identify citations related to AATD that were published since the 2003 comprehensive review, specifically evaluating publications between January 2002 and December 2014. Important, more recent publications were solicited from the writing committee members as well. The combined comprehensive literature reviews of the 2003 document and this current review comprise the evidence upon which the committee’s conclusions and recommendations are based. Results: Recommendations for the diagnosis and management of AATD were formulated by the committee. Conclusions: The major recommendations continue to endorse and reinforce the importance of testing for AATD in all adults with symptomatic fixed airflow obstruction, whether clinically labeled as COPD or asthma. Individuals with unexplained bronchiectasis or liver disease also should be tested. Family testing of first-degree relatives is currently the most efficient detection technique. In general, individuals with AATD and emphysema, bronchiectasis, and/or liver disease should be managed according to usual guidelines for these clinical conditions. documents.title: ATS clinical practice guideline diagnosis and detection of sarcoidosis

chunks.content: Search strategy and selection criteria References for this review were identified through searches of PubMed for articles published from January 1971 to May 2025, by use of the terms “sarcoidosis”, “bronchoscopic diagnosis”, “granulomas”, “airway involvement in sarcoidosis” and “endobronchial ultrasound”. Relevant articles published between 1918 and 1920 were identified through searches in the authors’ personal files, in Google Scholar and the Springer Online Archives Collection. Articles resulting from these searches and relevant references cited in those articles were reviewed. Introduction Sarcoidosis, first described by Jonathan Hutchinson in 1869 and later named by Caesar Boeck, is a complex multisystem granulomatous disorder of unknown aetiology [ ]. It affects individuals globally, with notable variability in prevalence, phenotype, radiographic presentation and prognosis across populations [ – ]. Pulmonary involvement occurs in over 90% of cases and is a leading contributor to both morbidity and mortality [ ]. Despite advances in imaging and clinical recognition, diagnosing sarcoidosis remains challenging, particularly in atypical presentations, extrapulmonary disease or advanced fibrotic stages [ , , ]. While characteristic clinical and radiologic features may suggest the diagnosis, histologic confirmation of noncaseating granulomas is often necessary to exclude alternative aetiologies and guide therapy [ – ]. Sarcoidosis is typically defined by non-necrotising granulomas; however, certain phenotypic variants, such as necrotising sarcoid granulomatosis, may exhibit a mixture of necrotising and non-necrotising granulomatous inflammation [ – ]. Bronchoscopy has transformed the diagnostic landscape by enabling minimally invasive access to the mediastinum, lung parenchyma and airways [ , ]. Over time, diagnostic yields have improved with the evolution from conventional transbronchial needle aspiration (c-TBNA) to convex probe endobronchial ultrasound (CP-EBUS) and transbronchial lung cryobiopsy (TBLC). More recent innovations, including mediastinal cryobiopsy endobronchial ultrasound (Cryo-EBUS), endobronchial ultrasound-guided intranodal forceps biopsy (EBUS-IFB), elastography and confocal laser endomicroscopy, offer additional diagnostic value, particularly in challenging or equivocal cases [ – ]. This review presents a structured, stage- and phenotype-based narrative on the bronchoscopic diagnosis of sarcoidosis. We integrate conventional and advanced modalities, highlight emerging tools and propose a practical diagnostic algorithm. Special emphasis is placed on stage 0 sarcoidosis, extrapulmonary presentations and bronchoscopic management of airway complications. Historical perspective The evolution of bronchoscopic techniques in sarcoidosis has mirrored the growing demand for safer, less invasive and more diagnostically precise tools ( ). In 1949, S chieppati [ ] published the first description of transbronchial needle aspiration (TBNA) in the Revista de la Asociación Médica Argentina , though his technique remained largely unrecognised in the English literature for over a decade [ ] . Performed via rigid bronchoscopy, Schieppati's approach enabled sampling of large subcarinal and paratracheal lymph nodes with a high diagnostic yield [ ]. Historically, mediastinoscopy was the gold standard for intrathoracic lymph node sampling. First introduced in 1954 by H arken et al. [ ] and refined by C arlens [ ] in 1959, mediastinoscopy offered direct access to key nodal stations [ ]. However, the requirement for general anaesthesia, procedural costs and a complication rate of 2–3% limited its broader applicability [ ]. The advent of flexible bronchoscopy in the 1970s revolutionised pulmonary diagnostics, enabling safer sampling of the airways and parenchyma through techniques such as transbronchial lung biopsy (TBLB), endobronchial biopsy (EBB) and c-TBNA [ ]. In the early 1980s, W ang et al . [ ] reintroduced TBNA using a flexible bronchoscope and needle. However, in the absence of real-time imaging, yield remained highly operator-dependent, particularly for mediastinal lymphadenopathy. The introduction of endobronchial ultrasound (EBUS) represented a major leap forward. Radial probe EBUS, pioneered by H erth, B ecker and E rnst [ , ] in the late 1990s, allowed indirect localisation of lymph nodes. This was soon eclipsed by the development of convex probe EBUS (CP-EBUS), by Y asufuku et al . [ ] in 2004, which enabled real-time transbronchial needle aspiration under ultrasound guidance (EBUS-TBNA) [ ]. EBUS-TBNA has since become the first-line procedure for evaluating stage I and II sarcoidosis [ , ]. Numerous meta-analyses and clinical studies confirm its superior sensitivity, safety and diagnostic accuracy compared to traditional approaches [ , , ]. This success has inspired the integration of transoesophageal ultrasound-guided fine-needle aspiration (EUS-FNA), echo-endoscope-guided FNA via the oesophagus (EUS-B-FNA) and hybrid approaches that combine EBUS and endoscopic ultrasound (EUS) in a single session [ , , ]. Recent innovations have further enhanced the diagnostic yield of bronchoscopy in sarcoidosis. These include TBLC, which offers high-quality parenchymal samples, and EBUS-IFB, which may improve histological architecture compared to needle aspiration [ , , ]. Bronchoalveolar lavage in sarcoidosis Bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL) remains a cornerstone adjunct in the evaluation of sarcoidosis, offering both diagnostic and prognostic insights. Performed most commonly in the right middle lobe or lingula using sequential aliquots of sterile saline, BAL facilitates assessment of immune cellularity, microbiology and soluble biomarkers [ – ]. Although not diagnostic in isolation, BAL provides a valuable immunologic “fingerprint” that complements histological confirmation and radiographic staging. The classical BAL pattern in sarcoidosis is lymphocytic alveolitis with a predominance of CD4 + T-helper cells, often reflected in an elevated CD4/CD8 ratio (>3.5) [ , , – ]. A markedly increased ratio, when integrated with compatible clinical and imaging features, strongly supports the diagnosis [ , ]. Nevertheless, the specificity of BAL is limited, as similar findings can overlap with hypersensitivity pneumonitis, chronic beryllium disease and other interstitial lung disorders [ , – ]. Thus, BAL is best viewed as a complementary tool rather than a diagnostic end-point. Beyond diagnostic support, BAL fluid (BALF) analysis provides important prognostic information [ – ]. Increased neutrophil percentages have been consistently linked to worse outcomes [ ]. Patients exhibit greater impairment in gas exchange, higher relapse rates and a greater likelihood of chronic or refractory disease [ , ]. D rent et al. [ ] demonstrated that elevated polymorphonuclear neutrophils were associated with the need for treatment escalation, poor corticosteroid responsiveness and, in some cases, progression to lung transplantation due to fibrotic remodelling. Z iegenhagen et al. [ ] similarly reported that higher neutrophil fractions predicted steroid requirements across both early and advanced radiographic stages. However, thresholds for defining “high” neutrophil counts vary between studies, ranging from absolute counts ( e.g. >0.2×10⁴ cells·mL −1 ) to relative percentages (>3%) [ , , , ]. Elevated eosinophil percentages have also been associated with more severe impairment in alveolar gas exchange, while increased natural killer cell proportions correlate with corticosteroid requirement, extrapulmonary involvement and progression to fibrotic stage IV disease [ , , ]. More recently, higher frequencies of circulating CD14 hi CD16 hi monocytes at diagnosis have been linked with chronic progressive disease, further emphasising the systemic immunologic derangements reflected in BALF profiles [ , ]. Ongoing work continues to refine BAL's role in sarcoidosis. Expansion of specific T-cell subsets such as CD4 + Vα2.3 + T-cells in HLA-DRB1*03-positive patients has shown potential as a biomarker for Löfgren's syndrome [ , ]. Similarly, multi-parameter immunophenotyping may allow BAL to serve as both a window into disease pathogenesis and a predictor of treatment trajectories. Unfortunately, most available studies include relatively small numbers of patients with advanced fibrotic sarcoidosis and the role of BAL neutrophilia in fibrotic progression remains incompletely defined. Conventional bronchoscopic techniques in sarcoidosis Endobronchial biopsy (EBB) EBB is a low-risk technique that samples bronchial mucosa and submucosal tissue. Its diagnostic yield is highly dependent on visible airway abnormalities ( ). When endobronchial lesions such as cobblestoning, erythema or nodularity are present, reported yields range from 54% to over 90%. By contrast, in patients with normal-appearing airways, yield typically falls to 30–40% [ , ]. Standard practice recommends obtaining at least three biopsies from the main or lobar carinas, or from visible endobronchial lesions, to maximise sensitivity [ ]. Narrow-band imaging (NBI) may help visualise endobronchial abnormalities, but data are inconsistent: a small randomised controlled trial (RCT) found no improvement in granuloma yield over white-light bronchoscopy and a prospective series showed only a nonsignificant trend toward better lesion detection; contemporary reports emphasise that NBI's role in sarcoidosis remains to be defined [ – ]. Although EBB rarely provides a standalone diagnosis, it remains a valuable adjunct, significantly enhancing yield when combined with TBLB or EBUS-TBNA. Importantly, EBB carries a low complication risk, with bleeding and airway injury being uncommon [ ]. Conventional transbronchial needle aspiration (c-TBNA) c-TBNA, first introduced in the 1970s, represented a milestone in minimally invasive mediastinal sampling [ ]. Using rigid or flexible bronchoscopy, it enabled access to hilar and mediastinal lymph nodes without surgical mediastinoscopy. However, its lack of real-time imaging contributes to wide variability in reported diagnostic performance. Yields range from 6% to 90%, with the highest success seen in stage I sarcoidosis and in patients with large nodal targets [ , – ]. Diagnostic performance depends heavily on operator expertise, nodal station and underlying pathology [ – ]. While meta-analyses have reported sensitivities ranging from 14% to 100%, specificity remains consistently high and false-positive results are exceedingly rare [ , ]. Combining c-TBNA with TBLB or EBB can raise diagnostic yield to 70–90%, but at the expense of longer procedure times and higher complication risk [ – ] In high-resource settings, c-TBNA has been largely replaced by EBUS-TBNA, which provides real-time ultrasound guidance and higher operator confidence. Nevertheless, in resource-limited environments, c-TBNA continues to play an important role due to its low cost and accessibility. Transbronchial lung biopsy (TBLB) TBLB is a cornerstone technique for the histologic confirmation of sarcoidosis, particularly in patients with parenchymal disease (radiographic stages II and III). Diagnostic yield is stage-dependent, ranging from 60–66% in stage I to 80–83% in stages II and III [ , ]. More recent series report yields of ∼62% for TBLB alone, with the addition of EBB contributing an incremental ∼20% and multimodal approaches (EBUS-TBNA+TBLB+EBB) achieving diagnostic yields approaching 90% [ ]. These findings underscore the complementary value of combining parenchymal, mucosal and nodal sampling to optimise diagnostic performance [ , – ]. To maximise yield, at least four forceps specimens are recommended irrespective of radiographic stage [ ]. Limitations of TBLB include the small sample size and susceptibility to crush artefact, which may obscure non-necrotising granulomatous and complicate histopathological interpretation. Complication rates are relatively low, with bleeding reported in 2–5% and pneumothorax in 1–10%, though risks vary with operator skill and patient characteristics [ ]. Despite advances in EBUS-guided and cryobiopsy techniques, TBLB continues to hold a central role in sarcoidosis diagnosis worldwide, particularly in centres where access to TBLC is limited. Current guidelines and reviews consistently affirm its utility as a safe, accessible and effective technique when applied within a multimodal bronchoscopic strategy [ , ]. Endosonographic imaging techniques for sampling guidance The introduction of CP-EBUS in the early 1990s pioneered less-invasive approaches to mediastinal lymph node evaluation [ , ]. Over the past two decades, the ability to sample intrathoracic lymph nodes under real-time ultrasound guidance, either through the airways or through the oesophagus, has transformed the diagnostic approach to sarcoidosis [ ]. CP-EBUS is performed with a flexible bronchoscope that incorporates an ultrasound transducer at its tip, allowing simultaneous direct visualisation of the airway and ultrasound imaging of adjacent mediastinal and hilar nodes [ ]. Cross-sectional images guide sampling and a balloon filled with saline at the probe tip improves acoustic coupling with the airway wall [ ]. EUS, performed by passing a flexible echoendoscope into the oesophagus or stomach, offers a wider scanning angle (up to 360° versus 60° with EBUS), higher resolution imaging and improved manoeuvrability for accessing small anatomical structures [ , ]. Transoesophageal EBUS (EUS-B), using a CP-EBUS bronchoscope via the oesophagus, extends access to mediastinal and even subdiaphragmatic structures and can be performed by pulmonologists trained in EBUS [ ]. Together, EBUS and EUS-B provide complementary windows into mediastinal sampling, with combined use in a single session significantly increasing diagnostic yield while reducing the need for surgical mediastinoscopy [ , ]. Endobronchial ultrasound-guided transbronchial needle aspiration (EBUS-TBNA) In 2020, the American Thoracic Society (ATS) published long-awaited guidelines on the diagnosis of sarcoidosis. EBUS-TBNA is now regarded as the preferred first-line technique for sampling mediastinal and hilar lymphadenopathy in suspected sarcoidosis [ , ]. It provides real-time access to nodal stations including 2R/L, 4R/L, 7, 10 and 11, and can be performed under moderate sedation or general anaesthesia with comparable outcomes [ , ]. A meta-analysis by T risolini et al . [ ] reported a diagnostic yield of 79% for sarcoidosis, with sensitivity rising to 84% in high-volume centres, underscoring the influence of expertise. Despite these strengths, EBUS-TBNA fails to establish a diagnosis in 20–40% of cases, particularly in stage III disease [ , ]. In such scenarios, complementary approaches such as TBLC, Cryo-EBUS, TBLB or EBUS-IFB may be considered [ ]. Technical refinements Efforts to optimise EBUS-TBNA have focused on needle design, sampling technique and cytologic support [ ]. Early studies showed no difference between 21G and 22G needles, but pooled analyses suggest 19G needles may improve sensitivity (up to 93.7% versus 84%) and preserve better tissue architecture [ , , ]. Technical refinements Efforts to optimise EBUS-TBNA have focused on needle design, sampling technique and cytologic support [ ]. Early studies showed no difference between 21G and 22G needles, but pooled analyses suggest 19G needles may improve sensitivity (up to 93.7% versus 84%) and preserve better tissue architecture [ , , ]. Newer designs, such as 22G side-cutting needles, have not improved performance in benign disease, whereas Franseen (crown-cut) needles appear to improve sample quality without increasing diagnostic accuracy [ , ]. Adjunctive technical modifications have yielded mixed results. A 2012 RCT found no improvement in sample quality, diagnostic yield, or accuracy with the use of suction during EBUS-TBNA [ ], a finding later confirmed in subsequent studies for both rapid on-site and final pathological assessment [ , ]. More recently, however, an RCT suggested that suction may enhance the diagnostic yield of cell blocks, though it does not improve cytology smears [ ]. Omitting the stylet during EBUS-TBNA does not compromise diagnostic accuracy and simplifies the procedure [ , ]. Similarly, increasing needle passes beyond 10 revolutions has no impact in benign conditions, although more passes can benefit molecular testing in malignancy [ , ]. ROSE, node features and passes Rapid on-site evaluation (ROSE) provides immediate cytologic feedback on sample adequacy and facilitates ancillary testing, but its impact on sarcoidosis diagnosis with EBUS-TBNA remains uncertain [ – ]. Multiple trials and meta-analyses confirm that it does not significantly improve sarcoidosis yield (86.0% versus 83.7% without, p=0.43) [ , , – ]. Nevertheless, it reduces the number of passes, shortens procedure time, lowers complication rates and minimises the need for repeat bronchoscopy, making it an operationally valuable adjunct [ ]. The influence of lymph node size and location is less clear. Sarcoidosis typically involves bilateral hilar and right paratracheal lymphadenopathy (“lambda sign”) [ ]. While older studies suggested that nodes ≥20 mm yield more tissue, the relationship between node size or station and EBUS-TBNA accuracy remains ambiguous [ ]. A 2025 multicentre analysis confirmed comparable diagnostic yields between hilar and mediastinal nodes (61.8% versus 65.5%, p=0.46) [ ]. Radiological features, such as symmetric bilateral hilar adenopathy, homogeneous nodes <27.5 mm and attenuation >48 Hounsfield units, favour sarcoidosis, while necrosis, low density and parenchymal consolidation suggest alternative diagnoses [ ]. An EBUS imaging study also found that lymph nodes exhibiting a granular (“sandpaper”) appearance with distinct margins had 99.3% specificity for sarcoidosis [ ]. As for the number of passes, most data support three to four aspirations per lymph node station, beyond which diagnostic yield plateaus [ , – ]. In the absence of ROSE, a higher number of passes may increase sensitivity, as illustrated by S un et al . [ ] (mean 7.2 passes·patient –1 ), though this comes at the expense of longer procedure time and potential complications. When ROSE is available, fewer passes are typically required, as sampling can be terminated once diagnostic material is confirmed [ ]. Safety profile Large registries and nationwide surveys consistently demonstrate that EBUS-TBNA is a highly safe procedure, with overall complication rates of approximately 1.2–1.4% [ , ]. The most common event is bleeding, requiring intervention in only 0.2% of cases [ , ]. The AQuIRE registry reported a rate of 1.44%, with pneumothorax in 0.53% of cases; risks were higher in patients over 70, inpatients, those undergoing concurrent transbronchial biopsy or procedures performed under deep sedation [ ]. Similarly, a Japanese survey of 7345 procedures found a complication rate of 1.23%, including haemorrhage (0.68%), infection (0.19%) and device damage (bronchoscope 1.33%, needle 0.2%) [ ]. Subsequent analyses corroborate these findings, reporting pneumothorax in ∼0.5%, mediastinal infection (0.1%), pneumonia (0.2%) and rare events such as acute respiratory failure (0.3%) or delayed fatal bleeding [ , – ]. Emerging and adjunctive techniques Building on TBNA, several newer modalities have been developed to address nondiagnostic cases or the need for larger histological samples. EBUS-IFB uses microforceps passed through a TBNA tract, yielding larger tissue cores and achieving 87–93% yield for sarcoidosis, with minor bleeding as the most common complication [ ]. Cryo-EBUS adapts cryotechnology to lymph nodes, producing larger, better-preserved core biopsies and early reports of up to 90% yield in sarcoidosis and lymphoma [ ]. Ultrathin bronchoscopy may also contribute in select patients without central airway findings. Transbronchial lung cryobiopsy (TBLC) Originally developed for neurosurgery in the 1960s, cryotherapy was later adopted in pulmonary medicine for tumour debulking [ ]. The introduction of flexible cryoprobes in the early 2000s enabled lung parenchymal sampling and led to formal descriptions of TBLC in 2009 [ ]. TBLC is typically performed under general anaesthesia. A flexible cryoprobe is introduced through the working channel and positioned under fluoroscopic guidance. The probe is then cooled to −121°F with nitrogen oxide for 5–6 s (3–4 s if sarcoidosis is suspected), followed by en bloc removal of the probe and bronchoscope to preserve tissue integrity. A Fogarty balloon is typically inflated post-biopsy to tamponade bleeding during reinsertion of the bronchoscope [ , , ]. Compared to conventional forceps biopsy, TBLC yields larger, better-preserved samples with fewer crush artefacts, improving histologic assessment in ILD, including sarcoidosis [ , , ]. In a study of 288 ILD patients, including 11 with nonfibrotic sarcoidosis, C hen et al . [ ] reported that three cryobiopsy samples were adequate for diagnosis. A ragaki- N akahodo et al . [ ] demonstrated equivalent sensitivity for TBLC and EBUS-TBNA (67%) in sarcoidosis, which reached 100% when both were combined. Notably, TBLC outperformed EBUS-TBNA in a subgroup of patients with parenchymal abnormalities (67% versus 11%). While TBLC shows promise, it is associated with higher complication rates than TBLB, including bleeding in up to 15% and pneumothorax in up to 11% of cases. The procedure also requires substantial expertise, with operator proficiency typically developing after approximately 70 cases [ , ]. Some experts argue against routine use in sarcoidosis, citing the already high diagnostic yield when EBB, TBLB and EBUS-TBNA are combined [ ]. A 2024 meta-review reaffirmed the diagnostic superiority of TBLC across ILDs. Despite superior tissue quality, TBLC lacks standardised protocols and robust sarcoidosis-specific data [ ]. In paediatric ILD, a recent systematic review showed a yield of 91.8% with a 6.5% major complication rate, suggesting the technique's potential across age groups when performed in experienced centres [ ]. Although evidence for TBLC in sarcoidosis remains limited, it may serve as a bridge between conventional bronchoscopy and surgical biopsy in select cases. Endobronchial ultrasound-guided intranodal forceps biopsy (EBUS-IFB) EBUS-IFB, or microforceps biopsy, enhances intranodal sampling by introducing biopsy forceps through a needle tract created during EBUS-TBNA to facilitate the insertion of small biopsy forceps in the lymph node ( ). This technique allows for extraction of larger core samples with improved tissue architecture, which is particularly helpful when cytology is nondiagnostic [ ]. A key element in the successful implementation of EBUS-IFB is the creation of a bronchial tunnel, which enables smooth entry of the biopsy forceps into the lymph node lesion. Some studies have incorporated a “hot tunnelling” approach, which has been shown to offer slight advantages in diagnostic yield, though no statistically significant differences were observed [ , ]. The size of the biopsy forceps used plays a crucial role in the ease of insertion and the adequacy of the tissue sample. Small forceps (0.8 mm) may more easily navigate the bronchial wall but tend to obtain smaller samples. Larger forceps (1.9 mm) provide larger tissue specimens, which may improve diagnostic accuracy but are more difficult to pass the bronchoscope's working channel [ , , ]. N akai et al . [ ] found that specimens obtained using 1.9 mm forceps were three times larger than those from 0.96 mm forceps, although both provided similar diagnostic yields for advanced lung cancer. Reported diagnostic yields for sarcoidosis range from 87% to 93% [ , ]. When combined with EBUS-TBNA, overall yield approaches 95% [ ]. The procedure is generally safe, with minor bleeding and rare complications such as mediastinal emphysema or arrhythmias [ , ]. Limitations include difficulty in tunnelling through thick bronchial walls and variability in tissue acquisition depending on forceps size and bronchoscopic channel diameter [ ]. While promising, EBUS-IFB is best reserved for cases where EBUS-TBNA is inconclusive and sufficient technical expertise is available. Larger, multicentre, prospective studies are necessary to establish clearer guidelines on the optimal forceps size, tunnelling technique and procedural standardisation to maximise diagnostic accuracy and minimise complications. EBUS-IFB based on transbronchial laser photoablation (EBUS-IFB-TLP) To overcome the mechanical limitations of tract creation, a novel refinement, EBUS-guided intranodal forceps biopsy via transbronchial laser photoablation (EBUS-IFB-TLP) has recently been introduced. In this approach, a diode laser fibre is used to create a precise tract into the node, facilitating forceps entry with reduced trauma to surrounding tissue. In a single-centre, prospective self-controlled study of 67 patients with mediastinal lymphadenopathy, sarcoidosis was diagnosed in 96.4% of cases using EBUS-IFB-TLP compared with 71.4% using standard TBNA (p=0.016). Overall diagnostic rates were 97.4% versus 78.9% (p=0.039), respectively. Although the laser-assisted approach was associated with a higher rate of moderate bleeding (23.9% versus 14.9%, p=0.109), no serious complications were reported [ ]. These developments signal a shift toward more architecturally informative biopsy techniques in patients with inconclusive TBNA results. EBUS-transbronchial mediastinal cryobiopsy (EBUS-TMC or Cryo-EBUS) Cryo-EBUS, or EBUS-transbronchial mediastinal cryobiopsy (EBUS-TMC), is an emerging alternative to EBUS-TBNA, obtaining larger, architecturally preserved tissue cores with fewer crush artefacts, particularly relevant for granulomatous diseases such as sarcoidosis and for lymphoproliferative disorders [ ]. EBUS-TMC can be performed either as a standalone sampling technique or in conjunction with EBUS-TBNA. When used as a standalone approach, access to the lymph node is created using a high-frequency knife or laser [ – ]. In the complementary setting, the cryoprobe is advanced into the node through the puncture tract established by the aspiration needle. Both 1.1-mm and 1.7-mm cryoprobes are commonly employed, with activation times typically ranging from 3 to 7 s [ – ]. The rapid freezing process causes the tissue to adhere firmly to the probe, permitting en bloc retrieval of the specimen together with the bronchoscope. A 2024 systematic review of 20 studies reported that Cryo-EBUS provided superior diagnostic yield and tissue adequacy compared with TBNA across sarcoidosis, lymphoma and tuberculosis, while maintaining a favourable safety profile [ ]. In a review of 555 patients, sample adequacy for molecular and immunophenotypic analysis improved to 97% versus 79% [ , ]. Large observational cohorts confirm that Cryo-EBUS consistently delivers more diagnostic tissue than TBNA [ – ]. Even in patients unable to undergo bronchoscopy, EUS-B-guided transoesophageal cryobiopsy has been performed safely, yielding high-quality core samples [ ]. Safety data are reassuring. In a 271-patient RCT, combining Cryo-EBUS with TBNA increased diagnostic yield (93% versus 81%) without higher complication rates [ ]. Minor bleeding is the most common event, reported in up to 85% of cases, justifying the use of a secure airway during the procedure [ , , , ]. Collectively, these data position Cryo-EBUS as a promising complement and, in some settings, a potential successor to TBNA, particularly when core tissue is required for diagnoses of sarcoidosis. Ultrathin bronchoscopy-guided small airway biopsy (UTB-SAB) Ultrathin bronchoscopy (UTB) enables direct visualisation and biopsy of small peripheral airways that may harbour granulomas [ ]. Small airway abnormalities are frequently observed in sarcoidosis. However, their visualisation and biopsy present technical challenges due to the small calibre, collapsibility of the bronchiolar lumen and limitations in image resolution. Small airway biopsy (SAB) is performed using 1.5 mm forceps under direct visualisation of subsegmental airways. In a prospective study of 79 patients with suspected sarcoidosis, bronchoscopies under general anaesthesia included systematic inspection of large and small airways with endobronchial and ultrathin bronchoscopes, six targeted or random biopsies of abnormal mucosa and EBUS-TBNA of hilar/mediastinal lymph nodes. All specimens were reviewed by blinded pulmonary pathologists with parallel microbiological testing to exclude infection. The final diagnosis of sarcoidosis was assigned by a multidisciplinary team based on clinical, radiological, microbiological and pathological findings; non-necrotising granulomas in at least one organ were required and if bronchoscopic samples were nondiagnostic, confirmation relied on surgical biopsy or clinical–radiological reassessment after 6 months. Small airway abnormalities were observed in 58% of those with parenchymal disease, compared to 23% of those with isolated lymphadenopathy [ ]. UTB-SAB yielded granulomas in 65% of patients with airway abnormalities versus 23% without [ ]. Further studies comparing UTB-SAB to conventional TBLB regarding diagnostic yield and safety are needed to better define its role in the bronchoscopic diagnosis of sarcoidosis. Imaging enhancements Adjunct imaging technologies are under investigation. Elastography is an ultrasound-based technique that assesses nodal stiffness, differentiating malignant (stiff) from benign or inflammatory (softer) nodes. Its value in sarcoidosis remains limited, as stiffness overlaps with other granulomatous diseases. A colour scale helps guide sampling by highlighting softer versus firmer regions, which can improve biopsy accuracy by avoiding necrotic areas or targeting the most representative tissue [ ]. Initial studies demonstrated excellent discriminative performance between benign and malignant nodes, with sensitivity and specificity of approximately 93% and 85%, respectively [ , ]. However, its application in sarcoidosis remains limited. Specifically, elastographic stiffness patterns have shown poor discriminatory ability in differentiating sarcoidosis from other granulomatous diseases such as tuberculosis [ ]. More recent evidence suggests some potential utility: granulomatous nodes (including sarcoidosis) tend to display lower elastography scores (type I and II), in contrast to malignant nodes which exhibit higher stiffness (type III) [ ]. These findings indicate potential, but still preliminary applications in sarcoidosis. Needle-based confocal laser endomicroscopy (nCLE) nCLE is a cutting-edge technique that enables cellular-level, real-time imaging at the needle tip during biopsy. In a multicentre trial involving patients with suspected sarcoidosis, distinctive granuloma patterns, homogeneous, well-demarcated, brighter-toned areas were identified. Trained observers distinguished granulomatous from malignant lymph node images with 88% accuracy, demonstrating substantial inter- and intra-observer reliability (κ≈0.63–0.70) [ ]. Importantly, nCLE facilitated immediate confirmation of granuloma presence and sampling adequacy during EBUS-TBNA, potentially reducing the need for repeat procedures [ , ]. Although nCLE is currently investigational, its safety, feasibility and diagnostic alignment with histologic findings make it a promising future tool, particularly in cases where tissue adequacy or rapid bedside interpretation is critical. Both EBUS elastography and nCLE represent promising imaging adjuncts for the bronchoscopic diagnosis of sarcoidosis. While elastography aids in lymph node characterisation, its role in granulomatous disease remains modest and nonspecific. In contrast, nCLE offers real-time, in situ granuloma visualisation and holds promise for enhancing procedural efficiency and diagnostic confidence. Given their current investigational status, routine incorporation into sarcoidosis evaluation awaits further validation and standardisation across centres. Bronchoscopic management of airway stenosis in sarcoidosis Symptomatic bronchial stenosis is an under-recognised manifestation of pulmonary sarcoidosis, reported in up to 8% of affected patients and contributing significantly to morbidity [ , ]. It frequently mimics asthma or chronic bronchitis, leading to diagnostic delay, especially in women and individuals of African descent, who appear disproportionately affected [ , ]. Airway stenosis in sarcoidosis arises either from granulomatous infiltration of the bronchial wall or from extrinsic compression by enlarged mediastinal or hilar lymph nodes [ ]. The right middle lobe is particularly susceptible because of its narrow orifice, sharp takeoff from the bronchus intermedius and the density of adjacent lymph nodes. Three principal patterns of airway involvement have been described, including isolated stenosis, multifocal lesions and diffuse narrowing, with the multifocal form being the most common [ ]. Bronchoscopy plays a pivotal role in both diagnosis and management. Visual inspection may reveal characteristic findings including cobblestone mucosa, endobronchial nodularity or concentric airway narrowing. The latter often reflects a progression from granulomatous inflammation to transmural fibrosis, a transition where systemic immunosuppression alone is rarely sufficient. At this stage, a tailored bronchoscopic strategy becomes essential. The cornerstone of intervention for fibrotic stenosis is mechanical dilation, via balloon bronchoplasty or rigid bronchoscopy [ , , ]. Balloon dilation is most effective in short, fixed stenoses and offers immediate symptom relief. However, the effect is often transient, with high rates of restenosis necessitating repeat procedures [ , ]. Rigid bronchoscopy enables more forceful dilation and is preferred for complex, longer-segment or central airway lesions. Importantly, it also permits simultaneous use of adjunctive tools, including lasers or stents [ , ]. Adjunctive therapies aim to prolong the benefits of dilation. Intralesional corticosteroid injections, most commonly triamcinolone, are often used post-dilation to mitigate local inflammation and reduce restenosis [ , , , ]. Importantly, it also permits simultaneous use of adjunctive tools, including lasers or stents [ , ]. Adjunctive therapies aim to prolong the benefits of dilation. Intralesional corticosteroid injections, most commonly triamcinolone, are often used post-dilation to mitigate local inflammation and reduce restenosis [ , , , ]. While widely practiced, the supporting evidence in sarcoidosis is limited to case series and extrapolation from other diseases such as granulomatosis with polyangiitis may not be valid due to differing pathophysiology. For stenoses dominated by mucosal granulation or web-like fibrosis, thermal modalities such as laser ablation and electrosurgery may be employed to restore luminal patency. These tools are particularly useful when mechanical dilation alone is inadequate [ ]. Cryotherapy offers a nonthermal alternative, inducing cell death via freeze–thaw cycles. Though its onset is delayed compared to thermal modalities, cryotherapy may be advantageous in friable or inflamed mucosa [ ]. A novel evolution is spray cryotherapy, which delivers liquid nitrogen in a non-contact, circumferential fashion [ – ]. Preliminary studies in benign airway stenosis, including post-intubation and post-transplant settings, suggest it may preserve mucosal architecture, delay restenosis and reduce procedural trauma [ – ]. When fibrotic remodelling leads to recurrent or refractory stenosis, airway stenting becomes necessary. Silicone stents are favoured for their removability and lower granulation risk compared to metallic options, but complications such as migration and mucus plugging are common. Stents are generally reserved for anatomically challenging or recurrent strictures unresponsive to other modalities [ ]. Long-term management of sarcoid-related airway stenosis requires close collaboration across specialties. Interventional pulmonologists, otolaryngologists, thoracic surgeons and sarcoidologists must coordinate therapy to balance procedural efficacy with systemic disease control. Selection of treatment modality is influenced by stenosis type (inflammatory versus fibrotic), airway location, patient comorbidities and centre expertise. A tailored, multimodal approach, incorporating both dilatory and ablative tools, is often required for durable symptom control. Stage-based diagnostic approach Accurate histologic confirmation of sarcoidosis is best achieved through a stage-adapted bronchoscopic strategy that maximises yield while minimising risk. The 2020 ATS/European Respiratory Society/World Association of Sarcoidosis and Other Granulomatous Disorders (WASOG) guideline [ , ] emphasises flexibility over rigid algorithms, encouraging diagnostic plans tailored to radiographic stage, clinical context and institutional expertise. In all those stages, it is paramount to exclude infectious, fungal, other granulomatous, malignancy and rheumatological diseases. Stage 0 (normal thoracic imaging) Patients with systemic features or extrapulmonary sarcoidosis but normal thoracic imaging represents the greatest diagnostic challenge. Some centres perform BAL, EBUS-TBNA, EBB and transbronchial biopsies despite a normal computed tomography (CT) scan result, though robust data are sparse [ , , ]. A small case series evaluating patients with suspected extrapulmonary sarcoidosis demonstrated that even when thoracic lymph nodes measured <10 mm on CT and in some instances appeared radiographically normal, EBUS-TBNA was suggestive of sarcoidosis in approximately 40% of cases [ ]. This finding underscores that radiographic “stage 0” disease does not exclude mediastinal involvement. However, given the limited sample size of the available data, larger studies are needed to confirm these diagnostic yields and to better define the role of EBUS-TBNA in this subgroup. UTB-SAB has demonstrated granulomas in ∼30% of patients with normal imaging and ∼65% when subtle small-airway abnormalities are present. In this setting, the authors advocate multidisciplinary discussion before proceeding, reserving invasive sampling for cases where histology will alter management. Stage I (isolated bilateral hilar/mediastinal lymphadenopathy) Endosonography is the diagnostic mainstay. EBUS-TBNA provides a pooled sensitivity of ∼84% across 21 studies, rising to ∼87% in high-volume centres. The GRANULOMA trial showed EUS-FNA achieves 88.6% yield, particularly useful in patients with difficult airways or sedation intolerance. Combining EBUS and EUS (or using EUS-B) consistently exceeds 90% yield with <1% complication rates. When TBNA is inconclusive, EBUS-guided IFB and Cryo-EBUS provide larger, architecturally preserved specimens, with early prospective studies reporting yields of 87–93% for sarcoidosis. These techniques remain adjunctive but are increasingly valuable in cases where cytology alone is insufficient ( ). Stage II (lymphadenopathy with parenchymal infiltrates) A multimodal bronchoscopic approach is recommended. In a prospective study of 151 patients, the combination of EBUS-TBNA, TBLB, EBB and BAL achieved an 88% diagnostic yield without major complications. In patients with typical pulmonary infiltrates, however, such as upper-lobe-predominant perilymphatic nodules, non-necrotising granulomas on EBUS-TBNA may be sufficient for the diagnosis. While not required in every case, TBLC can be considered when conventional techniques are nondiagnostic, particularly because it provides larger samples with preserved histology. Procedural risks, including pneumothorax (∼10%) and significant bleeding (∼5%), necessitate careful patient selection. Stage III (parenchymal infiltrates without adenopathy) Here, nodal sampling may not be feasible and diagnostic yield depends on parenchymal

a prospective study of 151 patients, the combination of EBUS-TBNA, TBLB, EBB and BAL achieved an 88% diagnostic yield without major complications. In patients with typical pulmonary infiltrates, however, such as upper-lobe-predominant perilymphatic nodules, non-necrotising granulomas on EBUS-TBNA may be sufficient for the diagnosis. While not required in every case, TBLC can be considered when conventional techniques are nondiagnostic, particularly because it provides larger samples with preserved histology. Procedural risks, including pneumothorax (∼10%) and significant bleeding (∼5%), necessitate careful patient selection. Stage III (parenchymal infiltrates without adenopathy) Here, nodal sampling may not be feasible and diagnostic yield depends on parenchymal tissue acquisition. Conventional TBLB provides ∼70% sensitivity, but TBLC increases yield to ∼89%, with superior tissue architecture that aids differentiation from other fibrosing interstitial pneumonias. TBLC is therefore increasingly favoured in some centres for this stage, provided adequate safeguards against pneumothorax and bleeding are in place. Stage IV (advanced fibrosis) Dense scarring and granuloma paucity reduce the utility of conventional bronchoscopic approaches. In many cases, a biopsy may not be needed due to the classic radiographic appearance and the low likelihood that a biopsy will change management. In cases where a biopsy is deemed indicated, TBLC remains a reasonable option, with yields around 58%, and can obviate surgical biopsy in more than half of patients. Where uncertainty persists and histology will meaningfully influence management, video-assisted thoracoscopic surgery remains the ultimate diagnostic recourse. The role of Cryo-EBUS or IFB is limited at this stage. Practical considerations In resource-limited environments, conventional bronchoscopy with BAL, TBLB and EBB remains the foundation of diagnosis. Where advanced tools such as Cryo-EBUS, IFB and TBLC are available, their use should be guided by stage and clinical context, not routine. Ultimately, the diagnostic pathway must be shaped by multidisciplinary consensus, balancing diagnostic yield, patient safety and institutional capability. Conclusion Bronchoscopy remains indispensable in sarcoidosis diagnosis, significantly enriched by recent technological advancements. A structured, stage-based diagnostic strategy, employing advanced modalities such as EBUS-TBNA, TBLC and Cryo-EBUS, as well as emerging techniques such as elastography, optimises diagnosis accuracy. Continued innovation, clinical training and procedural standardisation will further enhance diagnostic yield and patient outcomes. Points for clinical practice A step-wise, stage-specific strategy maximises yield while minimising morbidity. Endosonography dominates stage I and mixed nodal–parenchymal stage II disease. Cryobiopsy meaningfully improves diagnostic success in parenchymal-predominant (stage III/IV) presentations, albeit with higher procedure-specific risks. Even in patients with apparently “normal” chest imaging (stage 0), targeted small-airway or nodal sampling can establish the diagnosis in roughly one-third of patients.

chunks.content: Introduction Sarcoidosis is a chronic disease characterized by the formation of non-caseating granulomas in intrathoracic and/or extrathoracic organs ( , ). The prevalence and incidence of sarcoidosis both peak between ages 20 to 39 and are 4.6 to 64 per 100,00 people and 1.0 to 40 per 100,000 people per year, respectively. After idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis, it is the second most common interstitial lung disease ( ). In the United States, prevalence is higher among females than males as well as African American relative to Caucasian subjects. Sarcoidosis represents a multifactorial response to an unidentified, inhaled exposure with environmental, host immunologic, and genetic elements interacting to impact disease development ( ). It is an immunologically mediated disorder with pathogenesis requiring an exposure to an antigen which, with persistence, is presented to T lymphocytes (CD4+). There is upregulation of the immune response, activation of alveolar macrophages/dendritic cells, and sensitization culminating in granulomatous inflammation. Subsequently, direct exposure to an environmental agent with systemic distribution leads to multiorgan granuloma formation. Genetic factors participate in susceptibility ( , ). The specific mechanistic pathways that determine the induction, maintenance, and resolution of this systemic granulomatous inflammation remain poorly understood. Individuals experience disease remission within the first few years but over 30–50 % develop some form of a chronic disease requiring treatment to prevent progressive organ dysfunction and fibrosis. The major portal of entry for any etiologic agent of sarcoidosis is assumed to be the respiratory tract. Subsequently, the involvement of the lungs (~90%) and intrathoracic lymph nodes is greatest ( ). A significant proportion of individuals with sarcoidosis (~40 to 60%) are asymptomatic but the chest radiograph is abnormal in most patients (over 90%). The peripheral lymph nodes and liver are also commonly involved ( ). Other tissues which contact the external environment (e.g., eyes and skin) can also demonstrate increased involvement but virtually every organ in the body (e.g. liver, spleen, and heart) can be impacted ( ). The diagnosis of sarcoidosis, provided by the American Thoracic Society in 2020, is based on fulfilling several criteria: 1) a compatible clinical presentation, 2) the finding of non-necrotizing granulomatous inflammation in one or more tissue samples, and 3) the exclusion of alternative causes of granulomatous disease ( ). The last criterion requires that sarcoidosis be idiopathic ( , , ). Accordingly, sarcoidosis is not diagnosed if a specific etiology can be identified. After assigning causation to such an exposure, a descriptor (“sarcoidosis-like disease”, “sarcoid-like granulomatosis”, or “sarcoid-like granulomatous lung disease”) is frequently applied ( ). This assessment that sarcoidosis has no known cause has been challenged by numerous case reports, case series, and epidemiologic studies supporting associations of this disease with both occupations which include particle exposures and specific particles ( , ). We review the literature supporting particles in the pathogenesis of sarcoidosis. Methods A systematic review of the literature was performed using PubMed/MEDLINE, Web of Science, and TOXNET. All available years were included. Case reports, case series, epidemiological studies, editorials, reviews, and letters with a focus on pulmonary sarcoidosis associated with particle exposures were identified examining the databases. The initial search string (“Sarcoidosis”’[MeSH] and (“Environmental exposures”[MeSH] or “Silicon dioxide”[MeSH] or “Metals/adverse effects”[MeSH] or “Metals/toxicity”[MeSH] or “Oxides”[MeSH] or “Minerals”[MeSH] or “September 11 terrorist attacks”[MeSH] or “Soil”[MeSH] or Pollen”[MeSH] or “Smoking”[MeSH] or “Particulate matter”[MeSH] or “Air pollutants”[MeSH] or “Air pollution”[MeSH] or “Wood”[MeSH])). There were no filters used for species, sex, age, or language. This search resulted in 236 articles. Those articles not including either cases or epidemiological studies of sarcoidosis were excluded. Results Sarcoidosis and occupations Investigations have associated sarcoidosis and sarcoid-like granulomatous lung diseases with various occupations ( - ) ( ). This pulmonary disease can demonstrate epithelioid granulomas that are pathologically and clinically indistinguishable from sarcoidosis ( , , ). Granulomatous lung disease was reported in miners ( ) and construction workers ( ). Significant associations were demonstrated between occupational exposures including those with metal dusts and sarcoidosis mortality ( ). However, work with metals was also shown to be protective against sarcoidosis ( , ). In addition, construction and agriculture were suggested to increase the risk for sarcoidosis ( - ). Finally, in a study of 36 pediatric sarcoidosis patients matched with both 36 healthy controls and a group of 21 with sickle-cell disease, pediatric sarcoidosis was associated with indirect exposure to inorganic particles through someone living at home. Co-residents’ occupations included construction ( ). A metanalysis estimated that 30% of sarcoidosis cases can be attributed to occupational exposures ( ). It was not known whether these occupational exposures caused sarcoidosis, impacted the immune system to increase susceptibility, exacerbated subclinical cases, or triggered a granulomatous condition comparable to but distinct from sarcoidosis ( ). 36 healthy controls and a group of 21 with sickle-cell disease, pediatric sarcoidosis was associated with indirect exposure to inorganic particles through someone living at home. Co-residents’ occupations included construction ( ). A metanalysis estimated that 30% of sarcoidosis cases can be attributed to occupational exposures ( ). It was not known whether these occupational exposures caused sarcoidosis, impacted the immune system to increase susceptibility, exacerbated subclinical cases, or triggered a granulomatous condition comparable to but distinct from sarcoidosis ( ). Pulmonary sarcoidosis and particles. Specific particles associated with pulmonary sarcoidosis include silica, silicates, metals and metal oxides, and World Trade Center dust ( ). Silica and silicates. Prominent among particles which have demonstrated a relationship with sarcoidosis are silica and silicates. There have been several case reports and case series documenting this correlation. An early report recognized pulmonary granulomas in two workers exposed to Portland cement and to mica dusts ( ). Using histochemical and X-ray diffraction techniques, abundant inclusions of the inhaled material were identified within the pulmonary lesions. In another case, a 50-year-old woman presented with Lofgren syndrome, defined by an acute onset of erythema nodosum, bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy, fever, and migratory polyarthritis, and without granulomatous skin involvement. ( ). Computed tomography revealed a foreign body granuloma of the lung containing inhaled particles. Analysis of the particles showed non-crystalline silica, calcite monohydrate, and phenol resin. In a patient treated for hypertension, an association between exposure to anhydrous colloidal silica (used as a vehicle for capsules or tablets in drug formulations) and sarcoidosis was suggested ( ). Sarcoidosis was also reported after silica exposure in a tunnel worker, a denim sandblaster, iron-foundry workers, and a plasterer ( , - ). Two cases of lung and hepatic granulomas in workers exposed to artificial quartz conglomerates were initially diagnosed to be sarcoidosis but later considered consistent with silicosis ( ). In another case, pathologic examination of the lung revealed focally infarcted granulomas and chronic inflammation in an industrial worker with exposure to high levels of inorganic dust (most significantly silica, silicon carbide and aluminum compounds) for 28 years ( ). The tissue removed from the granulomatous involvement showed significant dust deposition. Despite the inorganic dust deposits, a diagnosis of necrotizing sarcoid granulomatosis was initially made but this was later changed to mixed-dust pneumoconiosis after detailed examination using scanning electron microscopy/energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (SEM/EDS) analysis of individual particles showed predominantly silicon (silica or silicon carbide) and aluminum particles (the latter being consistent with aluminum metal and/or oxide). Two cases of sarcoidosis were observed in a workforce of 30 metal-halide lamp manufacturing workers in Belgium ( ). Mediastinal lymph node and open lung biopsy specimens revealed noncaseating epithelioid granulomas. Birefringent particles were observed in the biopsied tissues and the exposures included amorphous silica and cristobalite. More recently, a patient who worked in cement processing with silica exposure had a lung biopsy which revealed sarcoid-like granulomas with birefringent particles under polarized light; there was no malignancy or infection ( ). Based on the pathological findings, he was diagnosed with silicosis-associated sarcoid-like granulomatous lung disease rather than sarcoidosis. Pulmonary manifestations improved after discontinuation of silica exposure and introduction of corticosteroid/azathioprine combination therapy. In another study involving mining, 12 cases of sarcoidosis were observed in a cohort of hard-rock miners in Northern Ontario, Canada: 5 included extrapulmonary sarcoidosis ( ). Workers at a plant in Iceland exposed to diatomaceous earth comprised of silica, alumina, and iron oxide) and cristobalite (crystalline silica) were reported to show an increased risk of sarcoidosis with an odds ratio of 13.2 ( ). Among samples from 50 patients with sarcoidosis collected by biopsy and/or autopsy sampling, silicon-containing dust particles were present in epithelioid cells and multinucleate giant cells in all ( ). In a cohort of exposed workers in Swedish iron foundries, moderate to high levels of silica exposure increased risk for sarcoidosis ( ). In an additional epidemiologic study, an elevated risk for sarcoidosis was observed in a group of construction workers specifically exposed to silica and silicates ( ). A case-control study of all individuals diagnosed with sarcoidosis in Sweden between 2007 and 2016 revealed that silica dust exposure correlated with an increased risk of developing this disease (with an odds ratio of 1.44 for exposure greater than 10 years among males older than 35 years) ( ). Using multivariable logistic regression in 238 patients, sarcoidosis limited to pulmonary involvement was demonstrated to be associated with exposure to inorganic dust ( ). Finally, an increased trend in incidence of pulmonary sarcoidosis was observed in epidemiologic investigation of those exposed to silica in the Danish working population followed 1977-2015 ( ).
