Haemodynamic instability was regarded as a barrier by 40%, followed by the risk of barotrauma (32%). Notably, patient discomfort was cited as a relevant contraindication by only 20% of respondents. Complications related to FB were systematically assessed by 83% of participants. The most frequently reported adverse events were respiratory deterioration ( S pO 2 <88%), minor bleeding (<100 mL) and bronchospasm. By contrast, arrhythmias, haemodynamic instability and major bleeding were observed less frequently ( ). Tracheostomy Less than half of the respondents (46%) reported performing percutaneous dilatational tracheostomy (PDT). Physicians certified in intensive care conducted the procedure more frequently than non-ICU-certified colleagues (67% versus 29%; p<0.001). The most commonly used technique for PDT was the cone-shaped dilatator system, applied by 34%. Notably, FB guidance during PDT was employed by only 56%, with no significant variation across continents. The most frequent complications during PDT were bleeding, respiratory worsening and fracture of tracheal cartilage ( ). Discussion This international survey provides a novel insight into current practice of FB in ICUs worldwide. First, the practice of FB varies substantially across countries, particularly with respect to formal training, sedation protocols and the presence of 24/7 on-call bronchoscopy services. Second, ventilatory settings during FB, especially PEEP adjustments, differ markedly between ICU-certified physicians and non-ICU-certified physicians. Gender-based differences were also observed, with female physicians significantly more likely to reduce the PEEP during FB. Third, while microbiological sampling was a key indication for FB, the methods ranged from simple suctioning to BAL, with the instillation of 60–120 mL of saline. Importantly, FB findings led to therapeutic changes in nearly half of the cases. Fourth, although PDT is often recommended to be performed under bronchoscopy guidance, this was the case for only 56% of respondents. Despite FB being performed among 11% of mechanically ventilated patients [ ], FB is often performed without standardised protocols or high-level evidence [ ]. Indeed, more than two out of five respondents reported no formal training for FB when managing patients in an ICU. This is in line with a recent study showing that programme directors reported substantial barriers to establishing structured educational formats for teaching [ ]. This lack of training may also explain the limited availability of on-call bronchoscopy services. A recent German survey reported similar findings, with 69% of secondary care hospitals offering such services [ ]. The lack of structured training underscores the urgent need for innovative educational strategies. Simulation-based training offers a standardised, safe and reproducible environment to acquire and refine bronchoscopy skills, with recent systematic reviews confirming its effectiveness [ ]. Beyond conventional simulation, artificial intelligence (AI)-guided supervision has emerged as a promising approach, with recent randomised data suggesting that AI-supported bronchoscopy training may outperform instruction by human experts [ ]. Incorporating such approaches into critical care training curricula could help address the current gaps in formal education and ultimately improve both trainee competence and patient experience. The structure of critical care training differs internationally, being a primary specialty in some countries and a subspecialty ( e.g. pulmonary medicine) in others [ ]. For this survey, nearly 50% of the respondents were certified in intensive care medicine. These physicians were more likely to adjust PEEP during FB, eventually aiming to reduce the risk of auto-PEEP and barotrauma. The development of auto-PEEP during FB in mechanically ventilated patients, which was reported more than two decades ago [ , ], may cause barotrauma [ ]. In addition, a significant proportion of respondents did not change sedation during FB, which may go against either bronchoscopy guidelines that recommend adequate sedation [ , ] or recommended light over deep sedation on ICU [ ]. However, this may reflect the discrepancy between available recommendations and real-world practice. Another notable finding is the increasing adoption of single-use bronchoscopes, driven by their convenience and reduced risk of cross-contamination. However, this trend must be carefully balanced against their potential environmental impact, as widespread use may contribute to medical waste and raises questions of sustainability. Importantly, the greenhouse gas emissions appear to depend on the frequency of bronchoscope use (either single or reusable). In addition, some studies indicate an advantage and others a disadvantage for single-use instruments in terms of the carbon footprint. This highlights that the environmental debate is complex, is context-dependent and requires further high-quality research. Hospitals and clinicians should therefore consider both infection control and sustainability aspects when selecting bronchoscopes [ , ]. PDT remains an important intervention for patients requiring prolonged mechanical ventilation or difficult weaning. Guidelines recommend the use of bronchoscopy guidance for accurate placement and prevention of complications [ ]. According to this survey, however, this was performed by only 56% of the respondents. This is remarkable since PDT is

studies indicate an advantage and others a disadvantage for single-use instruments in terms of the carbon footprint. This highlights that the environmental debate is complex, is context-dependent and requires further high-quality research. Hospitals and clinicians should therefore consider both infection control and sustainability aspects when selecting bronchoscopes [ , ]. PDT remains an important intervention for patients requiring prolonged mechanical ventilation or difficult weaning. Guidelines recommend the use of bronchoscopy guidance for accurate placement and prevention of complications [ ]. According to this survey, however, this was performed by only 56% of the respondents. This is remarkable since PDT is recommended under bronchoscopic guidance [ ], and correct placement can be easily identified with bronchoscopy, which greatly decreases complications [ ]. Known complications of FB include hypoxaemia, hypotension, pneumomediastinum and pneumothorax – particularly in patients with underlying critical illness [ ]. While haemodynamical instability and barotrauma were frequently cited as contraindications, such complications were rarely observed in practice. Nonetheless, if they do occur, they may lead to severe clinical deterioration in critical ill patients on an ICU. Diagnostic FB was most frequently performed for microbiological sampling. Particularly among immunocompromised patients, FB including BAL plays a pivotal role in diagnosing pulmonary infections [ – ] and guiding antibiotic stewardship. Substantial changes have been reported in the last two decades in Europe, with a higher rate of bronchoscopy procedures performed for the diagnosis of lower respiratory tract infections in invasive mechanically ventilated patients [ , ]. In nearly 50% of cases, the microbiological results prompted changes in clinical management. Previous studies in patients with respiratory failure have reported diagnostic yields ranging from 13% to 59% [ – ]. This underscores the clinical value of FB, provided the potential benefits outweigh the risks. In this survey, among ICU patients the main aliquot range for BAL was 60–120 mL and the recovery rate was 48±18%; this is comparable with non-ICU settings, where 100–300 mL is standard [ – ]. Similarly, data from Germany have shown a median instillation of 100 mL of saline [ ] with 50% recovery rates, exceeding the often recommended threshold of 30% in non-ICU populations [ , ]. However, BAL can temporarily worsen gas exchange [ – ], with alveolar oxygen tension ( P AO 2 )/ F IO 2 ratios decreasing in mechanically ventilated patients by up to 86 mmHg, independent of instillation volume [ – ]. The findings of this analysis must be interpreted in the light of the following limitations. First, the number of respondents per country was insufficient to allow for country-specific comparisons. Second, due to the design of the survey, differentiation between invasively ventilated patients and non-invasively ventilated patients was not possible. Third, the dissemination via the ERS may have biased participation towards respiratory specialists. Conclusion Substantial variability exists in FB practices across ICUs, particularly in training, sedation, ventilation adjustments and microbiologic sampling. Despite FB leading to changes in management, standardised approaches to FB are lacking. Notably, a considerable proportion of physicians perform FB without formal training, and on-call bronchoscopy services are not universally available. ICU-certified physicians were more likely to adjust ventilator settings during FB, particularly by reducing PEEP to avoid barotrauma. Despite these variations, FB frequently led to clinically relevant changes in management, underlining its diagnostic and therapeutic value in critically ill patients. These findings underscore the need for international consensus guidelines and structured training programmes to harmonise FB practices in critical care settings.

chunks.content: Fujishima ﻿Journal of Intensive Care (2023) 11:10 Journal of Intensive Care https://doi.org/10.1186/s40560-023-00658-3 REVIEW Open Access Guideline‑based management of acute respiratory failure and acute respiratory distress syndrome Seitaro Fujishima* Abstract Acute respiratory failure (ARF) is defined by acute and progressive hypoxemia caused by various cardiorespiratory or systemic diseases in previously healthy patients. Among ARF, acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS) is a serious condition with bilateral lung infiltration, which develops secondary to a variety of underlying conditions, diseases, or injuries. This review summarizes the current standard of care for ARF and ARDS based on current major guidelines in this field. When administering fluid in patients with ARF, particularly ARDS, restrictive strategies need to be con- sidered in patients without shock or multiple organ dysfunction. Regarding oxygenation targets, avoiding excessive hyperoxemia and hypoxemia is probably a reasonable choice. As a result of the rapid spread and accumulation of evidence for high-flow nasal cannula oxygenation, it is now weakly recommended for the respiratory management of ARF in general and even for initial management of ARDS. Noninvasive positive pressure ventilation is also weakly recommended for the management of certain ARF conditions and as initial management of ARDS. Low tidal volume ventilation is now weakly recommended for all patients with ARF and strongly recommended for patients with ARDS. Limiting plateau pressure and high-level PEEP are weakly recommended for moderate-to-severe ARDS. Prone position ventilation with prolonged hours is weakly to strongly recommended for moderate-to-severe ARDS. In patients with COVID-19, ventilatory management is essentially the same as for ARF and ARDS, but awake prone positioning may be considered. In addition to standard care, treatment optimization and individualization, as well as the introduction of exploratory treatment, should be considered as appropriate. As a single pathogen, such as SARS-CoV-2, exhibits a wide variety of pathologies and lung dysfunction, ventilatory management for ARF and ARDS may be better tailored according to the respiratory physiologic status of individual patients rather than the causal or underlying diseases and conditions. documents.title: ATS clinical statement implementation of low-dose computed tomography lung cancer screening programs

chunks.content: Abbreviations AUC area under the receiver operating curve CEACAM5 carcinoembryonic antigen‐related cell adhesion molecule 5 CXCL17 C‐X‐C motif chemokine 17 DANTE Detection and Screening of Early Lung cancer with Novel Imaging Technology DLCST Danish Lung Cancer Screening Trial ESTHER Epidemiologische Studie zu Chancen der Verhütung, Früherkennung und optimierten Therapie chronischer Erkrankungen in der älteren Bevölkerung ITALUNG Italian Lung Cancer Computed Tomography Screening Trial LASSO least absolute shrinkage and selection operator LC lung cancer LDCT low‐dose computed tomography LUSI German Lung Cancer Screening Intervention trial MILD Multicentric Italian Lung Detection Trial MMP12 macrophage metalloelastase NELSON Nederlands‐Leuvens Longkanker Screenings Onderzoek trial NLST United States National Lung Screening Trial NPX normalized protein expression PLCO m2012 Prostate, Lung, Colorectal, and Ovarian Cancer Screening Trial Model 2012 STARD Standards for the Reporting of Diagnostic Accuracy Studies USPSTF US Preventive Services Task Force WFDC2 WAP four‐disulfide core domain protein 2 1 Introduction Lung cancer (LC) is the leading cause of cancer mortality and the most common cancer globally, accounting for more than 1.8 million deaths and over 2.4 million cancer cases in 2022 [ ]. Randomized control trials have demonstrated the effectiveness of screening high‐risk individuals with low‐dose computed tomography (LDCT) in reducing lung cancer mortality [ , , , , ]. Various risk prediction models have been proposed, evaluated, and validated that when compared with previously suggested eligibility criteria might identify future LC cases and deaths with greater efficiency [ , , ]. The PLCO m2012 model that incorporates a comprehensive set of variables, such as demographic information, smoking history, and medical history, has demonstrated strong performance in predicting LC risk across diverse populations, including American and European cohorts [ , , ]. Blood‐based biomarkers that improve risk assessment may be useful as a prescreening eligibility test. Numerous biomarkers like proteins, microRNAs, and methylation of circulating tumor DNA have been proposed to enhance the selection of individuals for LC screening [ , , , ]. A risk‐informative, biomarker‐based prescreening test could potentially identify individuals who are at high LC risk despite not meeting current eligibility criteria. The current study aimed to evaluate if a blood‐based protein marker risk prediction model can improve the LC risk discriminatory performance of the established risk prediction model. For the derivation and independent external validation, the participants were selected from population‐based cohorts from the UK and Germany, using data and samples from the UK Biobank and the ESTHER cohort study, respectively. The proteins were quantified via proximity extension assay, a multiplex immunoassay in which paired oligonucleotide‐tagged antibodies binding the same antigen bring their DNA tags into proximity, allowing enzymatic extension and amplification for sensitive and specific protein measurement [ ]. 2 Materials and methods 2.1 Study design The protein marker model was developed in a two‐step approach, with selection of proteins and construction of a multi‐marker algorithm in a derivation set and independent evaluation and validation of findings in an external validation set. The derivation set included participants from the UK Biobank study. The validation set was exclusively based on participants of the population‐based ESTHER cohort study. 2.2 Study population: derivation set 2.2.1 The <styled-content style="fixed-case" toggle="no">UK</styled-content> Biobank cohort The UK Biobank study is a population‐based cohort study with over half a million adults recruited at ages 37–73 years across 22 assessment centers in England, Scotland, and Wales. All participants provided written informed consent and ethical approval was obtained from the North West‐Haydock Multicentre Research Ethics Committee (11/NW/0382), the National Information Governance Board for Health and Social Care in England and Wales, and the Community Health Index Advisory Group in Scotland. Detailed study protocols are available on the UK Biobank website ( https://www.ukbiobank.ac.uk/ ). In brief, during the baseline recruitment visit between 2006 and 2010, biological samples (blood, stool, and urine) were collected in addition to information on sociodemographic, health and medical history, and anthropometric and lifestyle factors. Follow‐up of health‐related outcomes, including death and cancer, was conducted through linkage to electronic health records from the UK National Health Service. For the current study, ever‐smoking participants aged 50–70 with no prior LC diagnosis were selected from 52 348 participants included in the Pharma Proteomics Project for whom comprehensive proteomic profiles are available [ ]. The complete Standards for the Reporting of Diagnostic Accuracy Studies (STARD) diagrams displaying the selection of study participants are shown in Fig. . The study population of the derivation set comprised of 200 ever‐smoking participants who were diagnosed with LC and 18 668 ever‐smoking participants without LC diagnosis during the 6 years of follow‐up. 2.3 Study population: validation set 2.3.1 ESTHER The participants in the validation set were selected from the ESTHER study (Epidemiologische Studie zu Chancen der Verhütung, Früherkennung und optimierten Therapie chronischer Erkrankungen in der älteren Bevölkerung) study, which is an ongoing state‐wide cohort study conducted in Saarland, Germany. Details of the ESTHER study

of Diagnostic Accuracy Studies (STARD) diagrams displaying the selection of study participants are shown in Fig. . The study population of the derivation set comprised of 200 ever‐smoking participants who were diagnosed with LC and 18 668 ever‐smoking participants without LC diagnosis during the 6 years of follow‐up. 2.3 Study population: validation set 2.3.1 ESTHER The participants in the validation set were selected from the ESTHER study (Epidemiologische Studie zu Chancen der Verhütung, Früherkennung und optimierten Therapie chronischer Erkrankungen in der älteren Bevölkerung) study, which is an ongoing state‐wide cohort study conducted in Saarland, Germany. Details of the ESTHER study design have been reported previously [ , ]. Briefly, in the context of a general health screening examination, 9940 men and women aged 50–75 years were recruited by general practitioners in Saarland, Germany, between July 2000 and December 2002 and were regularly followed up thereafter. At baseline, information on sociodemographic characteristics, lifestyle factors, and health status was obtained by standardized self‐administered questionnaires from both participants and their general practitioners. Additionally, blood samples were collected and stored at −80 °C until analysis. The prevalence and incidence of all types of cancer cases at baseline and follow‐ups were determined by record linkage with data from the Saarland Cancer Registry ( https://krebsregister.saarland.de/ ). All participants provided written informed consent, and the ESTHER study was approved by the ethics committees of the University of Heidelberg (Heidelberg, Baden‐Wuerttemberg, Germany) and of the state medical board of Saarland (Saarbruecken, Saarland Germany). The ESTHER study was conducted in adherence to the Code of Ethics of the World Medical Association (Declaration of Helsinki) for experiments involving humans. The evaluation of the protein markers in the current study was based on 101 ever‐smoking participants who were diagnosed with LC in the first 6 years of follow‐up and randomly selected 101 ever‐smoking participants without LC diagnosis during this time (Fig. ). 2.4 Sample selection and storage In the UK Biobank, blood was collected via venipuncture and the samples were centrifuged within 2 h of collection, aliquoted, and stored at −80 °C. In ESTHER, the blood samples were collected during the baseline survey, were transported to the laboratory within 24 h of collection, and then aliquoted and frozen at −80 °C. In both cohorts, there were no more than three freeze–thaw cycles until the protein measurements. 2.5 Proteomic assays and data processing Protein profiling in blood samples in both the derivation and validation sets was performed utilizing antibody‐based proximity extension assays. Details about protein profiling in the UK Biobank have been published elsewhere [ ]. Briefly, a total of 2 923 unique proteins were measured using Olink® Explore 3072 across eight protein panels. In the validation set comprising participants of ESTHER, the proteomic profiling of 5413 proteins was performed utilizing the Olink® Explore HT assays (which include almost all of the proteins covered by Olink® Explore 3072). Proximity extension assay has a broad dynamic range, being able to detect both high and low‐abundance proteins within the same assay and as the assay requires two antibodies binding to proximate epitopes and DNA extension, chances of nonspecific binding giving signal are reduced. Samples were processed across different plates, and each plate included a mix of study samples and controls to facilitate normalization and quality control [ ]. For proximity extension assays performed in both the derivation and validation sets, no batch effects, plate effects, or abnormalities in protein coefficients of variation were observed. The complete preprocessing and selection of biomarkers is presented in Fig. . For data preprocessing, proteins with more than 25% of values below the limit of detection, with more than 20% missing data and those that were highly skewed were excluded. For further analysis, 2025 proteins that were overlapping and available in both the datasets were considered. 2.6 Heavy smoking definitions and prediction models The criteria of heavy smoking used in previous LC screening trials and the US Preventive Services Task Force (USPSTF) guidelines like ≥ 30 pack‐years [ ], ≥ 20 pack‐years [ , , , , ], ≥ 15 cigarettes per day for ≥ 25 years or ≥ 10 cigarettes per day for ≥ 30 years [ , ], and ≥ 15 cigarettes per day for ≥ 20 years [ ] were used for comparison or combination of risk stratification in the current study. We furthermore used the Prostate, Lung, Colorectal, and Ovarian Cancer Screening Trial Model 2012 (PLCO m2012 model) [ ]. 2.7 Statistical analysis The linear protein values were log transformed to produce normalized protein expression (NPX) and one NPX represents a two‐fold change in protein concentration. The NPX values of each individual protein were compared between LC cases and control participants without LC diagnosis during follow‐up using the Wilcoxon rank‐sum test with adjustment for multiple testing by the Benjamini and Hochberg method. A logistic regression model was used to construct the prediction algorithm for each protein and the prediction accuracy was evaluated by calculating areas under the receiver operating curve (AUCs) and their 95% confidence intervals (95% CI). We used a predefined, multistep process combining univariate screening, penalized selection, and internal validation with bootstrapping to derive a protein marker model for prediction of incidence of LC. In the derivation set comprising UK Biobank participants, we first estimated the effective number of independent tests from a principal component analysis of the standardized NPX protein data using the Gao method and the significance threshold was adjusted by dividing 0.05 by effective number of tests. Only the protein biomarkers below this adjusted threshold in univariate logistic regression were carried forward. On the reduced set, we standardized predictors and applied least absolute shrinkage and selection operator (LASSO) with 10‐fold cross‐validation to select the tuning parameter. To enhance selection stability and correct for overfitting, we performed 1000 subsamples drawing 75% of observations each time, refitting LASSO, and recording variable inclusion and the protein biomarkers that were selected in at least 80% of replicates comprised the final set. We then carried out 1000 bootstrap splits (75% training, 25% testing) fitting logistic regression models on the final protein biomarkers and evaluating discrimination via area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC), reporting the mean bootstrap adjusted (AUC*s). Finally, we fit the model on the full data using the selected markers to report its apparent performance AUCs not adjusted for overfitting and 95% CI. All random seeds were fixed for reproducibility. Furthermore, we assessed if and to what extent the combination of the protein marker model with PLCO m2012 could enhance LC prediction as compared to the risk model alone. The DeLong test was performed to assess whether the difference between the AUCs obtained for the PLCO m2012 model alone and for the combination of the protein marker model with the PLCO m2012 model was statistically significant. The prediction potential of the protein marker model and the PLCO m2012 model, individually and in combination, to identify future LC cases, was compared with those of four different definitions of heavy smoking that were used as selection criteria by the LDCT trials and also the USPSTF 2020 guidelines. For that purpose, the cutoff of the models was adjusted to yield the same number of participants selected for LDCT screening as the respective trial criterion. Then, for each model, the sensitivity at this cutoff, defined as the proportion of incident LC cases selected for LDCT screening, was calculated and compared with the sensitivity of the respective trial criterion. McNemar test was performed to assess the statistical significance of the increase in sensitivity, as compared to the respective LDCT trial criterion. The comparative evaluations were further performed in an independent validation set consisting of ESTHER participants. For the variables that had unknown information for some participants (for variables like years smoked, years quit, cigarettes per day, pack‐years of smoking, education, family history of lung cancer, lung diseases), multiple‐imputation datasets were created to impute these variables with the r package ‘mice’ [ ]. All statistical analyses were performed with statistical software r language and environment (version 3.6.3, R Core Team) [ ] using r packages ‘dplyr’, ‘DTComPair’, ‘glmnet’, ‘lcmodels’, ‘ModelGood’, ‘poolr’, and ‘pROC’. Statistical testing was two‐sided, and P ‐values of 0.05 or less were considered to be statistically significant. 3 Results The derivation set consisted of 200 incident LC cases and 18 668 ever‐smoking participants without LC diagnosis from UK Biobank participants. The validation set included 101 participants with LC diagnosis and 101 controls free of LC from the ESTHER study. Characteristics of the study populations from both the derivation and the validation sets are shown in Table . Incident LC cases were often older as compared to those free of LC in both derivation (median age: 65.0 vs. 61.0 years) and validation sets (median age: 65.0 vs. 60.0 years). Current smokers represented 49.0% and 54.5% of LC cases in derivation and validation sets, respectively. Incident LC cases were often older as compared to those free of LC in both derivation (median age: 65.0 vs. 61.0 years) and validation sets (median age: 65.0 vs. 60.0 years). Current smokers represented 49.0% and 54.5% of LC cases in derivation and validation sets, respectively. The prediction performance of the 2025 proteins available in both datasets is presented in Table . After adjustment for multiple testing, the differences in protein concentrations between LC cases and participants that remained free of LC were statistically significant ( P ‐values < 0.05) for 551 proteins and 44 proteins, in the derivation and validation sets, respectively. AUCs ≥ 0.70 were observed for 11 and 9 proteins (highlighted in green in Table ) in the derivation and validation sets, respectively. The volcano plots displaying the differential expressions of all 2 025 proteins between incident LC cases and participants who did not develop LC during 6 years of follow‐up among participants of the UK Biobank and ESTHER are shown in Fig. . To identify a multi‐marker predictive signature distinguishing LC cases from LC‐free controls, we applied LASSO logistic regression on 2 025 protein biomarkers in the derivation set, with internal validation via bootstrap resampling. Although several biomarkers were differentially abundant in the derivation set, four proteins were selected by multivariate LASSO in at least 800 of 1 000 training sets and these four biomarkers were included in the final protein marker model. As shown in Table , the protein marker model predicted the incidence of LC in the derivation set with an AUC of 0.814 (95% CI, 0.785–0.843). The four proteins included in the protein marker model were carcinoembryonic antigen‐related cell adhesion molecule 5 (CEACAM5), C‐X‐C motif chemokine 17 (CXCL17), macrophage metalloelastase (MMP12), and WAP four‐disulfide core domain protein 2 (WFDC2). The estimates of β‐coefficients, odds ratios, and feature selection stability frequency of the four proteins selected in the final model in the derivation set are reported in the Table . In the validation set, an AUC of 0.814 (95% CI, 0.756–0.873) was observed for the protein marker model. As shown in Table , the AUCs for the four proteins CEACAM5, CXCL17, MMP12, and WFDC2 selected in the multi‐marker signature individually were 0.72, 0.76, 0.74, and 0.77 in the derivation set and 0.70, 0.70, 0.78, and 0.72 in the validation set, respectively. The violin plots displaying the distribution of the four proteins selected in the protein marker model among incident LC cases and participants who did not develop LC during 6 years of follow‐up among participants of the UK Biobank and ESTHER are shown in Fig. . The predictive performance of the protein marker model and PLCO m2012 model, alone and in combination, for the derivation and validation sets is presented in Table and Fig. . Individually, the protein marker model outperformed the PLCO m2012 model. The overall AUCs for the PLCO m2012 model in the derivation and validation sets were 0.758 (95% CI, 0.723–0.793) and 0.775 (95% CI, 0.710–0.841). When adding the protein marker model to the PLCO m2012 model, the AUC was estimated at 0.814 (95% CI, 0.785–0.843) in the derivation and at 0.832 (95% CI, 0.776–0.888) in the validation set. As shown in Table , the odds ratios per increase in the protein marker model by 1 standard deviation were 2.62 (95% CI, 2.36–2.92) for the derivation set and 4.79 (95% CI, 2.97–7.71) for the validation set, respectively. The sensitivities of the protein marker model, individually and in combination with the PLCO m2012 model, the four definitions of heavy smoking criteria used by different LDCT trials and the USPSTF 21 guideline, for predicting incident LC cases during a 6‐year follow‐up are provided in Table . Using the trial criteria and USPSTF guidelines in the derivation set, between 51.5% (NLST) and 62.5% (USPSTF 21) of LC cases would have been correctly identified as eligible for screening. At cutoffs yielding the same number of participants selected for LDCT screening as the respective trial criterion and guideline, the sensitivities (proportions of correctly predicted LC cases) would have ranged from 55.5% to 64.5% for the PLCO m2012 model and from 65.0% to 73.5% for the protein marker model, respectively (Table ). In the validation set, between 59.4% (NLST) and 73.3% (USPSTF 21) of LC cases would have been correctly identified as eligible for screening. The sensitivities ranged from 65.3% to 77.2% and from 66.3% to 79.2% for the PLCO m2012 model and the protein marker model, respectively. The increase in sensitivity compared to the trial criterion was highest for the DEPISCAN criterion (+16 and +12 percent units, P < 0.05 in the derivation and validation set, respectively). In the validation set, between 59.4% (NLST) and 73.3% (USPSTF 21) of LC cases would have been correctly identified as eligible for screening. The sensitivities ranged from 65.3% to 77.2% and from 66.3% to 79.2% for the PLCO m2012 model and the protein marker model, respectively. The increase in sensitivity compared to the trial criterion was highest for the DEPISCAN criterion (+16 and +12 percent units, P < 0.05 in the derivation and validation set, respectively). In the derivation and validation sets, the combination of the PLCO m2012 model with the protein marker model did not further improve the sensitivities as compared to the protein marker model alone. 4 Discussion In this study, we developed a novel protein‐based risk prediction tool which outperformed the PLCO m2012 model in both the internal and external validation cohorts of target use population for screening. A protein marker model comprising four markers was derived based on the participants from the UK Biobank study, and subsequently, the performance was evaluated in an independent validation set comprising participants of the ESTHER study. The protein marker model outperformed the PLCO m2012 model in both the derivation and validation sets. At cutoffs yielding the same proportion and number of participants selected for LDCT screening as the respective trial criterion, the protein marker model predicted occurrence of LC within 6 years with up to 16 and 12 percent units higher sensitivity compared to the trial criteria in the derivation and validation set, respectively. Following the demonstration of reduction of LC mortality by LDCT screening in large‐scale randomized trials, efforts to implement LC screening programs are ongoing in many countries. At the same time, major efforts are made to find ways to optimize the effectiveness and cost‐effectiveness of the programs by enhanced selection of participants most likely to benefit from screening. Apart from risk factor‐based risk prediction models, blood‐based biomarkers could be potentially promising, easy‐to‐implement tools in this context [ ]. In recent years, a wide array of blood‐based biomarkers have been proposed for LC risk prediction [ , , , ]. However, only a few of these biomarkers have been independently validated and none are widely used in screening [ ]. In this study, a four‐protein biomarker signature was derived and found to outperform risk factor‐based risk prediction models in both internal and external validation. The four proteins included in the LASSO‐derived protein marker model were CEACAM5, CXCL17, MMP12, and WFDC2. Expression of CEACAM5, a cell surface glycoprotein, has been identified in several cancers, including lung cancer. MMP12, which is a metalloproteinase secreted by macrophages, has been found to be aberrantly expressed in various tumors. Protein biomarkers like CEACAM5 and MMP12 have been previously included in protein biomarker risk prediction tools for LC risk prediction [ , ]. CXCL17 is a member of the chemokine family and its expression has been observed in patients with both nonmalignant and malignant diseases [ ]. In the current study, these four LC‐associated proteins performed equally well, individually and as a model, in both the UK Biobank and ESTHER for predicting LC among ever‐smoking participants. The primary strength of this study is the two‐stage design, utilizing prediagnostic blood samples from large population‐based cohorts. This study performed comprehensive protein discovery using blood samples from the UK Biobank study and then externally validated findings in participants from ESTEHR. Using next‐generation high‐throughput proteomics, in the form of Olink® Explore 3072 and Olink® Explore HT arrays, comprehensive protein expression patterns were screened to identify markers that could enable prediction of lung cancer up to 6 years before diagnosis. Advanced statistical machine learning algorithms were employed to simultaneously evaluate possible combinations and comparisons of the protein markers. Our analysis included LC cases occurring during up to 6 years of follow‐up which makes the results closely comparable to the PLCO m2012 which was designed to predict lung cancer incidence within periods of 6 years. From a clinical application standpoint, the protein marker model comprises only four proteins, making it easily applicable and efficient. Although the current study provided evidence of the potential of using protein biomarkers in lung cancer risk assessment to define screening eligibility, further validation of this risk prediction model using prediagnostic samples in a larger population is needed before the use of this risk prediction tool in practice. Validation in a further, larger cohort should also include more detailed analyses for specific subgroups, for example, defined by age and sex. In previous biomarker verification studies, proximity extension assays have been found to give higher throughput, good sensitivity, and easier workflows as compared to other protein detection methods like mass‐spectrometry or antibody‐based arrays [ , ]; nevertheless, replication of our findings using other quantification techniques should be aimed for. Furthermore,

Validation in a further, larger cohort should also include more detailed analyses for specific subgroups, for example, defined by age and sex. In previous biomarker verification studies, proximity extension assays have been found to give higher throughput, good sensitivity, and easier workflows as compared to other protein detection methods like mass‐spectrometry or antibody‐based arrays [ , ]; nevertheless, replication of our findings using other quantification techniques should be aimed for. Furthermore, validation research should also include absolute quantification of the protein biomarker concentrations, for example by ELISA, rather than the relative quantification used in our study. Finally, thorough cost‐effective and benefit–harm assessments in large population cohorts will be crucial to best define the role of use of the biomarkers in risk‐adapted LC screening. 5 Conclusion A protein marker model was developed to identify future lung cancer cases and its prediction potential was externally validated in an independent cohort. Using blood samples from population‐based cohorts, the protein marker model showed promising risk discriminative performance beyond the established PLCO m2012 model. Further research is required to define a potential role of using the blood protein‐based panel to enhance the effectiveness and cost‐effectiveness of LC screening. chunks.content: Introduction Chronic respiratory diseases (CRD) are chronic diseases of the airways and the other structures of the lungs. Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) and asthma are the most prevalent CRDs , . COPD is characterized by airflow obstruction that can progress to pulmonary heart disease and respiratory failure , . Asthma occurs due to inflammation and narrowing of the small airways in the lungs and may cause a cough, recurrent wheezing, shortness of breath, and /or chest tightness as presenting symptoms , . CRD is among the most common NCDs and continues to be a considerable public health problem in the world , . In 2019 alone, 7.4% of the world’s population was threatened with CRD in 2017 . Africa has a huge burden of CRD ; nonetheless, as compared to other NCDs, it is underestimated and neglected . One-third of Ethiopians have NCDs, and CRDs are among the most common diseases with increasing public health challenges – . Addressing chronic diseases is integral to the 2030 Agenda for sustainable development . Ethiopia is working by following the World Health Organization’s (WHO) global action plan to prevent and control NCDs by the year 2025 . Environmental exposure to tobacco smoke, indoor air pollution, and occupational clouds of dust, smoke, and chemicals are important risk factors for COPD – . Other studies have been investigating the impact of frequent long hours of exposure to smoke released from the incomplete combustion of wood leads to lung function impairment . A prior study reported that major clusters of high COPD hospitalization were observed in an area near high emissions of pollutants . Previous epidemiological studies of CRD morbidity in Ethiopia and similar settings have mainly examined the prevalence of the disease – . Investigation of possible disease clustering is fundamental to epidemiology, to detect the high-risk population , and examining diseases over time provides essential insight into overall disease burden , . However, spatial, temporal, and spatiotemporal variations of CRD have not been well explored in charcoal production areas, constraining the ability of policymakers to implement targeted and efficient interventions. Thus, this study was performed to assess the spatial, temporal, and spatiotemporal variations of CRD among adults in the charcoal-producing areas of northwest Ethiopia from 2012/13 to 2018/2019. Methods Study design and settings This spatial, temporal, and spatiotemporal study was conducted in three zones (Awi, East Gojjam, and West Gojjam) of the Amhara region, Northwest Ethiopia (Fig. ). The region has a total of 13 zones and is located between 9° 20’ and 14°20’ North latitude and 36° 20’ and 40° 20’ East longitude. The three study zones have a total of 47 districts and lower administrative areas under the zones. The three zones were selected because they are known for high charcoal production. A cancer study conducted in the Amhara region revealed that more than 10 million quintals of charcoal are sent from the study area to the big cities in Ethiopia . Moreover, about 164,648.2 tons of charcoal was produced between 2014 and 2018 by households from one of the 47 districts in the study area . Based on the 2007 national population and housing of Ethiopia, the projected population for 2019 in the study area was about 6,724,134, of which 3,297,159 (49%) were male, and 3,426,965 (51%) were female Study area map Data sources and extraction procedures We acknowledge that the present study is based on routinely collected surveillance data from the three zones of the Amhara region through the National Health Management Information System (HMIS) reported between 01 July 2012 and 30 June 2019 that have been used previously in a separate publication focusing on the trend, seasonality, and forecasting analyses . In contrast, the current study applies spatial and spatiotemporal analytical methods to examine the geographic distribution and clustering of the disease, addressing distinct research questions. These analyses provide complementary insights by identifying geographic heterogeneity and localized clustering that cannot be inferred from trend, seasonality and forecasting of CRD analysis alone. The current manuscript does not reuse any analyses from that publication but instead conducts an independent spatial, temporal and spatiotemporal investigation to assess geographic distribution and clustering. Chronic respiratory disease cases of the three districts established since 2016/17 were included in their mother district (make ready this sentence for deleting). We considered bronchial asthma and COPD cases in our analysis since these are the most prevalent types of CRDs , , . There is an integrated health information system from the bottom up through the HMIS. Health-related data based on the recommended WHO guideline ICD-10 are compiled at the district level and reported quarterly to the Zone Health Department offices, then the Regional Health Bureau, and finally to the Federal Ministry of Health . The annual morbidity report covers the period from July 2012/13 to 30 June

We considered bronchial asthma and COPD cases in our analysis since these are the most prevalent types of CRDs , , . There is an integrated health information system from the bottom up through the HMIS. Health-related data based on the recommended WHO guideline ICD-10 are compiled at the district level and reported quarterly to the Zone Health Department offices, then the Regional Health Bureau, and finally to the Federal Ministry of Health . The annual morbidity report covers the period from July 2012/13 to 30 June 2018/19. Data were collected by health management information system officers from October to December 2022. Data quality control A checklist was prepared based on the HMIS registry format to extract the data from the zonal health department office records. We tried to reduce misclassification by including ICD-10 codes and carefully checking the data for obvious mistakes. Despite these efforts, some underreporting or misclassification may still exist, and we acknowledge this as a limitation. The data collectors were informed about the project’s objectives and trained in the data collection procedure. Every day, after extraction, the data were checked for completeness and consistency by the principal investigators of the study. In addition, cross-checking activities with the quarterly and annual reports of the districts were carried out. Data were carefully entered into Microsoft Excel for further cleaning and analysis. The number of CRD cases together with their district was carefully geocoded based on address information from registers and using X and Y-coordinates. All district attributes were properly recorded and cross-checked before analysis. Data analysis Ethiopian administrative regions’ shapefile, district-level polygon map, and geographic coordinates were obtained from the publicly accessible DIVA-GIS database ( https://diva-gis.org/data.html ), and spatial data layers were created in ArcGIS 10.8. Spatial, temporal, and spatio-temporal analysis was employed using the Poisson model. The data represent all CRD cases registered from 44 districts of the three zones between 01 July 2012 and 30 June 2019 and archived in the Zonal Health Department offices. We included bronchial asthma and COPD cases in our analysis since these are the most prevalent types of CRDs , . An attribute table for districts was prepared by including location ID, name of districts, number of CRD cases, sex, and population of the district, and all the CRD records were geocoded based on their X and Y-coordinates of each district where CRD cases were residing. The SaTScan software V10.1 was used to detect the randomness of CRD distribution over space and time among adults aged 15 years and above, and cluster map s with CRD cases were plotted using ArcGIS V10.8. Spatial autocorrelation analysis Spatial autocorrelation (global Moran’s I) statistic was employed to assess whether the spatial pattern expressed by CRD cases is clustered, dispersed, or random in the study area . The significance of Moran’s I is identified based on the Monte Carlo method, which simulates the distribution according to random data. Moran’s I value lies between + 1 and -1, and when its value is greater than zero and p-value < 0.05 shows clustering, while, Moran’s I value of zero shows no spatial autocorrelation (the pattern is random) and less than zero shows the pattern is dispersed. The local Moran’ I and Getis-Ord Gi analyses were also done to locate the local cluster after detecting the global Moran’ I. The local Moran’ I describes spatial clustering of observations in high or low rates and outliers, and the Getis-Ord Gi statistic identifies local spatial clustering patterns, either “hot spots” (spatial clusters of high values) or “cold spots” (spatial clusters of low values). The statistical significance for local Moran’s I and Getis-Ord Gi was determined via hypothesis testing using standardized z-scores calculated for each observation and significant p-values. A spatial weight matrix was used to specify the spatial relationships between neighboring districts. Neighbors were defined using the first-order queen’s polygon contiguity, and districts sharing common borders and vertex were considered neighbors – . ArcGIS was used to explore the distribution of CRD cases in terms of their geographic relations , . Spatial clusters We used Kulldorff’s SaTScan software version 10.1 to employ the spatial, temporal, and spatiotemporal scan statistics to depict the purely spatial, temporal, and spatiotemporal clusters as described previously , using the attribute table prepared for districts. Kulldorff’s scan statistics also help to calculate the log-likelihood ratio (LLR) and relative risk (RR), and provide a p-value using Monte Carlo Simulations. In this SaTScan statistics, the Poisson model was employed, where the number of cases is compared to the background population data and the expected number of cases in each unit is proportional to the size of the population at risk . The observed CRD cases were compared with the expected cases inside and outside of

scan statistics to depict the purely spatial, temporal, and spatiotemporal clusters as described previously , using the attribute table prepared for districts. Kulldorff’s scan statistics also help to calculate the log-likelihood ratio (LLR) and relative risk (RR), and provide a p-value using Monte Carlo Simulations. In this SaTScan statistics, the Poisson model was employed, where the number of cases is compared to the background population data and the expected number of cases in each unit is proportional to the size of the population at risk . The observed CRD cases were compared with the expected cases inside and outside of each window and the risk ratios were estimated based on the Poisson distribution. The null hypothesis of the spatial scan statistic states that CRD is randomly distributed throughout the districts and that the expected event count is proportional to the population at risk. The purely spatial clusters were selected based on the likelihood ratio and p-value < 0.05. The LLR was calculated to measure the RR of CRD occurrence within the cluster when compared to the risk outside using Monte Carlo simulations. The maximum number of permutations for the Monte Carlo simulation was set to 999 to assess the sensitivity of significant locations to the number of permutations (p < 0.05 . The scanning window was a circle in the purely spatial pattern, and the upper limit for the maximum purely spatial was set to be 50% of the population at risk, which is important to detect small and large clusters. For each circle, the rejection of the null hypothesis is based on a likelihood ratio statistic. The p-value was calculated through Monte Carlo hypothesis testing, by comparing the rank of the maximum likelihood from the real data set with the maximum likelihoods from random data sets. To evaluate the statistical significance of the most likely cluster, the 999 random replications of the data set are generated under the null hypothesis . For each location and size of the scanning window, the alternative hypothesis is that there is a higher risk within the window as compared to outside. Under the Poisson assumption, the likelihood function for a specific window is proportional to: where; C is the total number of cases, c is the observed number of cases within the window, E[c] is the expected number of cases within the window under the null hypothesis. Note that since the analysis is conditioned on the total number of cases observed, C-E[c] is the expected number of cases outside the window . I( ) is an indicator function. When SaTScan is set to scan only for clusters with high rates, I( ) is equal to 1 when the window has more cases than expected under the null hypothesis, and 0 otherwise. The opposite is true when SaTScan is set to scan only for clusters with low rates. When the program scans for clusters with either high or low rates, then I( ) = 1 for all windows . The excess hazard (the ratio of observed to expected cases greater than one) for each district was calculated by dividing the observed cases by the expected cases and plotted using the geographic information system (GIS). The expected number of cases in each area under the null hypothesis was calculated using the following formula: E[c] = p*C/P , where c is the observed number of cases and p is the population in the location of interest, while C and P are the total number of cases and population respectively. SaTScan also identifies secondary clusters in the data set in addition to the most likely cluster and orders them according to their likelihood ratio test statistic. Secondary clusters are computed, based on the degree of overlap allowed in the cluster circles, and include the option of no geographical overlap , . Temporal clusters A purely temporal cluster analysis scanning was performed to detect the temporal clusters of CRD cases with high rates, representing the whole geographic area, but with a one-year time aggregation length. The temporal scan statistic uses a scanning window, a time interval that moves in one dimension. The upper limit for the maximum was specified to be 50% within the study period for purely temporal cluster analysis. To identify clusters, a likelihood function was maximized across all locations and times. The maximum likelihood indicates the cluster is least likely to have occurred by chance (primary cluster). The p- value is obtained through Monte Carlo hypothesis testing. For purely temporal analyses, only the most likely cluster is reported . Space–time clusters The space–time scan statistic was employed to detect clusters in both space and time. The time of the space–time cluster analysis was set to the time frame from 2013 to 2019. The space–time scan statistic was defined by a cylindrical window with a circular

temporal cluster analysis. To identify clusters, a likelihood function was maximized across all locations and times. The maximum likelihood indicates the cluster is least likely to have occurred by chance (primary cluster). The p- value is obtained through Monte Carlo hypothesis testing. For purely temporal analyses, only the most likely cluster is reported . Space–time clusters The space–time scan statistic was employed to detect clusters in both space and time. The time of the space–time cluster analysis was set to the time frame from 2013 to 2019. The space–time scan statistic was defined by a cylindrical window with a circular (or elliptic) geographic base and with a height corresponding to time. The base is defined exactly as for the purely spatial scan statistic, while the height reflects the time of potential clusters. The cylindrical window is then moved in space and time so that for each possible geographical location and size, it also visits each possible time interval, where each cylinder reflects a possible cluster . Thus, this method enables simultaneous detection of the location and time of a cluster occurrence. A likelihood ratio was calculated for each space–time window to indicate to what extent the rate of cases inside the area is higher than expected. Monte Carlo hypothesis testing is then used to indicate the significance level of specific space–time windows. For each space–time window, the likelihood ratio was calculated to determine whether the rate of observed cases inside the area was higher than expected cases. By considering the number of observed and expected cases inside the window, the software identifies and assesses the statistical significance of space–time clusters. The Monte Carlo simulation technique is used to estimate the p-value. The maximum number of permutations for the Monte Carlo simulation was set to 999 to assess the sensitivity of the significant locations to the number of permutations . This means that SaTScan will generate 999 random permutations of the data to compare with the real data . The cluster with the maximum LLR was defined as the most likely cluster (a cluster with the highest LLR test means a cluster least likely to have occurred by chance). Likewise, for purely spatial analysis, in space–time analyses, SaTScan also identifies secondary clusters in the data set in addition to the most likely cluster and orders them according to their LLR test statistic. A standard of no geographical overlap and hierarchical cluster type was selected to report secondary clusters (separation of clusters). Statistical significance for the presence of clusters was reported when the p-value was < 0.05. A discrete Poisson-based model was used to analyze annually reported CRD cases following the Poisson distribution . Results Distribution patterns of CRD cases over time During the seven years (2012/13 to 2018/19), CRD cases were reported from 44 districts in three zones of the Amhara region, and the overall morbidity rate was 4,641 (95%CI: 3,903–5379) cases per 100,000 population at risk. CRD shows no substantial sex differences, with the rate among males slightly higher and accounting for 51%. The CRD morbidity rate was 6,508(95%CI: 2,933–10,082), 4,208(95%CI:1,714–6702), and 3,202 (95%CI:1852–4552) per 100,000 population in Awi, West Gojjam, and East Gojjam zones, respectively. Purely temporal cluster analysis detected a significantly higher rate of purely temporal CRD clusters. Only one peak period of an identified primary cluster occurred in all districts (with 86,410 observed and 55,822.41 expected CRD cases, LLR = 10,866.30, P < 0.001) from 2018 to 2019. The distribution patterns of adult CRD morbidity rate for each year and district varied and the highest morbidity rate (7314/100,000 population) was reported in Dangila town in 2018/19, followed by Finote Selam town (4275/100,000 population) in 2018/19, and Mota town (3626/100,000 population) in 2017/18, while the lowest observed in Yilmana Densa district (62/100,000 population at risk) in 2015/16 (Table ). Across all districts, for seven years, a significantly higher morbidity rate (19,967 /100,000 population) was reported in Dangila town (Awi zone), while the lowest was observed in Gonji Kollela district (West Gojjam) (746/100,000 population) (Fig. ). Spatial clustering of CRD cases Spatial autocorrelation analysis Spatially, the distribution of CRD cases was non-random (global Moran’s I = 0.277148, Z-score = 3.6597, p < 0.001), indicating that the distribution pattern of CRD morbidity was clustered (Fig. ). Since the global spatial autocorrelation showed clustering, we employed further analysis to identify spatial cluster features with high or low values (cluster and outlier analysis) and to identify hot spot areas using Anselin’s local Moran’s I and Getis-Ord Gi * methods respectively. The result from Anselin’s local Moran’s I analysis revealed that the high-high cluster was located in the districts of the Awi zone. The low-low clusters and outliers were also detected in most districts of East Gojjam and Awi zones (Fig. ). The hot spot analysis (Getis-Ord Gi) demonstrated that hot spot areas

CRD morbidity was clustered (Fig. ). Since the global spatial autocorrelation showed clustering, we employed further analysis to identify spatial cluster features with high or low values (cluster and outlier analysis) and to identify hot spot areas using Anselin’s local Moran’s I and Getis-Ord Gi * methods respectively. The result from Anselin’s local Moran’s I analysis revealed that the high-high cluster was located in the districts of the Awi zone. The low-low clusters and outliers were also detected in most districts of East Gojjam and Awi zones (Fig. ). The hot spot analysis (Getis-Ord Gi) demonstrated that hot spot areas were located primarily in the northwest and southwest of the study area (Fig. ). Hotspot Districts Purely spatial clusters of adult CRD cases Ten statistically significant purely spatial clusters, one most likely cluster, and nine secondary clusters were detected in the study period. The most likely cluster which comprises 11 districts was located in two zones (8 in the Awi Zone and 3 in the West Gojjam Zone). The cluster window was centered at 10.967700N, 36.925500 E, and the radius of the window was 48.37 km. There were 92,597 observed and 33,716 expected cases (LLR = 47,274, p-value < 0.001), with a relative risk (RR) of 4.37 in this cluster window (Table ). Secondary clusters are computed based on the degree of overlap allowed in the cluster circles, and include the option of no geographical overlap criteria for reporting secondary clusters. Among the nine secondary clusters observed, five, one, and three clusters were located in the East Gojjam zone, Awi zone, and West Gojjam zone respectively, during the study period 2012/2013 to 2018/2019. In this spatial distribution, most of the clusters were shown in the northwest and southwest parts of the study area (Fig. ). The relative risk compares what is the risk inside the cluster to the risk outside the cluster, while the observed /expected compares what is the number of cases inside the cluster to what would have been inside the cluster had the null hypothesis been true . People living in the most likely cluster had a 4.37-fold higher risk of the disease (about 337% higher) compared with those outside the cluster. Nine more significant secondary clusters for the high occurrence of CRD cases were detected in the study area, and most of the districts were from the West Gojjam zone (Table ). Spatial–temporal clusters A total of three clusters (one most likely and two secondary clusters) were identified in thirteen cluster locations by space–time cluster analysis. The most likely cluster with 51,423 observed and 14,825.69 expected cases (LLR = 31,406.98, RR = 4.37, P-value < 0.001) was detected from 2017 to 2019 from the Awi zone (Faggeta Lekoma, Injibara town, Banja, Chagni town, Guagusa Shikudad, Ankasha, Dangila town, and Dangila Zuria) and three districts from the West Gojjam zone (Sekla, Bure town, and Finote Selam town). The risk of getting CRD in the most likely cluster was 4.37 times higher than people residing outside of this cluster. Secondary clusters were identified in two districts of East Gojjam zone in Mota town (secondary cluster 1 with 9910 observed and 431.28 expected cases, LLR = 21,821.89, RR = 24.17, p-value < 0.001) from 2018 to 2019 and Debre Markos town (secondary cluster 2 with 4110 observed and 1364.33 expect cases, LLR = 1806.45, RR = 3.06, p-value < 0.001) detected during 2013 to 2015 cluster year (Table ). Discussion To our knowledge, this study is the first to apply GIS and SaTScan analyses to depict the spatial, temporal, and spatiotemporal variations of CRDs in the Amhara region. The study revealed that the spatial, temporal, and space–time distribution patterns of CRD morbidity rate in the study districts were non-random. The possible spatial variations might be explained by the difference in exposure to risk factors for CRD. The population within these districts has been exposed to massive charcoal production and indoor biomass fuel use. Investigating risk factors of CRD in the surrounding districts is an area of research. This is in agreement with a spatial analysis that revealed COPD case clustering observed in areas with higher firewood exposure, greater smoking exposure, and in households with closer proximity to local roads . Congruently, other studies also showed respiratory health outcomes with charcoal production and utilization , NCD deaths accounted for 43% in the Amhara region, and CRDs were among Ethiopia’s leading causes of death in 2019 . The purely spatial and spatiotemporal model identified that most of the districts included in the most likely cluster were from the Awi zone, and the secondary clusters were located in districts of the East Gojjam zone

The purely spatial and spatiotemporal model identified that most of the districts included in the most likely cluster were from the Awi zone, and the secondary clusters were located in districts of the East Gojjam zone and the West Gojjam zone. Moreover, hot spot clusters were detected in the northwest and southwest of the study area. This clustering of CRD cases coincides with areas of high charcoal production , , , in these areas, in addition to the other contributing factors. This is in agreement with a study that showed morbidity rate attributed to CRD was commonly observed in areas with higher firewood exposure , . Based on the analysis of records from 2012/13 to 2018/19, the annual morbidity rate of CRD showed an increase of 139.7%. Increasing numbers of health facilities and improving the diagnostic capacity which leads to early detection and prevention of progression of CRDs, could be the reason for increasing CRD morbidity rates. In our study area, the number of hospitals increased from five to twenty since 2015/16 onwards due to the initiatives for the establishment of primary hospitals in districts in the country . This increase is in agreement with the results from a global data 1990–2017 and systematic review , . Hence, we acknowledge that diagnostic capacity for chronic respiratory diseases may have improved during the study period due to expanded access to health services, increased training of health workers, and better availability of diagnostic tools across districts. Due to these reasons, some degree of misclassification or temporal variation in diagnostic accuracy may persist, and this is acknowledged as an inherent limitation of routine surveillance data. Despite the increment in the annual morbidity rate of CRD, it might be still underestimated because the average readiness of health facilities for CRD service was 45% in 2016 . A finding from the spatial analysis showed inappropriate medication users lived at a distance from their preferred health facilities compared to appropriate users . A study on NCDs reported that 60.4% of CRD mortality is attributed to modifiable risk factors including indoor and outdoor air pollution, the existence of exposure to biomass smoke, and road traffic vehicle exposure , . In our study population, wood charcoal production which is known to emit high levels of CO 2 appears to be the main factor associated with CRD morbidity and mortality . This is supported by studies revealing a higher proportion of CRD cases reported in areas exposed to biomass smoke , Our study found that CRD morbidity rates vary from 62 to 7314 per 100,000 population among districts. The reason for this variation is not clear and needs further study, but the potential effect of the volume of charcoal production and meteorological variables may be important. The geographic variations in CRD morbidity have been observed in other countries – . Nevertheless, the magnitude of these geographical inequalities also highlights the importance of geographically manifesting factors in understanding the CRD burden in the study area. In contrast, even if the number of CRD cases is still increasing, CRD mortality declined among Global Alliance Respiratory Disease member countries from 2000 to 2015 , . This might be due to strong advocacy for the reduction of cigarette smoking interventions, utilization of clean fuel sources, and early detection and treatment. Our study revealed that CRD distribution among males and females was similar. This is in agreement with a study reported in China . On the contrary, some studies have shown that CRD morbidity is higher in men than women , . This might be explained by the fact that the former studies were conducted among factory workers, and males were more involved than females in this occupation. Congruently, the mortality rate of CRD in males was higher than in females. The population within these districts has been exposed to massive charcoal production and indoor biomass fuel use. Investigating risk factors of CRD in the surrounding districts is an area of research. This is in agreement with a spatial analysis that revealed COPD case clustering observed in areas with higher firewood exposure, greater smoking exposure, and in households with closer proximity to local roads . Congruently, other studies also showed respiratory health outcomes concerning charcoal production and utilization , . We employed different spatial statistical analyses to identify the true cluster of districts with CRD. Identifying clusters and hot spot areas in CRD has a paramount effect on receiving priority attention from public health planners for the allocation of scarce resources and to devise interventions. This study, however, is not without limitations. Because we used routinely collected DHIS2 data, the CRD morbidity rate in the study area may be underestimated, as some people in the community may not have visited health facilities. In addition, the retrospective nature of the study, we lacked information on important environmental and lifestyle factors, such as smoking, household air pollution (PM₂.₅ data), or access to healthcare. In addition, our analysis was based on the presence of asthma and/ or COPD as a component of CRD. These might underestimate the magnitude of CRD cases and affect their spatial–temporal clustering in the zone. Despite these limitations, we believe the findings still provide useful insights into disease patterns in these areas. Conclusions The spatial distribution of CRD cases varied across districts rather than occurring at random. CRD morbidity also varied over time. CRD morbidity rates increased consistently in three zones, and the Awi zone reported the highest rates throughout the study period. This indicated that there is a need to have targeted interventions in the identified cluster areas with CRD morbidity. Therefore, increased efforts should be placed in the high-risk areas in the future for the allocation of scarce resources. Moreover, the clustering of CRD cases can occur for a variety of reasons. Since this study used aggregated data, future research should collect individual-level information to better understand personal exposures and other risk factors for CRD.

documents.title: ATS clinical practice guideline acute exacerbation of idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis

chunks.content: 1. Introduction The management of fibrosing interstitial lung diseases (ILDs) still presents with significant challenges, mainly due to the unpredictable clinical course and the lack of disease-modifying agents. Approximately one third of patients will develop a progressive fibrotic phenotype, with gradual clinical, radiological and functional deterioration; yet episodes of acute respiratory decompensation may complicate the disease course at any point [ ]. Acute exacerbation of fibrotic interstitial lung diseases (AE-fILDs) is defined as an acute worsening of respiratory status in patients with a previous or concurrent ILD diagnosis. It is characterized by marked respiratory symptoms and the appearance of new bilateral alveolar abnormalities on chest computed tomography typically of less than one month duration, which cannot be fully explained by fluid overload [ , ]. Although most commonly described in idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (IPF), exacerbations have also been reported in other fILDs, such as idiopathic nonspecific interstitial pneumonia (NSIP), connective tissue disease-associated ILDs (CTD-ILDs), and fibrotic hypersensitivity pneumonitis (HP), with a lower incidence compared to IPF [ ]. AE-ILDs can even occur in patients with preserved lung volumes and mild imaging abnormalities or with previously undiagnosed fibrotic ILDs [ , , ]. The diagnosis is based on clinical and radiological findings [ , ]. Triggering Factors may include infections, gastroesophageal reflux disease, drugs, air pollution, aspiration and in some cases perioperative lung injury [ , ]. Even though the pathogenetic mechanisms underlying AE-ILDs have not been fully elucidated, inflammation and immunity play a pivotal role. Elevated levels of pro-inflammatory cytokines, high cellularity of the bronchoalveolar lavage fluid, and histopathological findings of diffuse alveolar damage are highly suggestive of an aberrant inflammatory response interplayed with exuberant alveolar cell apoptosis. Inflammatory changes may extend beyond the lungs with systemic consequences and multi-organ dysfunction [ , , ]. Moreover, recent evidence highlights the role of antibodies in the pathogenesis of AE-ILDs through various mechanisms, including autoimmunity, complement activation, and direct cytotoxicity [ , , ]. AE-ILDs are associated with poor prognosis, significant morbidity, and mortality. The in-hospital and short-term mortality for acute exacerbation of IPF(AE-IPF) may exceed 50%, rising to 75–90% in intubated patients. Other ILDs generally have a better prognosis, though post-exacerbation mortality varies widely [ , , ]. Despite the devastating impact of AE-fILDs, established treatment strategies are majorly lacking. The latest IPF guidelines propose the use of corticosteroids, despite limited supporting evidence [ ]. Some retrospective studies indicate that corticosteroids may provide benefits in AE-IPF and other fILDs [ , , ]; yet results are still conflicting [ , ]. Importantly, as seen in a recently published global survey, the majority of physicians across the world apply pulses of methylprednisolone in AE-IPF [ ]. Other immunosuppressants, such as rituximab, cyclophosphamide, and azathioprine, are frequently used, although their efficacy remains uncertain [ ]. Additionally, considering the potential risk for typical or opportunistic infections, broad-spectrum antibiotics are often administered empirically [ , ]. Finally, concerning the use of antifibrotic agents in AE-IPF, evidence indicates that both anti-fibrotics exert a rather preventive rather than therapeutic role considering that nintedanib may prolong the time to the first AE-IPF, while pirfenidone could lower the risk of respiratory-related hospital admissions [ , , , ]. Based on the recent survey, for patients not previously treated with antifibrotics, physicians generally initiated such therapy after clinical stabilization. Conversely, for patients already on antifibrotic therapy at the time of AE-IPF, the majority of physicians continued the treatment [ ]. Intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIG) is a biologic component of pooled antibodies from healthy donors’ plasma. IVIG is used as a replacement treatment in immunodeficiencies, a hyperimmune treatment targeting specific infectious agents and in hematological, neurological, and rheumatological diseases, given its immunomodulatory and anti-inflammatory properties [ ]. Interestingly, IVIG is also used in some cases of rapidly progressive ILDs other than IPF, particularly in myositis-associated ILDs [ ]. IVIG therapy has been linked to both immediate and delayed adverse events. Immediate reactions typically occur within 30–60 min after infusion initiation. These are often transient and mild, such as headache, low-grade fever, or fatigue. Moderate manifestations, including nausea, vomiting, or chest discomfort, may also arise. Such reactions can usually be alleviated through symptomatic management, premedication with anti-inflammatory agents or antihistamines, reduction in infusion rate, dose adjustment, or discontinuation of therapy. More serious complications, though less frequent, include thromboembolic phenomena, hemolytic episodes, renal dysfunction, arrhythmias, marked fever, hemodynamic instability, dyspnea, or fluid overload. [ , ]. In light of the evidence that infections represent major causes of AE-fILDs [ , ], that patients with fILDs exhibit a state of immunosuppression, affecting both cellular and humoral immunity [ ], and that dysregulated inflammatory and immunological processes are major contributors in AE-fILDs [ ], we hypothesized that there is a profound rationale to investigate the safety and efficacy of IVIG treatment in AE-fILDs. 2. Materials and
