Therefore, multiple outcomes (e.g., patient- and family-centered measures) and implementation outcomes like adoption and sustainability and the use of newer study designs such as MOST (multiphase optimization strategy) ( ) are needed to examine which specific component(s) of the intervention are effective, including measuring specific impacts proximal to the intervention and potential harms ( ). Research is needed to identify when to initiate palliative care to achieve maximal benefit for patients and families for specific chronic respiratory illnesses (e.g., COPD) ( ). Effective telehealth-based palliative care delivery models that include sustainable payment models ( ) are critical to reaching patients living in rural and/or underserved communities. Developing and testing primary palliative care training interventions that are practical, scalable, and embedded within existing clinical settings is an additional priority. The critical shortage of palliative care specialists ( ) necessitates pulmonary–critical care clinician competency in fundamental palliative care skills. More work is also needed to develop models with integrated or comanagement of primary and secondary palliative care in ways that are acceptable, sensible, and efficient ( ). Application of novel methodologies and study designs are needed to improve the quality of palliative care evidence in pulmonary and critical care medicine. Examples include quasi-experimental/natural experiments, adaptive designs, hybrid and pragmatic trials, and mixed methods research. Pulmonary palliative care interventions that have been conducted in ICU settings can guide this work; however, further research is urgently needed for seriously ill patients and their caregivers managed in pulmonary outpatient clinics. Lastly, it is critical to include people of color, non-English speakers, and members of rural communities in future studies to ensure a better understanding of their unique palliative care needs ( ). Expanding funding for the cultural and linguistic adaptation of effective palliative care interventions to diverse populations offers a high-value opportunity to broaden the reach of palliative care. The “culture problem” of integrating palliative care into pulmonary and critical care medicine is a challenge that is not unique to the field. Despite recommendations from professional societies to offer palliative care to patients with advanced cancer, the adoption of palliative care is variable depending on the service and setting ( , ). Therefore, trials are needed to test the effectiveness of efficacious interventions with primary aims focusing on the outcomes of implementation science, such as clinician adoption of the intervention and sustainability in different practice settings. A clearer framework could help the field guide and successfully implement palliative care while enhancing its scalability. Palliative care interventions in the ICU and pulmonary outpatient settings appear promising, but more research is needed to understand the full range of patient, family, and healthcare system impacts ( ). Technological advancements, including the leveraging of electronic health record systems for useful clinical tasks and the use of methods such as artificial intelligence and machine learning, are likely to accelerate the conduct of future clinical research. Examples include patient identification for study criteria and outcomes collection. Technology in the form of telehealth can be used to support clinician education, patient self-management, and improved care delivery and disparities. A number of self-directed mobile app-based interventions targeting psychological distress and physical symptoms are also available ( – ). Lastly, researchers from around the globe can meet and collaborate without traveling by using available technology to access data and conduct collaborative research to accelerate innovation. Other important research priorities include characterizing the impact of clinicians engaging in early and regular GOC discussions on “in-the-moment decision-making” and goal concordant care ( , ). The palliative care field is making progress in developing measures of goal concordance ( ) and applying them in research studies. Approaches toward managing common symptoms in respiratory illnesses, such as acute breathlessness, cough, and fatigue, require further investigation to improve the efficacy of patient and caregiver self-care management as well as their QOL. For example, the effectiveness of specific opioid formulations and routes as well as target illnesses has not been established. Furthermore, the effects in daily life of supplemental oxygen in patients without hypoxemia and the use of heliox on dyspnea and functional ability are unknown ( ). In addition, studies on the effects of nonpharmacological approaches to symptom management, such as graded exercise therapy for fatigue, are important next steps to tailor care. Lastly, caregiver research is a priority as the demand for informal caregiver involvement in patient care increases while the caregiver population ages. Developing and evaluating dyad-targeted palliative care interventions for patients and caregivers

specific opioid formulations and routes as well as target illnesses has not been established. Furthermore, the effects in daily life of supplemental oxygen in patients without hypoxemia and the use of heliox on dyspnea and functional ability are unknown ( ). In addition, studies on the effects of nonpharmacological approaches to symptom management, such as graded exercise therapy for fatigue, are important next steps to tailor care. Lastly, caregiver research is a priority as the demand for informal caregiver involvement in patient care increases while the caregiver population ages. Developing and evaluating dyad-targeted palliative care interventions for patients and caregivers living with serious respiratory illnesses is important as they may improve QOL, and this research can inform state and federal policy initiatives on caregiver support. In summary, to comprehensively address the research priorities identified by the members of this committee ( ), it is imperative to engage a broad group of partners that includes patients, families, caregivers, policymakers, and funders (e.g., National Institutes of Health, Patient-Centered Outcomes Research Institute, and foundations) to help prioritize topics and ensure adequate funding ( , ). Conclusions Patients with serious respiratory illness and their caregivers suffer from significant physical, emotional, spiritual, and financial burdens and are in need of early palliative care to help guide treatment planning. Ideally, primary palliative care should be initiated by pulmonary–critical care clinicians early in the care continuum seamlessly alongside disease-directed treatments. Secondary palliative care has an important complementary role in supporting primary palliative care by providing interprofessional expertise as needed. Given the robust evidence-based support for palliative care in improving QOL among patients with serious illness, the provision of this care is a fundamental right for any patient and/or caregiver who may benefit. This multisociety policy statement presents essential palliative care recommendations, values, and guiding principles among patients with serious respiratory illness and is designed to provide guidance for clinicians and to inform policy initiatives.

documents.title: ATS Occupational Contribution to the Burden of Airway Disease

chunks.content: Contents Overview Key Conclusions Introduction Methods Occupational Burden of Asthma Incidence Occupational Burden of COPD and Chronic Bronchitis Occupational Burden of IPF Occupational Burden of PAP and Other Interstitial Lung Diseases Occupational Burden of HP (Extrinsic Allergic Alveolitis) and Other Granulomatous Lung Diseases, Including Sarcoidosis Occupational Burden of TB and CAP Conclusions Overview Occupational exposures are important, frequently overlooked, and modifiable contributors to the burden of respiratory disease. Quantifying the occupational contribution to this disease burden is critical to preventing disease and improving lung health. To date, the question of the occupational burden in respiratory disease at the population level has been addressed primarily in relation to asthma and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD). This document reviews and synthesizes existing data to quantify the occupational contribution to the burden of nonmalignant respiratory diseases across a range of conditions frequently unrecognized as potentially work related. Key Conclusions • A substantial evidence base indicates that the contribution of inhalational workplace hazards to the burden of nonmalignant lung diseases is substantial. • Conditions for which the estimated occupational burden is 10% or more include asthma, COPD, chronic bronchitis, idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (IPF), hypersensitivity pneumonitis (HP), other noninfectious granulomatous lung diseases (including sarcoidosis), pulmonary alveolar proteinosis (PAP), and community-acquired pneumonia (CAP). • These findings highlight the need for greater awareness that work exposures contribute substantially across a range of respiratory diseases. • Strategies are needed to improve the recognition and prevention of the substantial occupational burden of nonmalignant respiratory diseases. Introduction Inhalation of vapors, gas, dust, or fumes (VGDF) in the workplace is common worldwide, and occupation is an important global contributor to the burden of respiratory disease ( ). For asthma and COPD, the contribution of workplace exposures has been a particular focus of attention in previous American Thoracic Society (ATS) policy statements ( – ). Occupational exposures also contribute to the disease burden in a number of other conditions, including interstitial disease diagnosed as IPF, HP, other noninfectious granulomatous lung diseases such as sarcoidosis, other interstitial lung diseases, and selected respiratory infections ( – ). We synthesized data from multiple sources to quantify the occupational contribution to the burden of nonmalignant respiratory disease. The occupational burden in thoracic cancer (lung and pleura) has been well characterized elsewhere ( – ). Of note, the classic pneumoconioses (including silicosis, coal workers’ pneumoconiosis, and asbestosis) remain an important, unabating global health problem that is not addressed in this document because the occupational contribution to these conditions is essentially 100%. That does not detract, however, from their public health importance. In this statement, we assess the occupational burden in four categories of respiratory conditions: airway disease (asthma, COPD, and chronic bronchitis), interstitial lung disease (IPF as well as PAP and other uncommon interstitial diseases), granulomatous processes (HP and other noninfectious granulomatous diseases, including sarcoidosis), and selected respiratory infections (tuberculosis [TB] and CAP). Methods We searched the PubMed and Embase databases from their respective start dates through December 31, 2017, unless otherwise noted. A supplemental literature search was conducted covering January to September 2018. The search strategies, including start dates, rationale, and search terms, are shown in Table E1 in the online supplement. For asthma, COPD, and chronic bronchitis, searches took into account the previous ATS reports ( – ) and additional reviews ( – ). We also reviewed reference citations in identified publications to identify relevant papers. Except when stated explicitly, all data were population based and were not limited to a specific industry or exposure. For asthma, COPD, chronic bronchitis, and IPF, we estimated the occupationally related population attributable fraction (PAF) reported by or derived from case–control and cohort studies. When needed, we calculated the PAF using the odds ratio (OR) and proportion of cases exposed [PAF = pc(OR − 1)/OR, where pc is the proportion of cases exposed] ( ). We limited the analysis of asthma to incident data. For PAP, HP, and sarcoidosis, we extracted data from cases series in which the proportion of occupationally related cases was available. For TB, we used World Health Organization and World Bank databases ( – ) for data on country-specific general population rates to estimate relative disease incidence by occupation. For CAP, we examined both PAF estimates and, within exposure cohorts, the attributable fraction (AF). We pooled published or derived PAF values (asthma, COPD, chronic bronchitis, and interstitial lung disease) and the occupationally attributable burden (PAP, HP, and sarcoidosis) to obtain weighted summary estimates using the metaproportion command in Stata 14.2 software (StataCorp). We used the exact method to compute the 95% confidence interval (CI) for each pooled estimate. Because we recognized that the heterogeneity among the studies was high, we calculated the pooled PAF or proportion using random effects modeling with case numbers informing the weights. We also estimated statistical heterogeneity using the I 2

estimates and, within exposure cohorts, the attributable fraction (AF). We pooled published or derived PAF values (asthma, COPD, chronic bronchitis, and interstitial lung disease) and the occupationally attributable burden (PAP, HP, and sarcoidosis) to obtain weighted summary estimates using the metaproportion command in Stata 14.2 software (StataCorp). We used the exact method to compute the 95% confidence interval (CI) for each pooled estimate. Because we recognized that the heterogeneity among the studies was high, we calculated the pooled PAF or proportion using random effects modeling with case numbers informing the weights. We also estimated statistical heterogeneity using the I 2 statistic, which in each case was consistent with high heterogeneity, as we expected (values not presented). We also calculated the pooled estimate excluding the highest and lowest values in the group, as well as calculating the median of the observed PAF or occupational burden values. For TB and CAP, we did not calculate weighted pooled values, limiting summary data to the median values among the estimates considered. For consistency, we use the term “occupational burden” across the various disease outcomes analyzed, even though in some cases the burden was derived from PAF estimates, whereas in others the burden was derived from attribution in case series, incidence rate ratios (IRRs), or AF within a group. Occupational Burden of Asthma Incidence Work-related asthma is now the most commonly reported work-related respiratory disorder in many industrialized countries. Work-related asthma comprises occupational asthma, defined as asthma “caused” by the workplace, and work-exacerbated (or aggravated) asthma, meaning preexisting asthma with work-related worsening ( ). Cross-sectional (prevalence) studies have dominated previous estimates of the occupational burden of disease. To build on earlier estimates, we limited our search to longitudinal, population-based studies that reported incident asthma and occupational risk factors. We identified nine studies with longitudinal data relevant to occupation and incident asthma for inclusion ( – ) ( ). Of these, six had been included in a previous review ( ), including a study of Israeli military recruits (over 95% of the Jewish male population aged 18 yr) exposed across a range of vocations ( ). Three newer studies have been published since the previous review ( ). One study investigating asthma incidence among persons aged 13–44 years in Tasmania (Australia) reported a high cumulative incidence of asthma (37%) with a work-related job exposure matrix (JEM)-based PAF of 10% ( ). A second study, using the RHINE (Respiratory Health in Northern Europe) adult study population aged 20–44 years, estimated a JEM-based PAF for occupation of 14% for males and 7% for females ( ). A later reanalysis using a different JEM arrived at similar estimates (13% and 8% for males and females, respectively) ( ). A third longitudinal study analyzed data from the United Kingdom. 1958 birth cohort limited to those without asthma by age 16 with later follow-up through age 42 ( ). Using a JEM to assess exposure risk, the overall occupational PAF was 16%, with wide confidence intervals (95% CI, 3.8–27.1%). Pooling data from all nine studies yielded an estimated PAF for the occupational contribution to incident asthma of 16% (95% CI, 10–22%) ( ), which is comparable to prior estimates ( ). Overall, longitudinal data from which inferences can be drawn on the occupational burden of incident asthma are limited. Of note, the studies considered were largely done in developed economic settings. Sex-stratified longitudinal data are even more limited; we identified only two such analyses, both with lower PAF estimates for women than for men. Occupational Burden of COPD and Chronic Bronchitis Seven reviews published since the 2003 ATS statement ( , – , , ) identified 33 papers relating to the occupational contribution to COPD or chronic bronchitis. Of note, two of these found a median PAF for the occupational contribution to COPD of 15% ( , ); one meta-analysis estimated a pooled OR of 1.43 for COPD related to VGDF exposures ( ), whereas another meta-analysis observed minimal excess risks (1.04–1.15) for separate JEM-defined exposures ( ). The additional literature search for publications published between 2014 and 2017 identified a further 15 relevant citations not among the 33 included in the reviews noted above. We retained population-based studies that included a range of potential occupations or case–control studies that clearly reflected the general population. Studies were excluded if they lacked a clear definition of the disease endpoint (e.g., either COPD or chronic bronchitis) or when key data were missing (e.g., studies not presenting the number of subjects exposed that would have allowed for a PAF calculation). When a study reported multiple endpoints or measures of exposure, we preferentially considered risk estimates for COPD defined by spirometry (using lower limit of normal, if reported) over self-reported COPD, and, similarly, we considered JEM-defined risk over self-reported exposure. In studies stratified by smoking

a range of potential occupations or case–control studies that clearly reflected the general population. Studies were excluded if they lacked a clear definition of the disease endpoint (e.g., either COPD or chronic bronchitis) or when key data were missing (e.g., studies not presenting the number of subjects exposed that would have allowed for a PAF calculation). When a study reported multiple endpoints or measures of exposure, we preferentially considered risk estimates for COPD defined by spirometry (using lower limit of normal, if reported) over self-reported COPD, and, similarly, we considered JEM-defined risk over self-reported exposure. In studies stratified by smoking status, the ever-smoking stratum was the one used in the pooled analysis of PAF. When data from a never-smoking stratum were available (in some cases the entire cohort analyzed), we used these in a separate pooled analysis of PAF among never-smokers. Results presented only in a stratified manner (e.g., by sex) were considered as separate estimates of risk. We included 26 studies to estimate the contribution of occupational exposures to the burden of COPD ( – ) and 7 for the contribution to chronic bronchitis ( , , , , – ). summarizes the 26 COPD studies considered, including 28 estimates of risk (taking into account sex-stratified data). The pooled PAF for the occupational contribution to the burden of COPD (including cohorts with mixed smoking status, adjusted for smoking) was 14% (95% CI, 10–18%) ( ). The occupational PAF for COPD among never-smokers (not shown in table), estimated from six studies including stratified data ( , , , – ), yielded a pooled PAF of 31% (95% CI, 18–43%). summarizes the seven chronic bronchitis studies used (eight estimates of risk). The pooled PAF for chronic bronchitis was 13% (95% CI, 6–21%) ( ). Only two studies allowed estimation of the occupational PAF for chronic bronchitis among never-smokers, yielding values of 8.3% ( ) and 12% ( ). Several publications excluded from the tables nonetheless warrant mention. Accelerated annual decline in FEV 1 in males with early COPD was observed in association with occupational exposures ( ). An ecological analysis of three large international studies estimated a 0.8% increase in COPD prevalence per 10% increase in occupational exposures, taking into account the concomitant prevalence of smoking ( ). Several large population-based studies have addressed the association between various occupations and COPD ( , , ). Also of note, other researchers have investigated large occupational cohorts, including construction workers exposed to dust ( , ). In summary, an impressive body of new data on the occupational burden of COPD, and to a lesser degree chronic bronchitis, has been published since the original 2003 ATS statement. In aggregate, participant numbers are large and international in scope. The pooled estimates of the occupational PAF of 14% for COPD and 13% for chronic bronchitis are in line with those of the previous ATS statement and interval reviews. Moreover, the higher occupational PAF for COPD among never-smokers (31%) suggests that occupational exposures contribute more substantially to the burden of COPD in nonsmokers. Occupational Burden of IPF IPF is a diagnosis of exclusion made in the presence of a usual interstitial pneumonia pattern on biopsy or with a consistent appearance on a high-resolution computed tomographic scan. The IPF diagnosis presumes that known causes of interstitial lung disease have been excluded (e.g., drug toxicity; connective tissue disease; and domestic, occupational, or environmental exposures) ( ). Therefore, studies of cohorts with a diagnosis of IPF presumably already exclude persons with a recognized occupational cause of fibrosis, such as asbestosis. We identified four reviews of occupational exposures in IPF ( , – ) that collectively included 10 relevant case–control studies. One of these, a meta-analysis of six studies, reported a PAF for several exposure categories ranging from 3.5% (silica) to 20% (agriculture) ( ). Adding more recent citations ( n = 5), we identified a total of 15 relevant case–control studies addressing the question of occupational exposures associated with IPF ( – ). Four of the 15 publications were not included in our PAF estimates: one because data were not available on the proportion of cases with specific occupational exposures ( ), two because of methodological issues in exposure assignment ( , ), and one because of overlap with an included study ( ). We initially included one publication that appeared in abstract form only ( ), because we were aware that the full paper was forthcoming ( ). The remaining 11 case–control studies provided data permitting analysis of occupational exposures in five exposure categories: VGDF, metal dust, wood dust, silica dust, and agricultural dust. For the IPF analysis, VGDF represents an inclusive category combining any of multiple exposures, defined variously by each study. Thirty-nine risk estimates from 11 studies (1,229 IPF cases in total) contributed to these pooled PAF

( , ), and one because of overlap with an included study ( ). We initially included one publication that appeared in abstract form only ( ), because we were aware that the full paper was forthcoming ( ). The remaining 11 case–control studies provided data permitting analysis of occupational exposures in five exposure categories: VGDF, metal dust, wood dust, silica dust, and agricultural dust. For the IPF analysis, VGDF represents an inclusive category combining any of multiple exposures, defined variously by each study. Thirty-nine risk estimates from 11 studies (1,229 IPF cases in total) contributed to these pooled PAF estimates ( ) ( , – , , , , ). The burden of each pooled exposure type was based on 5–11 individual risk estimates ( ). The pooled OR for agricultural work (five studies) was elevated but not statistically significant (OR, 1.6; 95% CI, 0.8–3.0), with a PAF of 4%. The pooled ORs for each of the remaining exposure categories were elevated and statistically significant. These pooled PAFs were as follows: silica (3%), wood dusts (4%), metal dusts or fumes (8%), and VGDF (26%). A forest plot for the estimates for VGDF, the broadest exposure category, is presented in . In summary, our findings suggest that occupational exposures contribute substantially to the burden of disease otherwise considered idiopathic and labeled “IPF.” It is also interesting to note that in one Korean study, patients with IPF who had been occupationally exposed to dust had earlier onset of disease and worse prognosis ( ). A major challenge in assessing the occupational burden of IPF disease is differentiating between disease misclassification (e.g., chronic HP or one of the classic pneumoconioses [e.g., asbestosis, silicosis] misdiagnosed as IPF) and a causative role of work exposures in usual interstitial pneumonia–like processes. Another important challenge is exposure misclassification, especially when estimating chronic inhalational work exposures over many years. For example, asbestos exposure was common in metal and wood industries and could have contributed to these exposure-associated PAFs for IPF. Occupational Burden of PAP and Other Interstitial Lung Diseases PAP has been categorized as primary (idiopathic), secondary, or congenital ( , ). Primary PAP involves autoantibodies to granulocyte–macrophage colony–stimulating factor ( ); secondary PAP is attributed to a variety of occupational exposures, most notably silica ( – ). Cases of autoimmune PAP have been reported in occupationally exposed persons ( , , – ). We included 29 relevant publications since 1958 subsuming 1,539 PAP cases (with a range of 10–241 cases per series) ( – ), excluding overlapping reports ( – ). The reported occupational exposure prevalence ranged from 0% to 67%, with a pooled prevalence of 29% (95% CI, 21–37%) ( ). A range of exposures was reported, including vapors or gases (cleaning fluids, gasoline, hairspray, paint, and pesticides), inorganic dusts (asbestos, cement, chalk, coal, glass fiber, and silica), organic dusts (cotton, flour, wood, and wool), and metal dusts or fumes (aluminum, copper, indium, iron, and zirconium). Among 19 publications that specifically reported on silica (786 PAP cases), the exposure prevalence ranged from 0% to 22%, with pooled prevalence of 5% (95% CI, 2–8%) ( , – , – , , , – , , ). Among the five publications describing 345 autoimmune PAP cases, occupational exposure prevalence ranged from 26% to 55% ( , , , , ). Although PAP has a more robust literature relevant to the occupational burden of disease, there are a number of other respiratory syndromes in which occupational associations have been observed in disease outbreaks, in certain work settings, or after suspect exposures ( , – ). Table E2 provides selected examples of these reported associations, which include bronchiolitis and the flavoring chemical diacetyl; cryptogenic organizing pneumonia and textile dye (“Ardystil syndrome”); and diffuse pulmonary hemorrhage and trimellitic anhydride ( , – ). Occupational Burden of HP (Extrinsic Allergic Alveolitis) and Other Granulomatous Lung Diseases, Including Sarcoidosis We synthesized data from 15 relevant publications for HP, the earliest paper dating from 1983 ( see ). We excluded case series limited to a single avocation or occupation (e.g., bird fanciers or machinists) ( , ), if there were insufficient data to determine the proportion due to an occupational exposure ( ), or if there were overlapping cases ( ) that were included in another publication ( ). The studies included ( – ) were all case series (or registries), except for one case–control design ( ), but used variable criteria for diagnosing HP and assessing causation. For the case series, we considered the work-related cases within a larger series to represent the occupational burden of disease. The estimated occupational burden of disease ( ) ranged from 0% to 81.3%, with a weighted metaproportion of 19% (95% CI, 12–28%). In addition to HP, we also considered the occupational burden of other noninfectious

or if there were overlapping cases ( ) that were included in another publication ( ). The studies included ( – ) were all case series (or registries), except for one case–control design ( ), but used variable criteria for diagnosing HP and assessing causation. For the case series, we considered the work-related cases within a larger series to represent the occupational burden of disease. The estimated occupational burden of disease ( ) ranged from 0% to 81.3%, with a weighted metaproportion of 19% (95% CI, 12–28%). In addition to HP, we also considered the occupational burden of other noninfectious granulomatous lung diseases. Inhalation of beryllium can cause granulomatous lung disease that mimics sarcoidosis; other metals have also been associated with granulomatous responses; and sarcoidosis prevalence has been reported to be elevated among various occupational groups, including firefighters, navy recruits, workers in the lumber industry, rock or glass wool workers, salespeople, and World Trade Center disaster emergency responders ( , ). Several large case-referent studies of patients with sarcoidosis who were not beryllium sensitized have found that occupational exposures to organic dusts, bioaerosols, and metals increased risk of sarcoidosis ( – ). A study of sarcoidosis prevalence in Switzerland found higher frequencies in regions with metal industry and intense agriculture ( ). In a large U.S. study using national death certificate data, sarcoidosis mortality risk was significantly elevated in association with metalworking, health care, teaching, sales, banking, and administration ( ). Mortality data also suggest that occupational exposures may increase risk for a more severe sarcoidosis phenotype ( ). Epidemiological evidence on the proportion of chronic beryllium disease misdiagnosed as sarcoidosis is limited to a few case series ( – ) and one case-referent study ( ). Combining beryllium-focused studies of sarcoidosis with other studies that estimated occupational risk, we identified seven studies to use to estimate the occupational burden of sarcoidosis ( ) ( , , , – , ). The pooled estimated occupational proportion of sarcoidosis ranged from 0% to 54%, with a weighted metaproportion of 30% (95% CI, 17–45%). Occupational Burden of TB and CAP Certain occupational groups are at increased risk for TB infection or bacterial CAP. The occupational burden of these infectious diseases, however, has been infrequently quantified ( – ). Searching back to 1990, we identified 9 silica-related and 17 healthcare worker (HCW)-related relevant studies for inclusion in this analysis ( – ) ( and ). We excluded studies that dealt exclusively with latent TB, did not use diagnostic criteria for TB, or were reviewed in previous analyses (and thus were not included in our estimates) ( , ). We considered TB in two distinct occupational risk groups: those exposed occupationally to silica and those exposed as HCWs. For TB among the silica exposed, three U.S. studies and six South African studies allowed estimation of an occupation-associated burden of disease ( – ). For the U.S. studies, the estimated burden ranged from 3.2% to 4.9%. For the South African studies using gold miner cohorts, the occupational burden was estimated by deriving an IRR for miners relative to national rates of disease; the median silica-associated burden was 2.3% (range, 0.8–7.9%) ( ). One other estimate of the occupational burden from an Iranian study, strikingly higher than all other studies (36%), was omitted because selection bias may have been present ( ). As shown in , we found little consistency in estimates of the occupational burden of TB in HCWs. In five studies, the incidence rate among HCWs was lower than that of the general population ( , , , , ), yielding an estimated burden of zero. Among those with an appreciable burden (IRR ≥ 1), the occupational burden ranged from 0.1% ( ) to 8.9% ( ). In one of these studies ( ), even though there was an increased TB IRR overall, this was accounted for by foreign-born HCWs, and work-acquired infection was confirmed in only a handful of cases. Based on all 17 HCW studies, the overall median estimate was 1.0% (range, 0–8.9%) ( ). A previous review of TB among HCWs ( ) reported similar occupational burdens of disease among low– and high–TB incidence countries. We identified 15 publications relevant to the occupational burden of CAP. Six were population-based case–control studies estimating CAP risk ( – ). Of these, the earlier of two overlapping publications from the same Spanish research group was excluded ( ), as well as the earlier of two related publications from Canada ( ). The four remaining case-referent studies ( ) yielded a median PAF of 10% (range, 3–45%) for the occupational burden of pneumonia. We identified nine cohort studies focusing on specific exposures or a single industry ( – ). Seven estimated risk of pneumonia in welders or in individuals with metal fume exposure ( ,

the occupational burden of CAP. Six were population-based case–control studies estimating CAP risk ( – ). Of these, the earlier of two overlapping publications from the same Spanish research group was excluded ( ), as well as the earlier of two related publications from Canada ( ). The four remaining case-referent studies ( ) yielded a median PAF of 10% (range, 3–45%) for the occupational burden of pneumonia. We identified nine cohort studies focusing on specific exposures or a single industry ( – ). Seven estimated risk of pneumonia in welders or in individuals with metal fume exposure ( , , – ); two also estimated risk for inorganic dusts ( , ). For metal fume/welding exposures, the median AF was 52.5% (range, 38–73%). Four studies considered risk associated with inorganic dust ( – ). The AF estimates from these studies varied widely ( ). Conclusions This comprehensive literature review and analysis of nonmalignant respiratory disease demonstrates a substantial occupational burden for multiple respiratory conditions not typically considered potentially work related ( ). The findings for asthma, COPD, and chronic bronchitis build on prior estimates and reinforce the validity of an occupational PAF in the 15–20% range. The occupational contribution to the burden of cases diagnosed as IPF, other interstitial lung diseases, HP and other noninfectious granulomatous diseases (including sarcoidosis), and selected respiratory infections has not been estimated previously using an in-depth literature review and data synthesis approach. One limitation of this review is that we censored study eligibility for the purposes of data synthesis after December 2017. To address this potential shortcoming, after completing the main analyses, we performed a supplemental literature review covering January through September 2018, identifying three additional publications that would have met criteria for inclusion to estimate occupational burden, one each relevant to COPD, chronic bronchitis, and HP ( – ). All three studies’ results were consistent with our original findings. A 20-year longitudinal follow-up study of 3,343 participants of the population-based European Community Respiratory Survey found that work exposures, assessed by JEM, increased the risk of developing COPD ( ). The PAF for VGDF yielded by the data from this study was 14.1%, consistent with our estimate. A cross-sectional study of 5,539 Colombians reported increased risk of chronic bronchitis associated with self-reported VGDF exposure, yielding a PAF of 16.1% ( ), also consistent with our findings. The final recent publication, a U.S. retrospective health claim–based study that estimated the incidence and prevalence of HP, found that 17.0% of HP cases had occupational exposure–associated International Classification of Diseases codes, also consistent with our findings ( ). Several other limitations of this in-depth literature review and data synthesis should be noted. The literature we identified was extremely heterogeneous and not amenable to a formal systematic review that could apply all of the PRISMA (Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses) criteria. Thus, we have avoided applying the label “systematic review” to this analysis. In particular, we made no attempt to formally grade publication quality, to apply methodologic restrictions on acceptability (beyond limiting the asthma analysis to prospective studies), or to weight results (beyond taking into account study size in pooled estimates). Study heterogeneity necessitated using differing approaches (e.g., PAF and prevalence) to estimate the occupational contribution to the burden of the various respiratory conditions. Study heterogeneity also likely contributed to the wide range in the observed values for the estimated occupational burdens within the conditions we studied. To better assess this potential limitation, we also estimated all of the pooled burdens, excluding the highest and lowest values, as well as calculating the median rather than the pooled value. Reanalyses after excluding outlying values yielded point estimates that were similar to the original pooled estimates, as were the median values, neither of which were consistently lower or higher than the initial estimates (data not shown). Across conditions, a differential in burden estimates is biologically plausible, consistent with differing potencies of risk depending on the nature of the exposure and the pathogenesis of the disease in question. It would be speculative, however, to make causal inferences from these findings, precisely because of the within- and across-condition variability that characterizes this literature. Yet another limitation of this analysis is that it lacks data that might serve to estimate disability-adjusted life-years lost, a metric that could provide more quantitative assessment of the health impact of different work exposures and comparison across populations. Also of note, this analysis does not include classic pneumoconioses such as silicosis and asbestosis. These are conditions for which the occupational contribution is essentially 100%, obviating the need for an analysis of the estimated burden of those diseases. The pneumoconioses remain important, underrecognized global health problems associated with considerable morbidity and mortality ( – ). This assessment of the occupational burden of nonmalignant respiratory disease has

is that it lacks data that might serve to estimate disability-adjusted life-years lost, a metric that could provide more quantitative assessment of the health impact of different work exposures and comparison across populations. Also of note, this analysis does not include classic pneumoconioses such as silicosis and asbestosis. These are conditions for which the occupational contribution is essentially 100%, obviating the need for an analysis of the estimated burden of those diseases. The pneumoconioses remain important, underrecognized global health problems associated with considerable morbidity and mortality ( – ). This assessment of the occupational burden of nonmalignant respiratory disease has clinical, research, and ultimately policy implications. There is a pressing need to improve clinical recognition and widen public health awareness of the contribution of occupational factors across a range of nonmalignant respiratory diseases. Greater attention should be given to reducing this occupational disease burden by identifying and implementing effective preventive interventions. In that light, the importance of preventing these diseases needs to be recognized. Policy makers, especially those who set regulatory standards and oversee their enforcement, should reassess current protections for workers around the world who are exposed to recognized hazardous inhalational exposures. chunks.content: INTRODUCTION Type two diabetes mellitus and insulin resistance are associated with worse outcomes in asthma, but the specific pathophysiology is unknown. Epidemiologically, these conditions are associated with a preserved ratio impaired spirometry (PRISm) pattern —a lower forced exhaled volume in the first second (FEV1) and forced vital capacity (FVC) with a normal FEV1/FVC ratio. This relationship has been variously postulated to be due to restrictive lung disease, secondary to fibrosis or neuromuscular weakness, or to decreased chest wall compliance from obesity. However, results are inconsistent across studies, and the principal explanation for this pattern remains unknown. Small airways dysfunction (SAD) is a complex physiologic signature present in all severities of asthma, characterized by non-participation of the small airways secondary to bronchiolar or alveolar narrowing, remodeling, and inflammation. Individuals with asthma characterized predominantly by small airways involvement can present with PRISm rather than obstruction on spirometry. , Insulin resistance and hyperglycemia are two core features of diabetes. In animal models, hyperinsulinemia which arises from insulin resistance increases peri-bronchial and alveolar septal membrane collagen deposition and airway smooth muscle mass. Hyperglycemia induced by streptozotocin also increases bronchiolar and alveolar septal thickness and causes non-allergic airway inflammation. If such effects occur in humans, these changes may manifest as small airways dysfunction. Advancement of high-throughput technologies have led to the discovery of numerous prognostic biomarkers for diabetes complications; interrogated through Mendelian randomization, many of these biomarkers are implicated as having a causal relationship, suggesting that they may represent mechanistic pathways involved in end-organ injury. Should the lung be a target organ for insulin resistance and hyperglycemia, then biomarkers prognostic of diabetes end-organ complications may also associate with SAD. We hypothesized that insulin resistance and dysglycemia would be associated with SAD in asthma. We further hypothesized that biomarkers related to end-organ complications in diabetes may have value in identifying pulmonary dysfunction due to these conditions. To test these hypotheses, we performed a prospective cohort study of adult participants with asthma. METHODS Cohort description We recruited 65 adult patients with physician-diagnosed asthma from Baylor College of Medicine from January 2023 through July 2024. Recruitment sources were patients treated at the pulmonary clinic, study advertisements, and contact of prior research participants. Exclusion criteria were active smoking or former smoking of greater than 10 pack-years, major cardiovascular disease, lung disease other than asthma, and active or recent asthma exacerbation. Patients taking diabetes medications were initially excluded, but a protocol modification allowed enrollment of these patients to permit accrual of individuals with more severe insulin resistance, as long as they were not treated with insulin (n=2, both only treated with metformin). Participants were characterized by an in-person visit at baseline and a 3-month phone call for assessment of asthma outcomes. The study was performed with Institutional Review Board approval, and all participants gave written informed consent. Metabolic characterization At the baseline visit, we collected fasting blood for metabolic characterization. Serum insulin was measured by an electrochemiluminescence immunoassay (Elecsys insulin), serum glucose by a hexokinase assay (GLUC3), and hemoglobin A1c by a turbidimetric inhibition immunoassay (Tina-quant A1c) on Roche cobas analyzers. The homeostatic model assessment of insulin resistance (HOMA-IR) as an epidemiologic surrogate for insulin resistance was calculated from fasting glucose and insulin based on the formula (insulin [in mIU/L]) x glucose [in mg/dL])/405. Elevated fasting glucose was identified if its serum concentration was ≥100 mg/dL, elevated hemoglobin A1c if ≥5.7%, elevated HOMA-IR if >2.5, and elevated fasting insulin if ≥22 mIU/L (based on the local laboratory’s reference range). , We also examined these values as continuous variables, with HOMA-IR and insulin log-transformed, as a sensitivity analysis. Respiratory physiology characterization Participants were instructed to hold all asthma therapies prior to their baseline visit. The hold time was dependent on the half-life of each medication to allow adequate wash-out. Small airways function was characterized by respiratory oscillometry (Thorasys Tremoflo C-100; Montreal, Canada). In oscillometry, participants tidally breathe against a vibrating mesh which transmits pressure waves of varying frequencies into the respiratory system; the resultant pressure-flow relationships are analyzed to determine the resistance (in-phase changes to pressure and flow) and reactance (out-of-phase changes to pressure and flow) of the lungs. High frequency (~30 Hz) waves mainly reflect the function of the large airways, while low frequency (~5 Hz) waves reflect function of the entire respiratory tree; thus, their difference represents the function of the small airways. SAD is identified on the resistance curve by a higher difference in airway resistance between high and low frequencies (also termed frequency dependence of resistance; R5-R20) and on the reactance curve by a more negative reactance at low frequencies (at 5 Hz for this study, labeled as X5), an increased area under the reactance curve (AX), and a higher resonant frequency (Fres). Percentage of predicted values for R5, R5-R20, AX, and Fres were calculated based on the equations of Oostveen and colleagues, which incorporated adjustment for sex, height, age, and weight. Pre-bronchodilator spirometry was performed according to technical standards (ndd EasyOne Air; Andover, MA). The forced exhaled volume in the first second (FEV1), forced vital capacity (FVC), and their ratio (FEV1/FVC) were measured. Percentage of predicted values were calculated based on the race-neutral Global Lung Initiative equations, which incorporated adjustment for sex, height, and age. PRISm was defined by a FEV1/FVC ≥0.7 with a FEV1 precent-predicted <80%. Patient-reported outcomes Participants answered questionnaires regarding their past medical history and active medication use. Asthma control was measured by the Asthma Control Test questionnaire, which ranges from 5–25 with a score of ≤19 indicating uncontrolled asthma, and an asthma exacerbation ascertained if the participant reported going to the emergency department, being hospitalized, or being prescribed a course of oral steroids for asthma. , Plasma proteomics The proteome from EDTA plasma was measured by the SomaScan 11k assay (SomaLogic; Boulder, CO). This assay utilizes modified single-stranded oligonucleotides, called aptamers, to measure relative protein concentrations with high sensitivity and dynamic range. After data quality control and standardization by SomaLogic, the relative fluorescence of proteins were log-transformed for analysis. For proteins measured by more than one aptamer, the mean fluorescence was taken after confirmation that all target measurements were correlated with each other. The panel of proteins causally associated with diabetes end-organ complications was chosen from a recent Mendelian randomization study which identified 15 proteins prognostic of at least one end-organ complication of type 2 diabetes and which had a significant causal effect. Of these, 13 were measurable by the SomaScan assay. The specific UniProt and SomaScan identifiers for these proteins are listed in . Receptor for advanced glycation end-products (RAGE) effector proteins Given initial proteomic results identifying the relevance of the receptor for advanced glycation end-products (RAGE) pathway, we sought to examine this pathway in closer detail. Absolute concentration of the soluble receptor for advanced glycation end-products (sRAGE) was measured in serum by automated ELISA using the Ella platform (Bio-Techne; Minneapolis, MN). We examined the Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes consensus pathway for RAGE activity and extracted SomaScan data for effector proteins related to RAGE activation: systemic non type-2 inflammation (IL-1, IL-6, IL-8, TNF-α, CRP), vascular adhesion and immune cell migration (ICAM-1, VCAM-1, MCP-1), angiogenesis (VEGF-A) and growth factors (TGF-β1). Statistical analysis Descriptive statistics and distributions were reviewed for plausibility and data error. Participant characteristics stratified by use of metabolic medications were generated, and statistical comparisons between the two groups were done using chi-square and t-test as appropriate. Due to known log-normal population distributions, the oscillometry parameters AX, X5, Fres, and R5 were log-transformed for analysis. Because X5 is negative, the absolute value of X5 was log-transformed and then made negative. The relationship between each metabolic parameter with spirometry, oscillometry, and patient-reported asthma outcomes was estimated with linear or logistic regression. We considered age, sex, body mass index, and steroid exposure as critical confounders (e.g. causally related to both insulin resistance and lung physiology); as age and sex were already represented in the spirometry and oscillometry predictive equations, covariate-adjusted models were additionally adjusted for BMI and steroid exposure, defined by inhaled steroid use or oral steroid use within the past 3 months. Further adjustment was limited by the risk of overfitting due to sample size. Differences in protein concentrations by metabolic parameters were compared by t-test after log-transformation. Pairwise correlations between proteins were represented by matrix plots. A two-sided p-value of <0.05 defined statistical significance. For protein analyses, no adjustments were made to multiple comparisons due to the exploratory nature of the analysis. All analyses were performed in Stata 18 (StataCorp; College Station, TX). Mean (SD) age was 42.3 ± 16.8 years, 50 (77%) were female, and 12 (19%) were of Hispanic ethnicity. Mean BMI was 32.7 kg/m 2 , which was within the obese range. Participants had spirometry values lower and oscillometry values higher than predicted from normative equations, both consistent with abnormal lung function from asthma. Using a HOMA-IR threshold of 2.5 to define insulin resistance, 42 (65%) were classified as insulin resistant. Despite a high prevalence of self-reported exacerbations in the year prior, approximately half were currently using inhaled corticosteroids and half had not well-controlled asthma. No participants reported using oral steroids chronically. Of the 65 participants, 22 (34%) reported being previously told that they had diabetes, dyslipidemia (high cholesterol or triglycerides), or hypertension; 12/65 (18%) were actively taking medications for these conditions. Specific to diabetes, 6 (9%) reported being diagnosed with this condition, of which 2 were drug-treated with metformin. reports data stratified by whether participants were using medications for dyslipidemia, hypertension, or diabetes. These individuals were older, more insulin resistant, and had higher fasting glucose and hemoglobin A1c levels. However, their asthma treatment and baseline lung physiology were not statistically different. Association of metabolic indices to baseline outcomes We found statistically significant interactions of the association of metabolic indices to study outcomes by whether the participant was taking medications for hypertension, diabetes, or dyslipidemia. Relationships of glucose, hemoglobin A1c, and HOMA-IR with Fres, of A1c and HOMA-IR with R5-R20, and of A1c with R5 and FEV1 percent predicted values were all weakened by use of these medications (p-interaction <0.05 for all comparisons). Stratified models were performed as a result. Among patients taking medications for these conditions, no association was identified between metabolic indices with study outcomes (not shown). shows relationships with percent-predicted spirometry and oscillometry values for the remaining subgroup of 53 patients who were not taking medications (relationships with raw values are shown in ). Elevated glucose and hemoglobin A1c were associated with higher percent-predicted total airway (R5) and frequency-dependent airway resistance (R5-R20) as well as exaggerated frequency dependence of airway reactance, reflected by a higher area of reactance (AX) and resonant frequency (Fres) ( ). With respect to spirometry, elevated hemoglobin A1c was associated with lower percent-predicted FEV1 and FVC and higher odds of PRISm. Associations with elevated fasting glucose were not statistically significant. With respect to asthma control, only HOMA-IR was associated with a higher odds of uncontrolled asthma, although point estimates for elevated A1c and glucose were in a concordant direction. Modeling of fasting glucose, hemoglobin A1c, log(HOMA-IR) and log(fasting insulin) as continuous variables showed similar relationships ( ). Of note, HOMA-IR was not statistically associated with asthma control in this model. Association of metabolic indices to follow-up outcomes Of the 65 participants enrolled, 36 (55%) responded to the three-month phone call. Of these, three participants (8%) reported an asthma exacerbation, and six (21%) had uncontrolled asthma. There was no association between the metabolic parameters with odds of uncontrolled asthma at baseline. Because of the rarity of exacerbations, no statistical adjustment was possible; however, all three participants who had exacerbations had an elevated A1c at baseline (Fisher’s exact p-value = 0.02). sRAGE as a candidate biomarker of hyperglycemia-associated lung dysfunction Next, we tested whether proteins prognostic of diabetes end-organ complications were associated with spirometry (represented by percent-predicted FEV1), oscillometry (represented by percent-predicted resonant frequency), and uncontrolled asthma (represented by ACT score ≤19) in multivariable linear and logistic regression models, adjusted for BMI and steroid exposure. At a nominal p-value of <0.05, lower AGER/RAGE (receptor for advanced glycation end-products), lower HSPA1B (heat shock protein family A member 1B), and higher PTPN9 (tyrosine-protein phosphatase non-receptor type 9) were associated with lower (worse) percent-predicted FEV1. Higher GCKR (glucokinase regulator) was associated with a higher (worse) percent-predicted resonant frequency ( ). There were no proteins associated with asthma control. RAGE, HSPA1B, and GCKR were directionally consistent with their prognostic associations with diabetes progression and end-organ complications. Of these, only RAGE has prior literature supporting a role in lung disease and asthma. Therefore, we examined RAGE in detail and measured its absolute concentration by ELISA. Mean sRAGE was 961±429 pg/mL. Participants with elevated hemoglobin A1c had lower circulating levels of sRAGE (mean difference −272.9 pg/mL; 95% CI −532.8 to −13.0 pg/mL), consistent with its protective relationship with diabetes and diabetes end-organ complications ( , panel A). Participants with elevated hemoglobin A1c had lower circulating levels of sRAGE (mean difference −272.9 pg/mL; 95% CI −532.8 to −13.0 pg/mL), consistent with its protective relationship with diabetes and diabetes end-organ complications ( , panel A). Lower sRAGE was not associated with differences in oscillometry ( , panel B for resonant frequency, for other measures) but was associated with lower percent-predicted FEV1 and FVC ( , panel C for FEV1, for FVC ). With additional adjustment for BMI and steroid exposure, a one standard-deviation increase in sRAGE was associated with a 7.72% (1.52% to 13.91%) improvement in FEV1 and a 6.78% (0.47% to 13.1%) higher FVC. Next, we examined correlations of sRAGE with effector proteins of RAGE activation. We found that serum sRAGE was inversely correlated with IL-6 (p<0.01) and CRP (p=0.03), markers of metabolic inflammation, but positively correlated with VCAM-1 (p=0.04) and MCP-1 (p<0.01), markers of immune cell adhesion and migration ( and ). DISCUSSION In a prospective study of adults with physician-diagnosed asthma, glycemic control was associated with small airways dysfunction and PRISm, but only among individuals not treated for metabolic disease. Our results, taken together with preclinical data, suggest that the physiologic consequences of metabolic dysregulation may be localized to the small airways. In exploratory analysis, we further nominated sRAGE as a potential biomarker which connects poor glycemic control with abnormal lung function ( for graphical summary of key results). The small airways represent the distal portion of the respiratory tree less than 2 mm in diameter. SAD is common in asthma and is histologically characterized by airway smooth muscle hypertrophy and hyperplasia, basement membrane thickening, changes in composition of the extracellular matrix, and an increase in luminal inflammatory cells. In pre-clinical models, hyperinsulinemia associated with insulin resistance and hyperglycemia can precipitate similar structural alterations in the small airways as described for asthma, but whether such findings are relevant to humans has remained unclear. , , Using oscillometry to directly interrogate the small airways, we found that hyperglycemia was associated with a pattern of changes in lung resistance and reactance consistent with SAD. Importantly, these relationships were independent of elevated body mass index as obesity has also been associated with peripheral airway dysfunction on oscillometry. , Our results raise the possibility that prior findings could be contributed to by differences in metabolic health secondary to obesity. Further work, especially incorporating more nuanced parameters of adiposity beyond BMI, is necessary to confirm this possibility. In exploratory analysis, we identified sRAGE as a candidate biomarker for hyperglycemia-associated lung dysfunction. RAGE is a transmembrane pattern receptor enriched in alveolar epithelial cells and whose activation induces cellular inflammation and oxidative stresss. Elevated glucose promotes the production of advanced glycation end products (AGEs) which directly serve as RAGE ligands. Parallel studies have implicated RAGE activation as important to asthma pathogenesis and both allergic and non-allergic inflammation, raising the hypothesis that the RAGE pathway is mechanistically involved in the pulmonary harms related to hyperglycemia. , sRAGE is produced by alternative splicing and proteolytic cleavage of RAGE and experimentally inhibits its activity by acting as a decoy receptor. , In our study, sRAGE was inversely correlated with IL-6 and CRP, supporting its role as an anti-inflammatory ligand sink, but studies in other chronic diseases have shown opposing directionality. sRAGE may also have a pro-inflammatory role through effects on monocyte function, consistent with its positive correlation with MCP-1 in our study. Whether sRAGE is a valid biomarker in adult asthma will require prospective study, particularly as its relationship with oscillometry endpoints were weaker than spirometry, which may reflect preferential associations with large airway function or limited power due to sample size. Prior epidemiological work by our group and others have shown an elevated hemoglobin A1c as a risk factor for asthma exacerbations; these results were thought to originate from insulin resistance. , However, while glucose and hemoglobin A1c were broadly associated with physiologic measurements, associations with insulin and HOMA-IR were neutral. One explanation is that glucose rather than insulin is principally responsible for prior studies which have implicated IR as a risk factor for worsened asthma outcomes. , Alternatively, because fasting insulin and HOMA-IR mainly identify central insulin resistance, they may not be an adequate representation of the exaggerated excursions in insulin in non-fasting and post-prandial conditions which are characteristic of poor peripheral insulin sensitivity. The magnitude of reduction in FEV1 and FVC associated with an elevated hemoglobin A1c was significantly higher than reported in other studies. , In our study, participants withheld their asthma medications prior to pulmonary function testing, implying that these large differences in spirometry may be reversible. Because bronchodilator responsiveness testing was not performed, a follow-up study is necessary to confirm this speculation. We found significant interactions by whether participants

The magnitude of reduction in FEV1 and FVC associated with an elevated hemoglobin A1c was significantly higher than reported in other studies. , In our study, participants withheld their asthma medications prior to pulmonary function testing, implying that these large differences in spirometry may be reversible. Because bronchodilator responsiveness testing was not performed, a follow-up study is necessary to confirm this speculation. We found significant interactions by whether participants were taking medications for conditions associated with metabolic syndrome. Metformin, statins, angiotensin pathway medications, and calcium channel blockers have been described to have effects on lung function, which may explain why metabolic indices are less predictive of physiological outcomes in these individuals. – Because of the low sample size of the stratum, the implications of this finding are not clear. Several limitations are acknowledged. Participants were metabolically and physiologically characterized in a single visit, and key results should be interpreted as cross-sectional rather than longitudinal. Participants were also enrolled based on a physician diagnosis of asthma, without physiological criteria such as prior evidence of airways hyper-responsiveness, which represents a risk of misclassification. Additionally, results related to the proteomic analyses should be considered exploratory, and many adjusted comparisons were underpowered, both due to the limited sample size. Despite accounting for what we considered the most influential confounders, sample size also prevented adjustment for a more comprehensive suite of covariates, such as air pollution exposure or physical activity. Finally, we did not measure lung volumes which are necessary to confidently exclude the presence of comorbid restrictive lung disease; however, participants in this study were relatively young without a significant smoking background, decreasing this likelihood. In conclusion, among a cohort of adult participants with physician-diagnosed asthma, elevated fasting glucose and hemoglobin A1c were associated with abnormalities in respiratory oscillometry and spirometry consistent with small airways dysfunction, only among participants not treated for dyslipidemia, diabetes, or hypertension. These results suggest that glycemic control is important to small airways physiology in asthma. Further research with more detailed longitudinal follow-up is necessary to define structural and clinical consequences of metabolic dysregulation in asthma. Supplementary Material Supplement

chunks.content: 1 Introduction Severe asthma is a clinically heterogeneous disease that has a major financial impact as well as a major impact on the daily lives of these patients with experience of asthma exacerbations, chronic symptoms of breathlessness and wheeze, and side effects from therapy, especially oral corticosteroid therapy [ ]. Pathologically, asthma involves inflammatory and structural cells that can lead to various pathophysiological expressions of the disease such as acute exacerbations and chronic airflow obstruction and airway wall remodeling. Several clinical phenotypes have been recognized, with the description of the Type‐2 high inflammatory phenotype, clinically recognized by biomarkers, such as blood eosinophil count or levels of nitric oxide in the exhaled breath. Analysis of transcripts and proteins from sputum samples has identified different molecular pathways characterizing distinct clinical phenotypes [ , , ]. Various approaches have been used to determine the differences in underlying molecular mechanisms among individuals with severe asthma. Weighted correlation network analysis (WGCNA) is a methodology that can construct gene coexpression networks or groups of genes that show similar behavior and have a common biological function or association [ ]. Previously, in the severe asthma cohort of the Severe Asthma Research Program, WGCNA was used to identify the expression of 3 coexpressed IL‐13/Type 2 signature genes associated with atopy, eosinophilic airway inflammation, and a response to inhaled corticosteroids [ ]. In this study of Chinese patients with severe asthma of the C‐BIOPRED cohort [ ], we applied WGCNA analysis of sputum protein expression profiled with clinical, physiologic, and inflammatory variables. Our analysis pinpointed a positive association of complement and coagulation cascades with blood and sputum eosinophil counts and fractional levels of nitric oxide in exhaled breath (FeNO), biomarkers of Type 2 inflammation, with upregulation of complement C5 and of C5 downstream proteins in eosinophilic asthma. We further examined the pathogenic role of complement C5 in an asthmatic mouse model to confirm its importance in eosinophilic inflammation in asthma. 2 Results 2.1 Characteristics of Participants The characteristics of the 276 severe asthma and 62 healthy controls that provided sputum samples of good quality are shown in Table . Ninety‐eight of the severe asthma patients returned at 1 year and provided another sputum sample. The severe asthma participants were older, were more overweight, and were more airflow obstructed than the healthy controls, with higher levels of NO in exhaled breath and higher blood and sputum eosinophil counts. Those who returned at 1 year had similar characteristics as the whole severe asthma group. 2.2 Eosinophilic Inflammation Associated Proteins Involved in Complement Activation Using weighted correlation network analysis (WGCNA), proteomic profiles from a total of 436 sputum samples (Table ) were clustered into seven modules (Figure ). As indicated, the blue module (MEblue) is positively correlated with the yellow (MEyellow) module, while it is negatively correlated with the turquoise (MEturquoise) module (Figure ). The brown module was significantly correlated with exacerbations ( ρ = 0.13; p = 0.006), and with eosinophilic inflammatory markers including blood eosinophil count ( ρ = 0.39; p = 8e −17 ) or blood eosinophil % ( ρ = 0.38; p = 3e −16 ), FeNO ( ρ = 0.31; p = 8 e−11 ) and sputum eosinophil % ( ρ = 0.48; p = 7 e−26 ). Blue and yellow modules were correlated with sputum macrophage % of 0.44 and 0.61, respectively. Red, black, and turquoise modules were positively correlated with the sputum neutrophil %, with correlation coefficients of 0.2, 0.25, and 0.34, respectively (Figure ). Further functional analysis of the brown module, which was strongly associated with eosinophilic inflammation, indicated that these proteins are mainly involved in complement activation and the coagulation cascade and in pathways of viral and bacterial infection activation (Figure ). Geneset scoring analysis (using KEGG Complement and Coagulation Cascades gene set and the sc.tl.score_genes function in Scanpy) revealed that the complement and coagulation cascades pathway was highly enriched in macrophages (Figure ). Immunofluorescence staining of bronchial biopsies showed a significantly higher percentage of macrophages expressing complement C5 in asthma patients compared to chronic cough controls (Figure ). The expression of the complement receptor C5aR (C5aR1) in macrophages (Figure ) and eosinophils (Figure ) of the asthma group was significantly higher than that in the control group, while the percentage of neutrophils expressing C5aR was not different (Figure ). 2.6 <styled-content style="fixed-case" toggle="no">C5</styled-content> Promotes Inflammation in Steroid‐Resistant Asthmatic Mouse Model We used a steroid‐resistant asthmatic mouse model of combined HDM and low‐dose LPS ( N = 5 each group) stimulation to mimic severe asthma (Figure ) [ ]. Airway responsiveness to acetylcholine challenge was increased in the mouse model, but the addition of recombinant C5 by intranasal administration caused further increases in airway responsiveness while the effect of the anti‐C5 antibody was to restore responsiveness to acetylcholine to baseline (Figure ). In addition, recombinant C5 administration in the model led to further increases in CD11c − SiglecF + eosinophil and CD4 + ST2 + Th2 cell counts in bronchoalveolar lavage fluid (BALF) while the administration of anti‐C5 antibody reduced both eosinophil and Th2 cells toward baseline values (Figure and Figure ). Additionally, anti‐C5 treatment suppressed the myeloid immune cells, including neutrophils, macrophages, mast cells, and CD4 + and CD8 + T cells, as well as CD19 + B cells (Figure ). Regarding the expression of C5a receptors, we found that recombinant C5 challenge increased C5a receptor expression on eosinophils in lung tissue (Figure ). In parallel, administration of anti‐C5 antibody reduced the levels of type 2 immune cytokines (IL‐4, IL‐5, IL‐13) and the Th17 cytokine IL‐17A in BALF, compared to levels observed after recombinant C5 treatment (Figure ). Additionally, the concentration of C5a in the BALF was significantly reduced following anti‐C5 antibody treatment compared to the model group, while it was notably up‐regulated in the recombinant C5‐treated group (Figure ). This was also accompanied by a reduction in the immune infiltration score and goblet cell metaplasia in the anti‐C5 antibody treated asthma model group (Figure ). These results indicate that endogenous C5 production in this asthma model may be responsible for the eosinophilic inflammation and that the neutralization of C5 can alleviate granulocytic and immune cell infiltration and mucus expression. 2.7 <styled-content style="fixed-case" toggle="no">C5</styled-content> Exacerbates Eosinophilic Inflammation by Activating Eosinophils in <styled-content style="fixed-case" toggle="no">IL</styled-content>‐5 Transgenic Mouse Recombinant complement C5 protein or phosphate‐buffered saline (PBS) was administered by nasal instillation to IL‐5 transgenic mice every 2 days for 2 weeks (Figure and Figure ). C5 administration resulted in an increase in baseline airway resistance caused by acetylcholine challenge compared to the administration of PBS alone (Figure ), elevated eosinophil numbers in BALF (Figure ), and increased levels of eosinophil granule enzymes including eosinophil peroxidase (EPX) and eosinophil cationic protein (ECP) in BALF (Figure ). Histopathological examination of lung tissues confirmed the presence of bronchial inflammation (Figure ) and goblet cell metaplasia (Figure ) in the C5‐administered mice. The effect of C5 was further assessed with a C5aR1 antagonist (PMX‐53), which was coadministered with recombinant C5 (Figure ). C5aR1 antagonism significantly reduced airway resistance to acetylcholine (ACh) challenge (Figure ), eosinophil infiltration in BALF (Figure ), reduced expression of EPX (Figure ) and ECP (Figure ), and mitigated the inflammatory changes in lung histology (Figure ). The use of the C5aR1 antagonist also led to a reduction in PAS‐positive cells, indicating a decrease in goblet cell metaplasia (Figure ). These findings demonstrate that C5 exacerbates eosinophilic inflammation in this model, and C5aR1 antagonism effectively mitigates the C5‐induced inflammatory response. 3 Discussion Using WGCNA analysis, we have shown that there was a strong association of the complement and coagulation cascade with blood and sputum eosinophil counts together with another Type 2 biomarker, FeNO, which was confirmed by the elevated levels of C5 in sputum in those with eosinophilic sputum compared to noneosinophilic sputum. Furthermore, there was also increased expression of other components of the complement cascade that include C1qb, C2, C4A, C4B, C7, C8a, C8B, C8G, C9, CFB, CFH, and CFI in the sputum of eosinophilic asthma compared to noneosinophilic asthma. This was accompanied by greater expression of the eosinophilic proteins RNASE2 (EDN), EPX, and RNASE 3 (ECP) as measured in severe asthma sputum proteome versus those from healthy control subjects, indicative of activation of eosinophils in a severe eosinophilic asthma phenotype. A small study has previously reported increased C5a levels in sputum of 10 asthmatic subjects [ ], whereas levels of C3a and C5a were reported in bronchoalveolar lavage fluid after segmental allergen challenge in allergic asthma subjects [ ]. These data are also in agreement with the data from U‐BIOPRED showing that the plasma levels of C1 and C9 together with CF1 and C8γ were significantly elevated in severe asthma compared to mild–moderate asthma and healthy controls, although this increase was not linked to eosinophilic inflammation [ ]. In further analysis using single‐cell RNA sequencing, we found that complement C5 expression was present in a large variety of cells including macrophages, dendritic cells, granulocytes, lymphocytes, and structural cells in patients with asthma, and whereas receptors C5Ra were also present on these cells, they were particularly increased in expression in macrophages and eosinophils in asthma patients compared to controls. However, single‐cell RNA sequencing analysis in this study was based on a small sample size (four severe eosinophilic asthma patients and four healthy controls), which may limit the generalizability of the findings. Although batch correction and data filtering were applied to minimize technical biases, the sample size may not fully represent the broader asthma population. Future studies with larger single‐cell datasets and more diverse asthma subtypes are needed to validate and extend these findings. As a result of these observations in the sputum samples from patients with severe asthma, we next examined the importance of C5a particularly in an allergen mouse model where the administration of recombinant C5 increased further airway hyperresponsiveness and Siglec F+ eosinophils and ST2+ Th2 cells, while the anti‐C5 antibody suppressed airway hyperresponsiveness and the eosinophilia. C5 also increased type 2 cytokines in bronchoalveolar lavage fluid together with IL‐17A, effects that were suppressed by the anti‐C5 antibody. Administration of C5 in IL5‐overexpressing transgenic mice also increased airway hyperresponsiveness and eosinophil infiltration in bronchoalveolar lavage fluid and in the airway wall, together with goblet cell hyperplasia. We also showed that C5 was cleaved to C5a and that C5a transduced its effects via the C5aR1receptor since a specific antagonist of the C5aR1 receptor inhibited eosinophil inflammation and airway hyperresponsiveness induced by C5. These studies are in accordance with a previous report that C5a enhances airway inflammation and airway hyperresponsiveness in an established inflammatory environment through an increased Th2‐polarized environment [ ]. Together, these murine studies support the direct effect of C5 in the activation of eosinophils in the airways, with an increase in the expression of C5 receptors, C5aR1 and 2, on eosinophils. In addition, C5a can induce chemotaxis and recruitment of eosinophils, particularly of the inflammatory eosinophils, an effect blocked by anti‐C5aR antibody [ , ]. C5a has also been shown to play a critical role in Treg and Th‐17 cell differentiation through regulation of DC function via the C5aR that provides an innate immune signal that regulates the differentiation of naïve T cells into Th1, Th17, and Treg [ ]. A direct role of the C5a/C5aR1 interaction on Th2 and Th17 differentiation in mice has been reported [ , ]. We also detected C5aR2 on eosinophils. C5aR2 (C5L2) has also been implicated as playing an important role in the development of airway hyperresponsiveness, airway inflammation, and Th2 cytokine production [ , ]. Complement is a part of the innate immune system that plays crucial roles in host defense against pathogens, tissue repair, and immune surveillance [ ]. The complement system can be activated by classical, lectin, and alternative pathways [ ], which leads to the formation of C3a and C5a, which are both important proinflammatory mediators and immune regulators [ ]. The C5b fragment initiates the formation of the membrane attack complex, which is responsible for the direct lysis of pathogens and cells [ ]. Complement activation is highly relevant to respiratory infections and related diseases, such as acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS) [ ] and COVID‐19 infection [ , , ] with
