chunks.content: 1. Introduction Tuberculosis (TB) remains one of the most common and lethal infectious diseases worldwide. Although its global incidence has declined in recent decades, more than 10 million new cases and over 1 million deaths still occur annually, particularly among immune suppressed individuals [ , ]. Tuberculosis is caused by a bacteria with unique microbiological characteristics that require multidrug therapy to ensure complete eradication. This becomes particularly challenging in the context of contacts exposed to multidrug-resistant tuberculosis (MDR-TB). According to the World Health Organization, MDR-TB accounts for approximately 3.2% of new cases and 16% of previously treated cases. These epidemiological data underscore the complexity of selecting an appropriate LTBI chemoprophylaxis regimen in contacts of MDR-TB, where treatment choices depend largely on the resistance profile of the index case. Latent tuberculosis infection (LTBI) refers to a state where Mycobacterium tuberculosis persists in an inactive form, with potential for reactivation during immunosuppressed states. In low-endemic countries such as Spain, LTBI remains the primary reservoir for active TB. Patients with immune-mediated inflammatory diseases constitute a highly heterogeneous group, including rheumatoid arthritis, psoriatic arthritis, ankylosing spondylitis, and various connective-tissue disorders. Although each condition has distinct immunopathological mechanisms, many share common clinical features such as arthritis, myalgia, and systemic manifestations that may affect multiple organs and potentially lead to functional impairment. Because of both the underlying immune dysregulation and the immunosuppressive treatments these patients response to infections, particularly Mycobacterium tuberculosis, may vary considerably. It is plausible that these disease specific characteristics influence not only the prevalence of latent infection but also the risk and presentation of active TB. This epidemiological pattern also accounts for the high proportion of women in our study population, consistent with the known female predominance in many rheumatic IMIDs. This is important not only because LTBI has a high prevalence among patients with IMIDs, but also because these individuals are particularly vulnerable to reactivation. Their increased risk is not solely attributable to the initiation of tumor necrosis factor inhibitors (TNFi); but also because the underlying immune dysregulation inherent to the disease itself further predisposes them to TB reactivation [ , ]. Guidelines from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), European League Against Rheumatism (EULAR), and Spanish Society of Pulmonology and Thoracic Surgery (SEPAR) recommend universal LTBI screening prior to immunosuppressive therapy and advise against initiation if LTBI remains untreated. Screening is usually performed via tuberculin skin test (TST) and interferon-gamma release assay (IGRA), with chemoprophylaxis recommended if results are positive [ ]. Most of the time, we assume that patients who initiate biologic therapy have not had recent exposure to active TB. For this reason, the standard LTBI regimen, isoniazid or rifampicin, remains the most widely used option, irrespective of previous exposure status. However, recently updated guidelines suggest that, depending on the type of TB contact and the resistance pattern involved, alternative initial regimens such as rifampicin, or even levofloxacin or moxifloxacin when rifampicin is not available, should be considered. Common LTBI regimens include isoniazid (INH) for 6–9 months, rifampicin (RIF) for 4 months in cases of INH intolerance, or weekly rifapentine plus INH for 12 weeks, though this latter regimen is less frequently used in Europe [ , , ]. It is important to notice that patients with prior TB treatment may experience two potential clinical scenarios: (1) true reactivation of latent infection or (2) reinfection following new exposure. These outcomes depend not only on epidemiological context but also on the patient’s immunological status. This highlights the clinical relevance of evaluating which chemoprophylaxis regimen is most appropriate for an individual patient, beyond the conventional single-drug approach with isoniazid. Although generally well-tolerated, these regimens may cause hepatotoxicity in up to 28% of patients [ ]. INH, the most widely used agent, inhibits mycolic acid synthesis and is effective against intracellular and extracellular bacilli [ ], with neuropathy and drug-induced liver injury (DILI) as the main associated toxicities. INH-induced hepatotoxicity is idiosyncratic, dose-independent, and may lead to acute liver failure or death [ ]. Initially attributed to metabolic idiosyncrasy via acetyl hydrazine [ ], later studies suggest that INH itself may produce reactive metabolites that trigger immune-mediated hepatic injury. In fact, two clinical phenotypes have been described: a self-limited, mild form and a severe variant associated with anti-cytochrome P450 autoantibodies, potentially causing progressive liver damage or death [ ]. Several disease-modifying antirheumatic drugs (DMARDs), including hydroxychloroquine (HCQ), methotrexate (MTX), leflunomide (LEF), and sulfasalazine (SSZ), also may cause hepatotoxicity potential [ , , ]. MTX disrupts folate metabolism, lowers antioxidant enzyme levels (e.g., S-adenosylmethionine [SAM]), induces oxidative stress via reactive oxygen species (ROS), and promotes proinflammatory cytokine activity through methylenetetrahydrofolate reductase (MTHFR) inhibition [ ]. Risk factors for DILI include genetic susceptibility, age > 35 years, female sex, alcohol consumption, previous liver disease, and comorbid conditions such as human immunodeficiency virus

form and a severe variant associated with anti-cytochrome P450 autoantibodies, potentially causing progressive liver damage or death [ ]. Several disease-modifying antirheumatic drugs (DMARDs), including hydroxychloroquine (HCQ), methotrexate (MTX), leflunomide (LEF), and sulfasalazine (SSZ), also may cause hepatotoxicity potential [ , , ]. MTX disrupts folate metabolism, lowers antioxidant enzyme levels (e.g., S-adenosylmethionine [SAM]), induces oxidative stress via reactive oxygen species (ROS), and promotes proinflammatory cytokine activity through methylenetetrahydrofolate reductase (MTHFR) inhibition [ ]. Risk factors for DILI include genetic susceptibility, age > 35 years, female sex, alcohol consumption, previous liver disease, and comorbid conditions such as human immunodeficiency virus (HIV), diabetes, hepatic steatosis, TB, or cancer [ ]. Although not fully understood, the hepatotoxic risk associated with INH following DMARD-related DILI remains unclear and has been rarely reported; however, clinical practice often involves immunosuppression shortly after completing LTBI chemoprophylaxis, raising concerns about cumulative or synergistic liver injury [ , ]. Considering these factors, the objectives of this study were to identify the LTBI chemoprophylaxis regimens used in patients with R-IMIDs, estimate the incidence and risk factors for hepatotoxicity and other adverse events, and evaluate the risk of hepatic toxicity during INH and RIF administration in patients with prior DMARD-induced hepatotoxicity. 2. Materials and Methods 2.1. Patients and Study Design A retrospective observational study was conducted at a tertiary university hospital in northern Spain between January 2016 and December 2020. We included all patients with a diagnosis of R-IMID and a positive LTBI test. This was defined by a positive tuberculin skin test (TST) and/or interferon-gamma release assay (IGRA) (QuantiFERON-TB Gold Plus), marketed by the company QIAGEN, whose headquarters are in Venlo, The Netherlands. For those who received chemoprophylaxis prior to biological therapy (BT). Chemoprophylactic regimens included: (a) INH 5 mg/kg/day (maximum 300 mg) with vitamin B6 for 9 months; (b) RIF 10 mg/kg/day (maximum 600 mg) for 4 months; and (c) Levofloxacin 500 mg/day for 6–9 months. All patients underwent laboratory monitoring, including liver enzyme assessment at the first and third month, and thereafter at individualized intervals based on clinical judgment. We also included consecutive patients diagnosed with R-IMID who developed hepatotoxicity with INH following DMARD treatment between 2016 and 2020. Hepatotoxicity was defined as ALT and/or AST elevation ≥2× the upper limit of normality (ULN) after treatment initiation. Data retrieved from patient records included age, sex, R-IMID diagnosis, liver enzyme elevation over baseline, and treatments received. 2.2. Data Collection Data were extracted from electronic clinical records using a structured protocol specifically developed for this study to ensure uniformity and reproducibility of data collection. All variables of interest, including demographic characteristics, clinical history, immunosuppressive treatments, adverse events, and serial laboratory parameters were systematically recorded in predefined fields to minimize variability in interpretation. Data abstraction was performed independently by two trained reviewers, who were blinded to each other’s evaluations. Any inconsistencies or discrepancies between reviewers were resolved through consensus after re-examining the original clinical documentation, thereby ensuring accuracy and internal validity. The final dataset was stored in a secure, password-protected electronic database with restricted access limited to authorized study personnel. To minimize transcription errors, double data-entry procedures were implemented, and periodic quality-control audits were carried out during the study period to ensure completeness, internal consistency, and adherence to the predefined data-collection protocol. This study was conducted in accordance with the ethical principles of the Declaration of Helsinki and complies with national regulations regarding biomedical research and data protection. Ethical approval was granted by the Clinical Research Ethics Committee of Hospital Universitario Marqués de Valdecilla (Santander, Spain) (Protocol Number 2020.486), approved on 1 January 2016. Informed consent procedures followed institutional guidelines; given the retrospective design and anonymization of all patient data, the requirement of consent was waived by the Ethics Committee. 2.3. Statistical Analysis Descriptive statistics were used to characterize demographic, clinical, and therapeutic variables. Categorical variables were expressed as absolute counts and relative frequencies, whereas continuous variables were summarized using means and standard deviations or medians and interquartile ranges, depending on distribution. Liver enzyme levels (ALT and AST) were examined both as continuous measures and according to clinically relevant categorical thresholds (≥2×, ≥3×, and ≥4× ULN), in line with internationally accepted definitions of hepatotoxicity. Adverse events, including any degree of liver enzyme elevation, were recorded and summarized at predefined time points (month 1, month 3, and beyond month 3), as detailed in . Patterns of hepatotoxicity were further explored across treatment subgroups (MTX, LEF, SSZ, TNFi, tocilizumab, and JAK inhibitors), and their temporal trajectories are presented in and . The normality of quantitative variables was assessed using the Kolmogorov–Smirnov test. In cases where assumptions for parametric testing were not met, results were summarized using non-parametric descriptors. Missing data were addressed using complete-case analysis, given the low proportion of incomplete observations and the retrospective design of the study. All statistical analyses

All statistical analyses were conducted using IBM SPSS Statistics software package, v.25. A two-tailed p -value of <0.05 was considered indicative of statistical significance. 2.4. Literature Review Additionally, a literature review was conducted in July 2024 to identify studies on: (a) hepatotoxicity induced by INH in patients with LTBI and R-IMID; and (b) hepatotoxicity related to DMARDs to explore possible associations. The search aimed to estimate INH-related hepatotoxicity prevalence and its relationship to DMARD-related reactions. We searched PubMed, Embase, the Cochrane Library and others from 1 January 2010, to 31 July 2024, without language restrictions, using the following keywords: (“latent tuberculosis” OR “latent tuberculosis infection” OR “LTBI”) AND (“prophylaxis” OR “isoniazid” OR “chemoprophylaxis” OR “rifampicin” OR “rifampin” OR “levofloxacin”) AND (“adverse reaction” OR “adverse effect” OR “DILI” OR “metabolic idiosyncrasy” OR “hepatotoxicity”) AND (“epidemiology”) AND (“rheumatic-IMID” OR “rheumatic inflammatory disease” OR “rheumatoid arthritis” OR “systemic lupus erythematosus” OR “Behçet’s disease”) AND (“hepatotoxicity related INH and DMARDs” OR “INH and methotrexate”). Meta-analyses, reviews, cost-effectiveness studies, animal studies, and articles involving patients with active or presumed TB were excluded. According to this search strategy, nineteen articles met inclusion criteria, focusing on patients treated for LTBI and related adverse events in high-risk populations. 3. Results 3.1. Baseline Characteristics Of 7218 screened patients with R-IMIDs, 240 received LTBI chemoprophylaxis: 232 with INH and 8 with RIF. Among them, 64 patients (27.6%) developed hepatotoxicity attributed to INH and were included in the analysis. Most were women (70.3%), with a mean age of 53.4 ± 10.5 years. Pre-existing liver disease was documented in 18.8% of cases, and six of these patients showed enzyme elevations during INH therapy. Chronic alcohol consumption, defined as >210 g/week for men and >140 g/week for women. Only 6.7% of patients who developed hepatotoxicity met criteria for chronic alcohol use. Underlying diagnoses included axial spondyloarthritis/psoriatic arthritis (56.3%), rheumatoid arthritis (RA) (32.8%), connective tissue diseases (CTDs) (4.7%), and other inflammatory conditions (3.2%). Most of them (81%) were scheduled to initiate TNFi therapy; others were treated with tocilizumab, abatacept, or alternative DMARDs ( ). 3.2. Anti-Tuberculosis Chemoprophylaxis INH was prescribed in 232 patients (96.7%), while 8 (3.3%) received RIF. A subgroup analysis examined hepatotoxicity risk associated with prior DMARD exposure, with MTX, HCQ, LEF, and SSZ as the most frequently used drugs ( ). 3.3. Adverse Events DMARD-related hepatotoxicity occurred in 35.2% of previously exposed patients. INH was also associated with peripheral neuropathy (1.25%), managed with pyridoxine, and mild gastrointestinal manifestations (3.3%). RIF showed fewer adverse events; only one case involved mild hepatic dysfunction. Although the definition of acute liver failure may vary between the U.S. and Europe, it generally requires coagulopathy (INR > 1.7), bilirubin elevation (>3 mg/dL), prolonged jaundice (>3 days), and progression toward adverse outcomes such as hepatic encephalopathy, death, or need for liver transplantation. None of our patients developed acute liver failure or required hospitalization; all cases were managed on an outpatient basis. Most cases met criteria for mild to moderate hepatotoxicity, defined as ALT/AST elevations as defined as ALT/AST elevations <4× ULN. 3.4. Treatment Discontinuation INH was discontinued in 10.3% of exposed patients: 17 due to hepatotoxicity, five due to gastrointestinal intolerance, and two for nonadherence. RIF was withdrawn in only one patient due to mild transaminase elevation. 3.5. Subgroup Analysis: Hepatotoxicity and DMARDs Among the 64 patients with INH-induced hepatotoxicity, 34 had previously received MTX. Of these, 35.3% experienced MTX-related liver injury: eight required dose reductions and four MTX discontinuation. Peak transaminase elevations appeared approximately in the third month of INH therapy ( and ). 3.6. Literature Review Data The literature review ( ) supported the clinical link between INH-related hepatotoxicity and prior or concurrent DMARD therapy, particularly MTX. Hepatotoxicity ranged from asymptomatic transaminase elevations to significant liver injury requiring therapeutic intervention. From 378 records, 19 studies met inclusion criteria after systematic screening. These included randomized trials, cohort studies, registries, abstracts, and consensus documents. provides a summary of reported hepatotoxicity rates, which ranged from 1% to 41% among the included studies [ , , , , , , , , , , , , , , , , , , ] with higher risk associated with MTX, SSZ, TNFi, and use of polymedication. Examples include the study by Sung et al.,

and prior or concurrent DMARD therapy, particularly MTX. Hepatotoxicity ranged from asymptomatic transaminase elevations to significant liver injury requiring therapeutic intervention. From 378 records, 19 studies met inclusion criteria after systematic screening. These included randomized trials, cohort studies, registries, abstracts, and consensus documents. provides a summary of reported hepatotoxicity rates, which ranged from 1% to 41% among the included studies [ , , , , , , , , , , , , , , , , , , ] with higher risk associated with MTX, SSZ, TNFi, and use of polymedication. Examples include the study by Sung et al., which reported that INH treatment for LTBI in patients with RA initiating TNF-inhibitors was associated with an increased occurrence of liver function tests (LFT) abnormalities [ ]. In contrast, the study by Cansu et al. found that INH chemoprophylaxis was generally well tolerated in rheumatic patients receiving DMARDs, with a comparable rate of hepatotoxicity ( n = 2, 3.3% vs. n = 1, 3.8%; p = 0.85) [ ]. Unfortunately, the literature exploring this specific association is very limited. Few studies have evaluated whether hepatotoxicity induced by conventional DMARDs increases susceptibility to INH induced hepatotoxicity. Although combination therapy with DMARDs and LTBI prophylaxis is generally considered safe, isolated reports describe adverse events [ , , ]. To this date, however, no published evidence demonstrates that patients who develop MTX induced hepatotoxicity are more likely to develop INH induced hepatotoxicity. Only one study did describe an increased risk of hepatotoxicity in patients receiving anti-TNF therapy in conjunction with DMARDs, but this does not specifically address the MTX–INH interaction [ ]. 4. Discussion Our findings underscore the clinical relevance of INH-induced hepatotoxicity in patients with R-IMIDs undergoing LTBI chemoprophylaxis prior to BT. Although INH remains the preferred chemoprophylactic agent, its hepatic safety profile requires closer evaluation, especially in immunosuppressed individuals previously treated with DMARDs. In this cohort, 27.5% of patients receiving INH developed liver enzyme elevations. Most cases were mild and reversible, though five patients required discontinuation. This incidence exceeds prior estimates and reinforces current recommendations for liver function monitoring during the initial three months of treatment. Although prescribed in only 3.3% of cases, RIF showed a more favorable hepatic profile, with only one case of mild transaminase elevation. It is important to emphasize that the number of patients receiving rifampicin was small and therefore this study does not allow reliable comparative interpretation. Nevertheless, the available literature suggests that rifampicin remains a safe alternative in this population. These findings align with previous evidence suggesting a lower risk of hepatotoxicity with RIF compared to INH [ ]. However, clinicians must weigh its enzyme-inducing potential and pharmacologic interactions in patients receiving multiple immunosuppressive therapies. Its hepatic tolerability profile suggests it may represent a safer alternative in patients with prior DMARD-related liver injury. RIF should be considered in patients with prior MTX-related liver toxicity, given the observed recurrence rate of nearly 50%. A key observation was the increased incidence of hepatotoxicity in patients previously exposed to DMARDs, especially MTX. Among those with INH-induced liver injury, 35.3% had a documented history of MTX-related hepatotoxicity. This recurrence rate suggests a clinically relevant overlap in hepatotoxic mechanisms between MTX and INH, including mitochondrial dysfunction, oxidative stress, and impaired hepatic repair [ ]. Additional risk factors, including alcohol consumption, obesity, and ageing, were prevalent and likely contributed to hepatic vulnerability [ , , ]. Although patients with known liver disease were excluded, subclinical hepatic compromise may still predispose individuals to additive injury from immunosuppressant drugs [ ]. Current evidence suggests that lifestyle factors, comorbidities, genetic susceptibility, and prior DMARD-related liver toxicity increase the risk of hepatotoxicity following initiation of INH prophylaxis. Nonetheless, heterogeneity across reviewed studies limits direct comparisons. While some studies suggest that combining these drugs may be safe, others advise against it, particularly in patients with prior DMARD-induced hepatotoxicity. Despite potential confounders, our data suggest that patients with prior MTX-induced DILI are at increased risk of hepatotoxicity with INH. This association, which emerges as a key finding in our analysis, has not been clearly reported elsewhere. Most hepatotoxic events occurred in the third month of INH prophylaxis. This late temporal pattern is consistent with mechanisms such as cumulative metabolic stress, oxidative injury, and synergy with concomitant DMARDs. However early toxicity is related to pre-existing liver abnormalities and risk factors such as alcohol consumption, metabolic syndrome, or idiosyncratic susceptibility. Highly consistent with our findings. These findings carry practical implications: patients with prior MTX-induced liver injury appear at high risk for INH-related hepatotoxicity across varying degrees of severity. In such cases, alternative prophylactic agents like RIF may help avoid treatment interruption, reduce monitoring burden, and prevent delays in disease control. Management may include enhanced monitoring, temporary interruption, or permanent discontinuation of INH. This may open several avenues for future

cumulative metabolic stress, oxidative injury, and synergy with concomitant DMARDs. However early toxicity is related to pre-existing liver abnormalities and risk factors such as alcohol consumption, metabolic syndrome, or idiosyncratic susceptibility. Highly consistent with our findings. These findings carry practical implications: patients with prior MTX-induced liver injury appear at high risk for INH-related hepatotoxicity across varying degrees of severity. In such cases, alternative prophylactic agents like RIF may help avoid treatment interruption, reduce monitoring burden, and prevent delays in disease control. Management may include enhanced monitoring, temporary interruption, or permanent discontinuation of INH. This may open several avenues for future research, including the evaluation of whether a shared pathophysiological mechanism exists between these two drugs and whether this relationship is specific to patients with IMID. It also highlights the need to compare safer therapeutic alternatives tailored to the treatments commonly used in this population, including regimens based on fluoroquinolones. Additionally, the development of clinical risk-score models incorporating relevant variables could help predict which patients are more likely to develop hepatotoxicity. Strengths of this study include a well-defined R-IMID cohort, standardized monitoring protocols, and integration of a targeted literature review to enhance external validity. As shown in several reviewed studies reported elevated hepatotoxicity risk in patients receiving INH and hepatotoxic immunosuppressant agents, including MTX, SSZ, and TNFi [ ]. The limitations of our study include the retrospective, observational design, lack of histologic confirmation of hepatotoxicity in most of the patients, and limited representation of other alternative prophylactic agents such as levofloxacin or extended RIF-based regimens. The absence of pharmacogenetic stratification, such as NAT2 genotyping [ ], also constrains individualized risk assessment. It is important to acknowledge a relevant limitation in the analysis and interpretation of our data. In most instances, patients who developed mild hepatotoxicity did not require discontinuation of therapy; instead, they were managed with closer monitoring of liver function tests. However, for analytical purposes, these episodes were still recorded and classified as mild hepatotoxicity cases. This should be taken into account, as it may influence the interpretation of the severity and the actual clinical impact of the hepatic abnormalities observed. 5. Conclusions In summary, isoniazid remains the first-line agent for LTBI prevention in patients with R-IMIDs; however, hepatotoxicity affects more than one quarter of exposed individuals, particularly those with a history of MTX-induced liver injury, an association that had not been clearly described until now. Given that nearly half of these patients experienced recurrent hepatotoxicity with INH, our findings suggest that rifampicin or other regimens may represent better-tolerated alternatives in this subgroup. Nevertheless, the small number of patients treated with rifampicin in our cohort precludes robust comparative conclusions. Overall, these results support the adoption of individualized prophylactic strategies, highlight the need for close hepatic monitoring to enhance safety and long-term outcomes, and raise the possibility of a shared pathophysiological mechanism underlying hepatotoxicity in MTX and INH in patients with IMID.

documents.title: ATS Clinical Practice Guideline on Polysomnography in Pediatric Sleep

chunks.content: 1 Introduction Obstructive sleep‐disordered breathing (oSDB) encompasses a spectrum of sleep related disorders, ranging from primary snoring to its most severe form, obstructive sleep apnea (OSA), and affects approximately 3%–12% of all children [ , ]. Untreated oSDB can lead to adverse neurological, cardiovascular, and developmental outcomes, highlighting the importance of early identification and management [ , ]. Polysomnography (PSG) is the gold standard for diagnosing oSDB and assessing its severity [ , ]. In children, treatment typically involves adenoidectomy and/or tonsillectomy, as adenotonsillar hypertrophy remains the most common cause of pediatric OSA [ , , ]. However, the reported success rate of tonsillectomy and adenoidectomy varies widely, ranging from 27.2% to 82.9% [ , ]. While factors such as obesity and comorbidities are known to influence oSDB severity and treatment outcomes, the specific PSG characteristics and risk factors across different pediatric age groups remain underexplored [ , , ]. Given that age‐related differences in sleep physiology and comorbidities may influence disease severity and treatment response, a more detailed, age‐based analysis is warranted. Age has been associated with varying tonsillectomy and adenoidectomy outcomes: children under 3 years of age experience higher rates of postoperative respiratory complications, while older, obese children are more likely to experience persistent OSA [ , ]. Although general age‐related trends in PSG parameters–such as declining total sleep time–have been documented, how these patterns present in children with oSDB, and how they change after surgery across different pediatric age groups, remain poorly understood [ , ]. Furthermore, sleep undergoes rapid changes particularly in the first 2 years of life, as children shift from a polyphasic pattern to more consolidated nocturnal sleep [ , ]. The primary aim of this study was to characterize age‐related differences in PSG parameters, with a focus on N3 sleep and AHI as key markers of sleep architecture and OSA severity. By identifying these differences across different pediatric age groups, we hope to inform more precise clinical decision‐making regarding surgical intervention and long‐term management of pediatric OSA. We hypothesize that AHI changes significantly among different age groups even when accounting for other factors. 2 Methods We performed a retrospective cohort study at Children's Medical Center of Dallas of pediatric patients aged 1–18 who had tonsillectomy performed between January 2021 and July 2021. This time period was selected to capture a window following the resumption of elective surgical cases and PSG availability after COVID‐19‐related restrictions at our institution, balancing adequate sample size with a relatively uniform practice environment. At our institution, preoperative PSG is obtained for all patients being considered for tonsillectomy due to oSDB, consistent with AAP guidelines, and is not limited to patients with specific comorbidities. This study was approved by the Institutional Review Board (IRB) at UT Southwestern and was exempt from consent due to its retrospective nature. Patients were excluded if they had a prior tracheostomy, underwent PSG solely with continuous positive airway pressure (CPAP), or if they had no preoperative PSG. A total of 303 patients were included, and 133 patients completed a follow‐up PSG, which was analyzed in a postoperative subgroup. Follow‐up PSG was generally recommended for patients with a preoperative AHI ≥ 5 events/h, those with significant comorbidities (e.g., obesity, Down syndrome, craniofacial anomalies), and patients whose caregivers reported persistent symptoms postoperatively. The median interval from surgery to follow‐up PSG was 104 days (IQR 73–147 days; range 41–820 days). Demographic data collected include age at PSG, age at operation, body mass index (BMI), area deprivation index (ADI), sex, race, ethnicity, and insurance type. Patients were stratified into age groups based on AAP guidelines: 13 months–2 years, 2–5 years, 6–11 years, and 12–18 years [ ]. Weight status was categorized based on BMI percentiles (underweight: < 5th percentile, normal: 5th–85th percentile, overweight: 85th–95th percentile, and obese: > 95th percentile). For patients with a BMI above the 95th percentile, BMI was expressed as a percentage of the 95th percentile value. Comorbidities documented include asthma, gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD), Down syndrome, craniofacial disorders, prematurity, and allergies. Tonsillar hypertrophy, defined as tonsil size of either 3+ or 4+ before removal, was also noted. GERD was identified based on clinical diagnosis documented in the electronic medical record and may include cases diagnosed empirically without confirmatory pH probe or impedance testing. Patients with syndromic conditions (Down syndrome, craniofacial disorders) were included and reported separately; patients with primary neuromuscular disorders were rare in our surgical population and were not specifically excluded. PSG parameters recorded were total sleep time, sleep efficiency, sleep latency, rapid eye movement (REM) latency, REM sleep duration, non‐REM (NREM) sleep duration, Stage 1 NREM sleep (N1) duration, Stage 2 NREM sleep (N2) duration, Stage 3 NREM sleep (N3) duration, arousal events per hour, obstructive apnea (OA) events, obstructive hypopnea (OH) events, AHI (apnea–hypopnea index), obstructive AHI (oAHI), central apnea index (CAI),

empirically without confirmatory pH probe or impedance testing. Patients with syndromic conditions (Down syndrome, craniofacial disorders) were included and reported separately; patients with primary neuromuscular disorders were rare in our surgical population and were not specifically excluded. PSG parameters recorded were total sleep time, sleep efficiency, sleep latency, rapid eye movement (REM) latency, REM sleep duration, non‐REM (NREM) sleep duration, Stage 1 NREM sleep (N1) duration, Stage 2 NREM sleep (N2) duration, Stage 3 NREM sleep (N3) duration, arousal events per hour, obstructive apnea (OA) events, obstructive hypopnea (OH) events, AHI (apnea–hypopnea index), obstructive AHI (oAHI), central apnea index (CAI), time spent with oxygen saturation (SpO 2 ) < 90%, lowest recorded SpO 2 (SpO 2 nadir), mean SpO 2 , peak end tidal carbon dioxide (CO 2 ), average CO 2 levels, percent of total sleep time with end‐tidal CO 2 > 50 mmHg, and periodic limb movements of sleep per hour (PLMS). Sleep efficiency was defined as the percentage of time asleep out of total sleep time, sleep latency was the time to sleep onset, and REM latency was the time to first REM period. AHI, oAHI, and CAI were reported as events per hour of sleep. For patients with OSA, severity was determined by AHI and categorized as severe (AHI > 10/h), very severe (AHI > 24/h), or profound (AHI > 50/h). All PSGs were performed as attended, in‐laboratory overnight studies at the Children's Medical Center of Dallas sleep laboratory, which is accredited by the American Academy of Sleep Medicine (AASM). Sleep stages and respiratory events were scored by registered polysomnographic technologists according to the AASM Manual for the Scoring of Sleep and Associated Events, using pediatric scoring rules for patients under 18 years of age. No home sleep apnea tests were included in this study. Sample‐size calculations were performed assuming six age strata and a medium effect (Cohen f = 0.24, equivalent to an 8–10 events/h difference in mean AHI). A total of 239 participants (39 per group) provide 80% power at α = 0.05. Accounting for the uneven age distribution observed in our population, the required total sample size was estimated to be approximately 300. A multiple regression analysis was performed to assess the effects of various parameters on sleep architecture. A correlation matrix was created to assess the association between sleep parameters, age, and BMI. p values were calculated using chi‐squared for categorical variables and linear regression for continuous variables when compared across age groups. For our primary hypothesis and the relationship between AHI and age groups, we performed a one‐way analysis of variance. If statistical differences were found, we performed multiple comparisons using the Tukey–Kramer method. For secondary analysis of other sleep measures, we applied the Bonferroni correction. For all other comparisons, we considered them exploratory and reported the p values, but the findings should be held in caution and considered for future research hypotheses. All statistical analyses were performed using Stata Statistical Software, Version 18, College Station, Texas. 3 Results Of the 303 pediatric patients who met inclusion criteria for this study, 6.6% were aged 13 months to 2 years, 50.5% were aged 2–5 years, 22.1% were aged 6–11 years, and 20.8% were aged 12–18 years. Demographic data is listed in Table . The average age of the cohort at surgery was 7.2 (4.6) years old, and the average BMI of the population was 22.8 (9.0) kg/m 2 . Given the skewed age distribution, with more than 50% of patients in the 2–5 year group, the median age at PSG was 5.5 years (IQR 3.2–10.3), and median BMI was 20.0 kg/m 2 (IQR 16.3–27.0). There was a significant increase in BMI percentile and z score with increased age ( p < 0.001), with obesity prevalence peaking at 75.8% in the 12–18‐year‐old category ( p < 0.001). Socioeconomic status, as measured by ADI, differed significantly across age groups ( p = 0.044), with the highest ADI in the 6–11‐year group and the lowest in the 12–18‐year group. The cohort was majority male (60.5%) and predominantly white/Caucasian (62.0%) or black/African American (27.7%), with 54.3% of the total cohort identifying as Hispanic. Comorbidity data collected is also summarized in Table . GERD and premature birth were significantly more prevalent in the 13 month to 2‐year group compared to the other age groups (GERD: 35.0%, p = 0.005; premature birth: 30.0%, p = 0.023). Other comorbidities and tonsillar hypertrophy prevalence were not significantly different between the age groups. Preoperative PSG parameters are documented in Table . Total sleep time and NREM followed inverse U‐shaped patterns ( p < 0.001), peaking in the 2–5‐year group, while REM sleep significantly decreased with age ( p < 0.001). REM latency was lowest in the youngest group at 102.0 (82.6) min and highest in the 6–11‐year group at 140.8 (75.4)

were significantly more prevalent in the 13 month to 2‐year group compared to the other age groups (GERD: 35.0%, p = 0.005; premature birth: 30.0%, p = 0.023). Other comorbidities and tonsillar hypertrophy prevalence were not significantly different between the age groups. Preoperative PSG parameters are documented in Table . Total sleep time and NREM followed inverse U‐shaped patterns ( p < 0.001), peaking in the 2–5‐year group, while REM sleep significantly decreased with age ( p < 0.001). REM latency was lowest in the youngest group at 102.0 (82.6) min and highest in the 6–11‐year group at 140.8 (75.4) min ( p = 0.004). Sleep latency and sleep efficiency did not differ significantly between age groups. N1 increased with age ( p < 0.001), from 15.9 (11.0) min in the youngest group to 25.4 (14.8) min in the oldest group. N3 followed an inverse U‐shaped distribution ( p < 0.001), peaking in the 2–5‐year group at 115.2 (30.0) min. Arousal events per hour, OA events, obstructive AHI, AHI, and time spent with SpO 2 < 90% all followed U‐shaped distributions, peaking in the 12–18‐year group ( p < 0.001, p = 0.010, p < 0.001, p < 0.001, and p = 0.018, respectively). The prevalence of severe, very severe, and profound OSA were highest in the oldest group ( p = 0.010, p = 0.017, and p < 0.001, respectively). OHs also followed a U‐shaped pattern, though the difference was not statistically significant ( p = 0.084). Mean SpO 2 and average CO 2 levels also featured inverse U‐shaped patterns ( p = 0.004 and p = 0.013). Correlations among key sleep parameters are presented in Table . Preoperative N3 time was moderately and negatively correlated with age ( r = −0.435), BMI ( r = −0.411), AHI (r = −0.383), and oAHI (r = −0.376). These relationships were confirmed in multiple regression analysis (Table ), with age ( β = −1.90, p < 0.001) and AHI ( β = −0.41, p < 0.001) showing statistically significant effects. BMI showed a nonsignificant trend ( β = −0.54, p = 0.071). These negative correlations strengthened in the postoperative cohort (age: β = −4.24, p < 0.001; BMI: β = −0.81, p = 0.027; AHI: β = −0.87, p = 0.001). Additional correlations revealed significant positive correlation between preoperative N3 time and sleep efficiency ( r = 0.332), total sleep time ( r = 0.477), and REM sleep ( r = 0.309). Age at PSG was positively correlated with both AHI ( r = 0.232) and oAHI ( r = 0.235) and negatively correlated with sleep efficiency ( r = −0.152), total sleep time ( r = −0.276), and REM sleep ( r = −0.334). Of the 303 patients, 133 (43.9%) completed a follow‐up PSG. A comparison of baseline characteristics between patients who completed follow‐up PSG and those who did not was performed to assess for potential selection bias. Patients who completed follow‐up had significantly higher mean preoperative AHI (24.6 vs. 9.3 events/h, p < 0.001) and were more likely to have severe OSA (78.2% vs. 25.3%, p < 0.001). Mean BMI was also higher in the follow‐up group (24.1 vs. 21.8 kg/m 2 , p = 0.028). No significant differences were observed in age at PSG ( p = 0.57), sex ( p = 0.45), race ( p = 0.18), ADI ( p = 0.60), or insurance type ( p = 0.68). These differences indicate that the postoperative subgroup overrepresents patients with more severe preoperative disease, and postoperative findings should be interpreted accordingly. Postoperative PSG results for the subset of 133 patients are presented in Table . Total sleep time and NREM sleep now decreased with age ( p < 0.001). N1 adopted a U‐shaped pattern, while N3 maintained its inverse U‐shaped distribution, peaking again in the 2–5‐year group ( p < 0.001). REM sleep continued to decrease with age ( p < 0.001), and arousals maintained a U‐shaped distribution. OAs were no longer significantly different between age groups, but OH increased with age and became statistically significant ( p = 0.011). AHI also increased with age postoperatively ( p = 0.004). Time spent with SpO 2 < 90%, mean SpO 2 , and average CO 2 were no longer significantly different between age groups. 4 Discussion This study demonstrated significant differences in PSG parameters across age groups in a cohort of 303 children with oSDB. A U‐shaped pattern in AHI and other respiratory variables (including arousals, OA events, oAHI, and time spent with SpO 2 < 90%) suggests differing mechanisms of disease severity across age groups. Increased BMI percentile with age likely contributed to higher AHI values in older children, reflecting the established association between obesity and OSA severity [ , ]. Furthermore, we found an inverse U‐shaped pattern

SpO 2 , and average CO 2 were no longer significantly different between age groups. 4 Discussion This study demonstrated significant differences in PSG parameters across age groups in a cohort of 303 children with oSDB. A U‐shaped pattern in AHI and other respiratory variables (including arousals, OA events, oAHI, and time spent with SpO 2 < 90%) suggests differing mechanisms of disease severity across age groups. Increased BMI percentile with age likely contributed to higher AHI values in older children, reflecting the established association between obesity and OSA severity [ , ]. Furthermore, we found an inverse U‐shaped pattern with N3 duration, highlighting distinct age‐related sleep parameter differences in pediatric patients with oSDB. Normative studies in healthy, nonsurgical pediatric populations have documented age‐related declines in N3/slow‐wave sleep and total sleep time across childhood and adolescence [ , ]. Our observed patterns are broadly consistent with these normative trends but appear more pronounced, suggesting that oSDB may amplify normal developmental changes in sleep architecture. Importantly, the U‐shaped AHI distribution observed in our cohort is not a feature of healthy populations and likely reflects the distinct pathophysiology of oSDB at different ages. Future studies incorporating nonsurgical control groups would help delineate the independent contributions of oSDB versus normal development to the age‐related sleep architecture patterns observed here. Prior studies have demonstrated the link between obesity and OSA severity, as well as the risk of residual OSA post‐tonsillectomy in older, obese patients [ , , ]. The persistence of elevated AHI postoperatively in the oldest age group in our study supports these findings. In contrast, the elevated AHI in the youngest group may be attributed to adenotonsillar hypertrophy and a greater prevalence of comorbidities such as prematurity and GERD, both of which have been previously associated with more severe OSA [ , ]. These results emphasize the importance of considering age‐related factors, including BMI and comorbid conditions, in the evaluation and management of pediatric oSDB, and they suggest that obese pediatric patients may require additional interventions beyond tonsillectomy to achieve optimal resolution of OSA. When comparing sleep architecture, REM sleep decreased with increased age, while NREM followed an inverse U‐shaped pattern, peaking in the 2–5‐year age group. Although N2 did not differ significantly, N1 increased with age, and N3 followed an inverse U‐shaped distribution. N3, or slow wave sleep, is associated with important development processes, including synaptic plasticity, insulin sensitivity, and autonomic regulation [ , , ]. Reduced N3 sleep has been associated with adverse metabolic outcomes, including increased risk for hypertension and type 2 diabetes [ , , , ]. Previous studies have noted general decreases in NREM and N3 duration with age in children, particularly during adolescence [ , ]. Our findings extend these observations across a broader pediatric range and demonstrate a moderate negative correlation between N3 duration and both age and BMI. However, the drop in N3 time in the youngest group compared to the 2–5‐year group could suggest that OSA may be associated with greater changes in N3 sleep time in very young children. These findings imply that both developmental changes and OSA severity may contribute to sleep architecture changes across pediatric age groups and raise questions about the long‐term impact of oSDB on sleep architecture, given the important neurocognitive processes that occur during slow‐wave sleep. Additional observations in the preoperative PSG data in Table revealed statistically significant differences in REM latency, mean SpO 2 , and average CO 2 between age groups. REM latency, defined as the first REM sleep after sleep onset, was longest in the 6–11‐year‐old group and shortest in the youngest group. Though there is limited research on REM latency and pediatric OSA populations, prematurity—most prevalent in the youngest group in our cohort—has been associated with shorter REM latency times [ ]. While both mean SpO 2 and average CO 2 followed similar reverse U‐shaped distributions preoperatively, all group means (SpO 2 : 96.7%–97.7%, CO 2 : 41.6–44.7 mmHg) remained within normal PSG‐documented clinical values [ ]. These observations indicate that while these physiologic differences exist across age groups in our cohort, their clinical relevance should be further explored. Limiting factors for this study include its retrospective design and the lack of a non‐OSA control group, which restricts generalizability. The absence of a control group prevents clear differentiation between OSA‐related PSG changes and normal age‐related sleep development. Additionally, because all patients were referred for surgery, this cohort may overrepresent children with more severe oSDB. Unequal age group distribution, particularly the small number of patients in the youngest group, may have affected statistical analyses. We also observed significant differences in ADI across age groups, with higher values in the 6–11‐year group. This may reflect disparities in timing of referral or access to care, while the lower ADI in the oldest group could reflect a

non‐OSA control group, which restricts generalizability. The absence of a control group prevents clear differentiation between OSA‐related PSG changes and normal age‐related sleep development. Additionally, because all patients were referred for surgery, this cohort may overrepresent children with more severe oSDB. Unequal age group distribution, particularly the small number of patients in the youngest group, may have affected statistical analyses. We also observed significant differences in ADI across age groups, with higher values in the 6–11‐year group. This may reflect disparities in timing of referral or access to care, while the lower ADI in the oldest group could reflect a shift in indication driven by obesity and more severe AHI. However, these findings may not reflect the general pediatric population with OSA. The study period of January–July 2021 coincided with the COVID‐19 era, which may have affected case mix, access to PSG, and surgical indications; delays in referral during the preceding year may have resulted in a shift toward more severe presentations due to deferred care. GERD diagnoses were based on clinical documentation and may not have been confirmed by objective testing such as pH probe or impedance monitoring, which could overestimate GERD prevalence in our cohort. The duration of OSA prior to diagnosis is unknown and may differ across age groups; it is plausible that older patients had a longer duration of untreated disease, which could independently affect sleep architecture and treatment response. The inclusion of patients with syndromic conditions (Down syndrome, craniofacial disorders) may introduce heterogeneity in OSA phenotype, as these patients may have a higher likelihood of mixed or central apnea events. Only 133 of 303 patients (43.9%) completed follow‐up PSG, representing a selected subgroup that overrepresents patients with more severe preoperative disease (mean preoperative AHI 24.6 vs. 9.3 events/h, p < 0.001) and higher BMI; the results of this comparison are detailed in the Results section. Additionally, the median interval from surgery to follow‐up PSG was 104 days (IQR 73–147; range 41–820 days), and this variability in follow‐up timing may influence postoperative sleep parameters, particularly in younger children where sleep architecture changes rapidly with development. While some postoperative findings were significant, only a subset of patients had post‐op PSG data, with only a few in the youngest group, limiting longitudinal conclusions and accurate comparisons with preoperative parameters. Future studies should include patients with both pre operation and multiple post operation PSGs, and ideally a control group, to better characterize persistence and clinical significance of age‐related PSG differences and investigate whether addressing sleep architecture could improve long‐term cognitive and metabolic health in pediatric oSDB patients. 5 Conclusion This study highlights age‐related differences in PSG parameters in children with oSDB. We observed a U‐shaped pattern in AHI and an inverse U‐shaped pattern in N3 sleep. Obesity appears to be associated with increased OSA severity in older children, as well as residual OSA after tonsillectomy. In contrast, OSA may be associated with greater changes in N3 sleep in younger pediatric patients, though this relationship warrants further investigation given the limited postoperative sample size. These findings emphasize the need for age‐specific approaches to the diagnosis and treatment of oSDB and support further research into the long‐term effects of obesity, age, and sleep architecture on pediatric OSA outcomes. documents.title: ATS-ERS official statement key concepts and advances in pulmonary rehabilitation

chunks.content: An official American Thoracic Society/European Respiratory Society statement: key concepts and advances in pulmonary rehabilitation. Pulmonary rehabilitation is recognized as a core component of the management of individuals with chronic respiratory disease. Since the 2006 American Thoracic Society (ATS)/European Respiratory Society (ERS) Statement on Pulmonary Rehabilitation, there has been considerable growth in our knowledge of its efficacy and scope. The purpose of this Statement is to update the 2006 document, including a new definition of pulmonary rehabilitation and highlighting key concepts and major advances in the field. A multidisciplinary committee of experts representing the ATS Pulmonary Rehabilitation Assembly and the ERS Scientific Group 01.02, "Rehabilitation and Chronic Care," determined the overall scope of this update through group consensus. Focused literature reviews in key topic areas were conducted by committee members with relevant clinical and scientific expertise. The final content of this Statement was agreed on by all members. An updated definition of pulmonary rehabilitation is proposed. New data are presented on the science and application of pulmonary rehabilitation, including its effectiveness in acutely ill individuals with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, and in individuals with other chronic respiratory diseases. The important role of pulmonary rehabilitation in chronic disease management is highlighted. In addition, the role of health behavior change in optimizing and maintaining benefits is discussed. The considerable growth in the science and application of pulmonary rehabilitation since 2006 adds further support for its efficacy in a wide range of individuals with chronic respiratory disease.

documents.title: ATS Official Statement Dyspnea Mechanisms Assessment and Management

chunks.content: An official American Thoracic Society statement: update on the mechanisms, assessment, and management of dyspnea. Dyspnea is a common, distressing symptom of cardiopulmonary and neuromuscular diseases. Since the ATS published a consensus statement on dyspnea in 1999, there has been enormous growth in knowledge about the neurophysiology of dyspnea and increasing interest in dyspnea as a patient-reported outcome. The purpose of this document is to update the 1999 ATS Consensus Statement on dyspnea. An interdisciplinary committee of experts representing ATS assemblies on Nursing, Clinical Problems, Sleep and Respiratory Neurobiology, Pulmonary Rehabilitation, and Behavioral Science determined the overall scope of this update through group consensus. Focused literature reviews in key topic areas were conducted by committee members with relevant expertise. The final content of this statement was agreed upon by all members. Progress has been made in clarifying mechanisms underlying several qualitatively and mechanistically distinct breathing sensations. Brain imaging studies have consistently shown dyspnea stimuli to be correlated with activation of cortico-limbic areas involved with interoception and nociception. Endogenous and exogenous opioids may modulate perception of dyspnea. Instruments for measuring dyspnea are often poorly characterized; a framework is proposed for more consistent identification of measurement domains. Progress in treatment of dyspnea has not matched progress in elucidating underlying mechanisms. There is a critical need for interdisciplinary translational research to connect dyspnea mechanisms with clinical treatment and to validate dyspnea measures as patient-reported outcomes for clinical trials.
